articles.title: Scott Bessent's Economic Turnaround
articles.author: Jason Zengerle
articles.description: The defining profile of the Trump administration's most consequential economic official: a Soros-made multimillionaire turned MAGA enforcer who picked fights with Musk, talked Trump down from firing Powell, and is now being whispered about for 2028.
articles.body:
One evening in early October, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sat in an empty meeting room at the Hershey Lodge in Pennsylvania, waiting to address 1,700 people at the state chamber of commerce dinner after warm-up acts Kevin Hart and Poison's Bret Michaels. It was a fitting scene for a man who seems an unlikely resident of Trumpworld: he built an estimated $600 million fortune managing money for George Soros, the liberal billionaire Trump supporters treat as a bogeyman, and likes to say he might otherwise have become a college professor. He and his husband, John Freeman, a former New York City prosecutor, have won preservationists' praise for restoring historic homes, including a pink mansion above Charleston Harbor. Yet in two years Bessent has become one of the administration's most consequential figures. A former White House official called him "the smartest person in the Administration, by far." Jason Miller, a longtime Trump adviser, said no other name comes up more often for vice president in 2028, and Steve Bannon went further, saying Bessent could be the Republican presidential nominee that year.

Bessent campaigned harder than any modern Treasury Secretary. In an unofficial Cabinet competition run by then-chief of staff Susie Wiles, awarding points for visiting swing states and competitive districts, he was a top performer — and the member best equipped to talk about the economy, the issue dogging Republicans. In Harrisburg he promoted Trump Accounts, the tax-free investment plans for children created by the One Big Beautiful Bill, telling a crowd they could compound from a couple of thousand dollars in kindergarten to roughly half a million by retirement. He insisted to the profile's author that the economy was good and the only problem was energy prices, driven by the war in Iran — "Gas could be at at least six or eight dollars if the Iranians had a nuclear weapon," he said — even as polls showed most Americans blaming Trump for high grocery, gas and health-care prices. "What I'm not going to do is say the American people don't know how they feel," he conceded, arguing that credit-card data showed strong spending and no rise in delinquencies: revealed preference versus stated preference, and only time would close the gap.

His portfolio extends far beyond Treasury's usual remit. He largely runs the administration's approach to Iran — in August he announced Operation Economic Outcast, a sanctions campaign that replaced the military one, and sketched a decay curve on a napkin to explain how Tehran would collapse "gradually, then suddenly," losing all leverage after the November 3 midterms. He manages much of the relationship with China, ran the process that made Kevin Warsh Federal Reserve chair, has overseen the I.R.S. since its Senate-confirmed commissioner left for an ambassadorship in August 2025, and turned down the job of White House "Super Intelligence" czar on A.I., taking instead a seat on the new Super Intelligence Force — "the impact without the responsibility," he joked. Unlike Steven Mnuchin, the loyal technocrat of Trump's first term, Bessent is willing to fight in the mud: he confronted Elon Musk in the Oval Office over a DOGE-installed acting I.R.S. commissioner, trading "fuck yous" before Musk shoved a shoulder into him, and at a Georgetown club dinner reportedly threatened housing-finance chief Bill Pulte — "I'm gonna punch you in your fucking face" — for bad-mouthing him to the President, a line he later softened in Senate testimony to "kick his ass."

The profile traces how he got there. Descended from two prominent Lowcountry families — Huguenots who arrived in 1680 and Bessents from Barbados in 1672 — he nonetheless grew up amid collapse: his developer father went bankrupt when Scott was eight, and at nine he was busing tables and putting up beach umbrellas to help. He turned down a Naval Academy appointment because of the ban on gay service members, went to Yale, lost a bruising race for editor of the Yale Daily News, and chose money management because "it's just your scorecard." In 1991 he joined Soros Fund Management, and within months was sent to London, where his insight — that Britain's adjustable-rate mortgages made it politically impossible for the Bank of England to raise rates to punish speculators — gave Stanley Druckenmiller the conviction to short the pound. On Black Wednesday, September 16, 1992, the fund put $10 billion on the trade and made around $1 billion. Soros's motto, "It takes courage to be a pig," became Bessent's too.

His politics drifted over decades: a 2000 fundraiser for Al Gore in East Hampton, then a turn toward establishment Republicans, $200,000 to John Kasich's super PAC in 2016, and a break with Wall Street's free-trade consensus after watching South Carolina textiles wiped out and hearing about Chinese manufacturing hubs nicknamed Sock City and Underwear City. Charles Murray's "Coming Apart" and two Uber drivers in Charleston who couldn't make ends meet pushed him toward Trump, as did Brexit. Bannon introduced him to Trumpworld in 2023, and he became a major fundraiser, calling Trump a "super stock" that "goes up on bad news" and assuring investors in a January 2024 memo that the tariff talk was mostly bluster — "the tariff gun will always be loaded and on the table but rarely discharged." His main rival for Treasury, Howard Lutnick, fought a public knife fight for the job, but Bessent won over Trump with quiet lobbying from J. D. Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Susie Wiles and Laura Ingraham. "The President loves a battle royal," a former ambassador said, "and he was impressed that Scott didn't get rattled."

In office, his first crisis came an hour after he was sworn in, when the top career Treasury official resigned after refusing DOGE access to the payment system, triggering a wave of departures by career and Senate-confirmed officials. One departing official left a copy of Umberto Eco's essay "Ur-Fascism" in her office. Bessent insists he defended the institution and that those who left "didn't want to work." On Wall Street he is regarded warmly — Jamie Dimon calls him "direct, honest, responsive, smart" — and he has played stabilizer, persuading Trump to pause the "Liberation Day" tariffs for ninety days and talking him down from firing Jerome Powell. But he has also stretched Treasury's powers: a $20 billion currency swap to keep Argentina from defaulting ahead of Javier Milei's midterms, $500 million in yen purchases to prop up Japan's currency, and in August and September a tripling of Treasury bond buybacks, from $2 billion to $6 billion, widely read as an attempt to push down long-term yields. It backfired — the ten-year yield hit 5.3 percent in late September, its highest since 2002 — and his old mentor Druckenmiller denounced it in a Wall Street Journal op-ed as "price management," not liquidity management, a "mistake." Bessent maintains it worked, since U.S. bonds did better than German, French or British ones: "If you and I are racing a bear, the important thing is that I beat you."

The piece closes after the midterms, with Democrats having retaken the House and the Senate, Trump having ousted Susie Wiles and installed Stephen Miller as chief of staff, and Bessent acknowledging a "vibe shift." He blames the defeat partly on the Iran war — "I think it was a reason. I don't think it was the reason" — and partly on the administration doing too little on housing costs and student loans. He has also been drawn into the Nvidia scandal: on November 5, in the Situation Room, he confronted Howard Lutnick over why Commerce had not put Megaspeed, the Singapore firm accused of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, on a restricted list, after C.E.O. Jensen Huang resigned over an affair with a Megaspeed executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy. Bessent, who recently moved from his Georgetown mansion onto a military base because of Iranian threats against his life, says he will stay at Treasury for the rest of Trump's term "if the President will have me." He claims no interest in running for office, though Representative Nancy Mace told the author, "He has any political future that he wants." Asked about his confidence after the midterm rebuke, he reached for boxing: he and Trump disagree over the greatest Ali fight — Trump says Ali-Frazier, Bessent says Ali-Foreman — "but we can both agree that Muhammad Ali always won on defense."

articles.title: The Scandinavian Compromise
articles.author: David Brooks
articles.description: David Brooks, a former Wall Street Journal editorial writer, argues the U.S. needs a new economic model that is hard on free markets and hard on economic security at the same time — and that Scandinavia already built it.
articles.body:
America lives in a divided nation and faces at least two more years of divided government, David Brooks writes, but he believes he has found a model that could give both the right and the left what they want — and, unusually for a former Wall Street Journal editorial page writer, he is looking to Scandinavia for inspiration. Drawing on Brink Lindsey's book "The Permanent Problem," he frames the country's crisis as two failures at once: inclusion and dynamism. On inclusion, both kinds of inequality are terrible — the top one percent's share of wealth, and the top twenty percent's caste system that rigs everything for the highly educated while leaving everyone else the scraps. Great nations decline when they become grossly unequal, and America is staring that possibility in the face. On dynamism, America's growth and productivity have been sluggish and disappointing for fifty years, retarding wage growth, feeding fiscal crises and eroding social mobility. The Brookings economist Isabel Sawhill calculates in her forthcoming book "Reviving the American Dream" that if America had sustained its 1948–1973 productivity growth and wages had kept pace, the average worker aged 25 to 54 would earn close to $180,000 a year; instead the average wage is under $70,000. The psychological toll — loss of trust, pessimism, alienation, class resentment, pervasive insecurity — is devastating.

Historically the two problems were divided between the parties: Republicans were the party of dynamism, Democrats the party of inclusion, each warning the other's medicine would poison the patient. Then Donald Trump offered a third framework based on protection — tariffs and immigration barriers would revive manufacturing — and it has manifestly failed: there are scarcely more manufacturing jobs now than when he first rode down the golden escalator. America no longer has a party making a full-throated case for economic growth; Republicans resemble an intellectual black hole approaching the post-Trump era, while Democrats are being pulled left by young socialists championing tried-and-failed policies like rent control, reminding Brooks of Richard Weaver's maxim that the problem with the younger generation is they haven't read the minutes of the last meeting.

The Scandinavians, he argues, simply don't carry America's mental categories. They see no contradiction between generous welfare states and aggressive free-market policies: in the libertarian Cato Institute's Human Freedom Index, which rewards rule of law, low regulation, free trade and property rights, Denmark, Finland and Sweden all rank above the United States. The Swedish economist Andreas Bergh divides his country's history into eras. From 1870 to 1970 Sweden rose from abject poverty to one of Europe's richest nations, helped above all by the nineteenth-century Bildung education policies that gave children complex inner lives suited to an industrial economy — "a human-capital grand slam." From 1970 to 1995 the country veered left, raising taxes and government size and shifting corporate ownership toward labor-connected funds — the version of Sweden the left valorizes, but not the end of the story. In the 1990s, across the political spectrum, Swedes realized their economy was tanking and tax revenues would not fund the welfare state, so they cut marginal and capital taxes and opened telecom, electricity, aviation, postal services and finance to competition — reforms adopted without partisan ruthlessness, Social Democrats accepting the need for dynamic capitalism while conservatives accepted the welfare state.

Today the region is full of arrangements that would horrify American partisans on both sides: countries with no wealth tax and no minimum wage that embrace school vouchers and low corporate taxes. The Fraser Institute ranks the United States as having the most progressive tax system in the developed world, with the Scandinavian nations clustered near the bottom. Denmark makes firing relatively easy, giving labor markets flexibility, but pairs it with substantial income protection plus retraining and job placement. Sweden funds education generously while letting parents choose schools, including for-profit ones, that compete for students, and cut corporate taxes while broadening the burden through consumption taxes. The Nordic nations pursue full employment with ideas that sound lefty in America — universal child care and parental leave — alongside strong unions and flexible labor markets.

Brooks is candid about the limits: copying and pasting Scandinavian arrangements onto America wouldn't work. Those are cohesive, high-trust, communal societies; American state capacity is in sharp decline; their middle classes will pay higher taxes for public support and it's unclear American ones will; Denmark has one of Western Europe's most restrictive immigration policies, inappropriate for a nation of immigrants. And in recent years several Scandinavian nations have tilted too far toward inclusion at dynamism's expense, with growth and productivity falling alarmingly. Still, they teach a general approach worth learning: you can build a productive workforce inside a generous welfare state, give people economic security while nurturing capitalist creative destruction, and protect people from disruption while encouraging modernization. Above all they teach two distinctions Americans blur — protecting people is not the same as protecting jobs, since you can give someone security without locking them to one employer, and who pays for a service is not the same as who performs it, since government can fund services that private firms compete to deliver. They also expose the limits of the American idea of freedom as freedom from the state: how free are you if you're free from Uncle Sam but live under the thumb of a manager you detest at Sam's Club and can't afford to switch jobs?

His proposed trade follows: progressives accept a world friendlier to corporations and billionaires than they'd like, and get the welfare policies they've demanded for decades; conservatives accept a bigger government than they'd like, and get flexible labor markets, free trade, low taxes on investment and productive workers. On the inclusion side he would back child tax credits and wage subsidies like the earned-income tax credit, child-care and family-leave policies, and stronger unions. On the dynamism side he would back every human-capital policy available — school reforms like those behind test-score surges in Republican states, charter schools, lifelong worker training, much larger public support for scientific research — and, having grown less impressed by tax cuts and more by deregulation, the abundance movement's push to deregulate home construction and the attack on regulatory capture documented by Lindsey and Steven Teles in "The Captured Economy": "State action, by suppressing and misdirecting entrepreneurship and competition, has rendered our economy less innovative and dynamic as well as less fair." He would pay for it with a tax on consumption rather than on savings and investment — Democrats will love consumption taxes when they see the revenue, Republicans when they see how regressive they are, though they can be designed not to be. The emphasis, he concludes, should shift from equality and freedom to agency: a society where people have more control over their lives and more opportunity to venture forth and build. Quoting the Nobel laureate Edmund Phelps in "Mass Flourishing" — the good life requires intellectual growth from engaging the world and moral growth from creating amid uncertainty — Brooks says Americans are suffering an uncharacteristic loss of national nerve, with venturesomeness replaced by fear and loss aversion. Getting an economy that encourages people to venture out and lead brave, satisfying lives will require compromises he wouldn't have considered a decade ago, because partisans cling to what he calls the idiot's primary delusion: that someday the other half of the country will be totally defeated and their side will get everything it wants.

articles.title: ‘It’s Not Just a Song on the Radio’: How Music Became a Main Character in ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’
articles.description: Billboard's cover story on the biggest entertainment launch in history: Rockstar spent 24 years chasing one song, built a game with 800+ tracks and a score by Justice, and turned music from background radio into playable story.
articles.body:
For decades, Rockstar Games was chasing one song. In 2002, while developing Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, the studio had secured classics like Michael Jackson's "Billie Jean" and Grandmaster Flash's "The Message" — but not the Cars' 1984 single "Drive," the band's highest-charting hit and a favorite of Rockstar co-founder Sam Houser, whose haunted synth sound captured the neon-soaked eighties world the game was building. Rockstar couldn't clear it then. More than two decades later, the wait is over: when players switch on the in-game radio in Grand Theft Auto VI, "Drive" is the first song they hear. For Rockstar's vice president of music Ivan Pavlovich, clearing it was more than a licensing win; it testified to the relationships and meticulous curation that turned Grand Theft Auto into one of the past twenty years' most culture-saturating and lucrative products. "Music," Pavlovich says, "is the through line through all of that."

That has never been truer than in GTA VI, which Pavlovich calls "the biggest project we've ever done": over 800 songs, 23 radio stations — 21 for music and two for talk — plus in-game podcasts and TV shows to watch in Leonida, the game's Florida stand-in. It launched November 19 after more than a decade without a mainline installment, with market researchers at Newzoo projecting $3.25 to $5.2 billion in first-week sales; first-day sales in fact reached $3.79 billion. The piece traces how music became the franchise's DNA. The original 1997 game, built by David Jones and Mike Dailly at Scotland's DMA Design, had little music to speak of, but Grand Theft Auto III's move to 3D in 2001 changed everything, and Vice City in 2002 made the radio dial a defining feature, from pop-driven Flash FM to hip-hop's Wildstyle Pirate Radio, with Ray Liotta voicing Tommy Vercetti. San Andreas in 2004 leaned into West Coast hip-hop with Interscope and recruited Chuck D, George Clinton and Axl Rose as DJs; Grand Theft Auto IV in 2008 added DJ Premier, Mister Cee and Green Lantern. By then Rockstar wasn't just licensing songs but creating original music: GTA V in 2013 introduced the series' first original score, with the Alchemist, Tangerine Dream, Oh No and Woody Jackson crafting more than 20 hours of music, while producers like Flying Lotus got their own stations.

For GTA VI, Rockstar had two missions: a score capturing the emotional journey of Jason and Lucia, the Bonnie-and-Clyde-like couple at the story's center, and a musical world for a reimagined Vice City. Pavlovich always had a gut feeling about French dance duo Justice — Xavier de Rosnay and Gaspard Augé — to write the score. "We went to them as fans first," he says. "There was nobody else who could do this but Justice." The duo spent four years on it, working in near-total secrecy with Pavlovich, Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson and Houser — de Rosnay jokes that when they started he had one child and when they finished he had three. Scoring a game meant abandoning how a score normally starts: "I would guess that usually when you start a score, you start defining a sound," de Rosnay says, but in a game that open, the score "has to cover as many styles and genres as there are parts of the cities, situations and variety of people." For every scene they had to cover every way a player might experience it — one minute for an expert, five for an average player, fifteen for someone lost — delivering 20 to 25 minutes of music per scene so nothing would ever sound artificial or repeat wrongly. They have no idea how many hours of their music are in the game. Much of it was written on the road during their 2024 Hyperdrama tour, in hotel rooms, airplanes and studios in Paris and New York.

The marching orders were to make music that created a spirit of fun even when the game gets dark, and to ensure it did "not sound like video game music." Rockstar pointed them toward their own catalog, especially the 2011 arena-rock album "Audio, Video, Disco," and their love of classic rock proved crucial — as did their idea of Miami, absorbed growing up in France through "Miami Vice" and "Scarface." "It's Florida and Miami seen through a very specific prism of a rock star," de Rosnay says. The thread runs through "Flower in a Hurricane," the score-and-soundtrack song Justice made supergroup-style with King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard, SZA and Tame Impala, whose opening riff — first seventies-styled, then shifting toward Dire Straits' "Money for Nothing" and classic ZZ Top — debuted at No. 2 on Billboard's Hot Dance/Electronic Songs and No. 62 on the Hot 100; U.S. on-demand streams rose 153.4 percent on launch day and the day after. Other collaborators include Gesaffelstein, drafted for a seven-minute, multimovement anxiety piece called "Pusher," and yacht-rock legend Michael McDonald, who recorded the opening-credits song "Starting From Zero" in a living room in Los Feliz in a single day. "He could have been a d–k and we wouldn't have minded, because he can, but the guy was so nice, so humble," de Rosnay says. The full score, 50 pieces, arrives December 11.

Alongside the score, Rockstar and Atlantic Records built the blockbuster soundtrack. Atlantic president Kevin Weaver, whose label has scaled the charts with soundtracks for "Barbie," "F1" and "Twisters," worked with Pavlovich from 2023 to find the right songs regardless of label affiliation — "They never pushed their own artists," Pavlovich says. The first artist Weaver approached was Travis Scott, flying to Houston for three days in the studio; his "RHYNO" hit the Hot 100 in September. The 34-track album, released November 20, features SZA, Tame Impala, JENNIE, Dua Lipa, Lana Del Rey, Young Thug and Cardi B, with Morgan Wallen's "Last Thing You Need" reaching the Hot 100 top 10 and Fuerza Regida's "Suzuki" hitting No. 5 on Hot Latin Songs; a surprise deluxe edition on November 23 added 23 tracks from Slayyyter, Anitta, The Dare, Offset and 21 Savage. Atlantic says it sold more vinyl and physical product in the first 24 hours than any soundtrack in its history. Licensing was detective work — for Kaleidoscope, a station of international covers of Western songs, Rockstar tracked down rights holders as far away as Thailand and Vietnam, licensing roughly three times as many songs as it used. And in a first for the series, Rockstar built missions around individual songs, weaving separate song stems into gameplay so players perform missions to the music rather than merely hearing it on the radio. "It's not just a song on the radio that's one of 20 or 30 or 40 or 50," Pavlovich says. "You are actually playing this mission to those songs. Those are the standout moments." The piece ends in Miami, where Pavlovich has just landed to streets covered in GTA VI imagery and a launch festival in Wynwood headlined by Travis Scott, Cardi B and Metro Boomin: "The hairs on my arms are standing up. I can't believe I'm actually here after all this time."

articles.title: The Internet Broke Our Taste. Will A.I. Destroy It for Good?
articles.author: Jonah Weiner
articles.description: The sharpest essay of the week on AI and culture: Silicon Valley has made 'taste' its obsession — the last human advantage over the machines, or just the next pattern for a model to learn.
articles.body:
In a world of slop capitalism, vibe-crafted culture and taste paranoia, why we like what we like feels harder than ever to know. That is the starting point of Jonah Weiner's New York Times Magazine feature, published November 20, which asks whether the internet already broke our taste — and whether A.I. will finish the job. "Taste" has become Silicon Valley's buzzword of the year: hailed by some as the last human advantage over the machines, dismissed by others as just another pattern a model will learn. A.I. labs are paying armies of freelancers to grade their output, with one firm reportedly spending millions of dollars a day, while tech's own elites — never known for refinement — try to buy taste through streetwear drops and designer knits.

Weiner spent months interviewing former Apple industrial design directors, ex-OpenAI product designers and cultural experts, and the piece splits the tech world's debate into two camps. One side enshrines taste as the ultimate differentiator in the A.I. era — the "new core skill" and a moat protecting humans from being usurped, on the grounds that computers can assemble materials quickly but their output will never possess a truly original and deeply resonant soul. The other side offers a cold reality check: computers excel at learning rules, and as models scale they will eventually cross the moat and learn what elegance means. One A.I. startup founder put it bluntly to Fast Company: "Those traits we were certain were uniquely human are being proven, one by one, to be nothing more than patterns that models can also learn." The deeper worry, Weiner argues, is ours. Playlists, influencers and feeds already tell us what to like; "starter pack" memes reduce whole sensibilities to checklists; and chatbots threaten to do our thinking for us. Ask several chatbots for the best novels or the best T-shirts and you get the same safe choices — an emerging chatbot-determined canon. Drawing on René Girard's idea that we want what we see others wanting, he asks what we will like, and who we will become, when the machines finish learning.

The piece's most piercing observation is psychological: Silicon Valley has created the first elite class in human history to be publicly equated with a total lack of taste. For centuries, ruling elites — European aristocrats, East Coast old money, Hollywood moguls — were also the arbiters of high art and popular aesthetics. The tech elite is a historical anomaly, and for moguls accustomed to an all-seeing STEM worldview, discovering a persistent "humanities blind spot" is jarring. So they are trying to spend their way out of it. OpenAI's recent limited-edition streetwear drop aped Supreme's scarcity marketing and street credibility, but to the cultural elite it felt stiff and awkward — as if the company believed it could package its taste blind spot by slapping a logo on a hoodie. Mark Zuckerberg has traded his signature gray T-shirts and hoodies for Prada loafers and sweaters from The Row, the pinnacle of "quiet luxury," in a conspicuous attempt to buy his way out of the classic tech-bro aesthetic.

Underneath the status anxiety sits a structural argument about how machines learn. Whether diffusion models or language models fine-tuned with human feedback, their essence is finding the greatest common denominator and historical consensus in training data. A.I. is excellent at mimicking any style with established rules — it can render precise Nordic minimalist interiors, write standard jazz chord progressions or generate outfits that fit current social media aesthetics. But true taste, through human cultural history, is often born from the precise betrayal of existing rules: someone senses a cliché while everyone else feels safe and steps toward the next unnamed frontier. Statistical models smooth out outliers and converge toward the high-scoring average, which is why A.I. images and videos so often have an uncanny, plastic feel. A system that revolves around the center of a probability distribution can only replicate yesterday's style; it cannot define tomorrow's taste. Weiner also draws on the dead-internet idea: A.I. feeds on the entire corpus of human culture and regurgitates it as weird digital corpse-flesh, feeding on itself in an inbred dynamic Microsoft researchers internally called a "doom loop."

The damage, Weiner argues, started before generative A.I. The last decade of short-video feeds, Spotify autoplay and "recommended for you" algorithms already homogenized global taste — walk into a café in Taipei, Tokyo, London or San Francisco and the industrial concrete decor, the lo-fi background music and the viral outfits look almost identical. That has left creative people with "taste paranoia" while most of us can no longer tell whether we truly love a song or have simply been brainwashed by an algorithm. As "vibe coding" and "vibe-crafting" collapse the cost of making things — anyone can type two prompts and get twenty posters, five soundtracks and three web prototypes in ten seconds — picking the one that feels right from a hundred passing A.I. drafts becomes the key skill, and the authority to define taste becomes more expensive. The scariest part, the piece concludes, is not that A.I. will suddenly become more tasteful than humans, but that humans will proactively surrender the courage to explore and fail for themselves, letting agents pick the highest-rated, trendiest option for restaurants, clothes, room decor and even writing perspectives until our aesthetic muscles atrophy. Former Apple design chief Jony Ive, whom Weiner interviewed, insists A.I. is merely a tool for quickly implementing ideas, with the starting point remaining his own pencil and thoughts. Taste, Weiner concludes, enables deep connection with others, whereas A.I. tends toward erasing the human element — and occasionally turning off the recommendation engine to preserve the friction of finding niche gems without an A.I. summary may be the simplest way to keep our taste from being completely formatted.

articles.title: Matt Salinger Doesn’t Know Where the Ducks Go
articles.author: Adam Gopnik
articles.description: The loveliest piece in the new issue: J.D. Salinger's son marks 75 years of 'The Catcher in the Rye' with an hour of duck-watching at the Central Park Pond — and a quietly devastating answer to Holden's famous question.
articles.body:
One recent afternoon in Manhattan, the actor and film producer Matt Salinger sat down for an hour's meditation at the Central Park Pond — the one Holden Caulfield says is "down by Central Park South." Matt is the son of J. D. Salinger, author of "The Catcher in the Rye," the book about a New York adolescent written in the boy's own demotic voice, which has improbably become perhaps the most successful literary novel of the past century. It celebrated its seventy-fifth anniversary this year; Holden first appeared in these pages as the hero of a short story, "Slight Rebellion Off Madison," in 1946. Matt, who has inherited his father's suspicion of the more lurid kinds of publicity, marked the milestone by ruminating on ducks in the park. He had been approached about any number of anniversary events that just felt "wrong. Yucky. Disgusting." What he wanted was "to be with Holden more than to be with my father — but, in a way, to be with both. You can't fully untangle one from the other. Holden is more recessive, but they're intertwined."

At sixty-six, Matt has his father's long gait and equine good looks — J.D. used to get mistaken for the actor Jason Robards — but a soft and achingly precise voice, as though a single slip in meaning could damage his hard-earned understanding of his father's work. "I try never to speak for him," he says. But he is alert to the fact that any number of adolescents — "and not just adolescents but people of all ages who are feeling confused or disappointed or going through some kind of grieving — gravitate to Holden." He remembers his father not as a mystical oracle hiding in New Hampshire but as a sometimes exasperating, deeply lovable man who spoke too loudly in public, had his share of peccadilloes and could be a wildly funny companion. J.D. was famously charming and social in his youth; Matt tells of a young Jerry, as friends called him, doing a handstand while drinking a Martini. "My father was different from Holden," he says. "He did have a great ear for people, and people tended to unload their problems on him fairly regularly. At gas stations, diners, at an ox-pulling contest at the county fair. But, if it was coming from an authentic place, he listened."

The central koan of "Catcher," as every reader remembers, is Holden's repeated question: where do the ducks in the park go when the pond freezes over? Holden gets several answers, including one from a cabbie who informs him that the fish, at least, "live right in the goddam ice. . . . Their bodies take in nutrition and all, right through the goddam seaweed and crap that's in the ice. They got their pores open the whole time." Holden responds, "I'm talking about the ducks." Where the ducks go in winter is a question that contains another question. "The real question Holden is asking," Matt reflects as he watches some ducks, "is, who protects the vulnerable, the lost, the confused? Gnawing at the edges of that is the knowledge that they're often not protected." He laughs. Like many sons of famous fathers, Matt lives in a liminal space where love and limits interact. He is wary of saying too much about his father's surviving manuscripts — except to assure that they are not being neglected — and he resists attempts to psychoanalyze Holden, to label him "neurotic" or to find a simple cause-and-effect reason for his angst, possibly stemming from Salinger's own war experience. "I don't believe that Holden's worrying over where the ducks go is merely, or even primarily, a knock-on effect of some specific wound or loss he's feeling," he says. "But it does evince someone who cares for the weak, the vulnerable, those decidedly non-'alpha' types. He feels things. He's empathetic. I'll take that any day in this time where tech bros are espousing testosterone supplements and how to keep one's body and psyche 'hard.'"

He looks at the ducks: "If these are mallards, then they're not big migrators. They might fly a short distance to find open water." The Central Park Conservancy does have an answer to Holden's question: if the pond freezes, the ducks fly off north about thirty blocks to the Reservoir — too big to ice over — and wait for spring. Then Matt's attention is caught by a flurry of activity near the pond. "Is this a proposal over there?" he asks. A small box is glimpsed, and then a young couple embracing. Suddenly a number of duck-watchers sitting on benches burst into applause, and so does Matt. It seems a Salingeresque benediction. "God damn it, there are nice things in the world," Zooey Glass says in "Franny and Zooey," having seen a little girl and her dog playing hide-and-seek on a Manhattan avenue. "We're all such morons to get so sidetracked." Matt settles back to enjoy this nice thing, knowing that it would probably have delighted Holden, and his father, too.

articles.title: What Happens After We Flush?
articles.author: Rebecca Mead
articles.description: A wonderfully strange book review that starts with a Victorian vicar's earth closet and ends with 'forever chemicals' in your garden compost: what happens to human waste after we flush — and who gets to pretend it just disappears.
articles.body:
When Henry Moule was appointed vicar of Fordington, a village in rural Dorset, in 1829, the locals did not greet the news with enthusiasm. Moule, then twenty-eight, was a vigorous evangelical, while his parishioners, mostly impoverished farmers, had "great contempt of religion." They resented his efforts to ban local horse racing and he even alienated the church choir, who quit en masse. Thomas Hardy, who grew up nearby, drew on the clergyman for the Reverend James Clare, the killjoy father of Angel Clare in "Tess of the d'Urbervilles." But when the village was repeatedly struck by cholera, Moule not only entered blighted homes to tend the sick but set out to remedy what he called "the evils of the water system of sewage": household waste draining directly into the nearby millpond. He filled in the vicarage's cesspool, dug trenches where ordure could be folded into the soil, and devised a wooden commode with a hopper releasing a measured amount of dry earth into a bucket below the seat — a system that eliminated odors and produced a mixture that, dried, served as valuable fertilizer. After it was installed at a local school for some seventy boys, a farmer paid ten shillings a month to cart away the shit-enriched earth. Moule patented his earth closet in the U.K. and the U.S.; the Dorset Museum has an example, a sturdy chairlike structure of polished wood with a galvanized-metal bucket and hopper, resembling the sort of gritty hardware that might decorate an artisanal restaurant today. But his innovation was doomed: toward the end of the nineteenth century the flush toilet arrived, using a burst of water to dispel waste swiftly, plus the eighteenth-century U-bend pipe, and, as one sanitary engineer acknowledged, it had "certain advantages" of comfort, convenience and health.

As earth closets gave way to flush toilets plumbed into large sewer systems, Americans in particular embraced what the anthropologist Nick Kawa calls, in "After the Flush: Rethinking the Future of Human Waste," a "flush and forget" mind-set. Societies set all sorts of norms around answering the call of nature: among the ruins of the ancient Roman port of Ostia is a communal toilet with twenty seats lining three sides of a large room — "everyone shitting together, tunics up, togas up, trousers down, chatting as they went," as the historian Mary Beard puts it. In "The Big Necessity" (2008), the journalist Rose George reports development workers in rural Shaanxi meeting resistance from farmers who think it alien and strange to have a toilet inside the home, and a Norwegian family whose children, raised with a composting toilet, were horrified at kindergarten to see shit floating in water — they were used to a black hole. Even the acceptability of talking about toilets has shifted: in Virginia Woolf's "Mrs. Dalloway," Peter Walsh notes a man writing openly in a respectable weekly about water-closets, something unthinkable ten years earlier. Now the Times runs headlines like "I Never Thought This Would Happen. But I Can't Stop Talking About My Toilet." We discuss the toilet as a consumer product — the Toto "smart toilet" with heated seat and bidet, once known in America only through travelers' lore from Japan, is now the gold standard for a celebrity-bathroom renovation — but, Kawa argues, once the handle is pulled we give no thought at all to the fate of our shit, a failure we can no longer afford.

Kawa, who teaches at Ohio State and has spent a decade studying waste treatment in the American Midwest, opens with the technicians who deal with what the rest of us hide, at the Jackson Pike Wastewater Treatment Plant on the south side of Columbus. Sewage workers think of themselves as farmers of bacteria, rearing "a hidden labor force that did essential work at treatment plants and composting facilities without a need for breaks, benefits, or monetary compensation" — microbes: nature's A.I. Raw sewage is screened for baby wipes and beer cans, settled in a clarifier tank where the heaviest solids sink and fats are skimmed, then piped to aeration tanks where microbes consume the organic material, producing what the industry calls "biosolids." Kawa's guide memorably tells him that "biosolids are not really shit at all but rather the remains of the 'great-great-grandchildren' of microbes that ate our shit." Presented this way, with kimchi and kombucha mainstream and the microbiome now monitored like any other bodily system, biosolids sound less like problematic waste than an untapped resource — the Moule mission, transposed to industrial scale. But much can't be filtered out. Even Class A biosolids, the most scrupulously treated grade, contain some heavy metals and pathogens, albeit at levels federal authorities deem acceptable, and plenty of other substances aren't tested for at all. And no microbe can abate PFAS — forever chemicals from all manner of modern conveniences — that end up in our soil, our blood and our feces. "It's all the shit in the shit that we need to worry about."

Kawa knew biosolids had been spread on fields as fertilizer for decades: Class B biosolids are regularly used to grow industrial crops like corn for ethanol, though farmers may not use them on store-bound crops like lettuce and kale. But he was surprised to find Class A biosolids distributed far more intimately, back to the very households they were flushed from. In Columbus they are mixed with wood chips and yard waste and repackaged as Com-Til, a soil amendment sold wholesale for twelve to sixteen dollars a cubic yard; Texas has Dillo Dirt, "Austin's homegrown compost." During the pandemic Chicago began offering its higher-grade biosolids as free compost to anyone who showed up with a bucket, and its treated waste now nourishes the waterfront Maggie Daley Park and the land-management programs of exclusive golf courses on the North Shore. The process by which matter that triggers disgust becomes material for elite spaces — promoted as sustainable and healthy — is, Kawa argues, an example of the sanitizing power of privilege: the affluent can afford to reencounter their waste without fear of taint, so long as it has been sufficiently transformed. An Oak Park sign asks, "What's that earthy smell?" to explain that an athletic field was treated with biosolids to keep it "robust and healthy." Across the Atlantic, Highgrove House, King Charles's Cotswolds home, channels sewage into bark-filled pits, filters it through a reed bed and discharges it into a pond irrigating the gardens — the monarch's haven nourished by the royal flush.

But not everyone is persuaded by narratives of sustainability. Given that the poor and disenfranchised are disproportionately exposed to pollution, organizations serving them may look skeptically on proposals to shovel shit, even treated remnants, into rather than out of their communities. "This issue has already been pooped on by the city, pardon my pun," a manager with a Chicago food-justice organization tells Kawa. He writes that his willingness even to entertain sewage reclamation as an environmental good reflects his privilege as a college professor from the Chicago suburbs. Catherine Coleman Flowers, founder of the Center for Rural Enterprise and Environmental Justice, argues that being able to "flush and forget" is a right her impoverished Alabama constituency deserves. Treating apprehension about biosolids chiefly as stigma also underplays how contentious it is: an environmental chemist at Chicago's Metropolitan Water Reclamation District, asked whether biosolids are safe given unregulated chemicals, replies that people should equally ask whether their fire-retardant mattress, their toothpaste or "the dioxins in the dust bunnies under the couch" are safe — not exactly reassuring. Nor is a district researcher telling Kawa in 2020 that "there's no way" the E.P.A. will limit agricultural biosolids, "because we've got nowhere to put it except on the land." Last year, in the waning days of the Biden administration, the E.P.A. issued an unprecedented warning about PFAS in what was once called sludge; four months ago it issued draft guidance that, while still insisting agricultural biosolids are safe, recommended landowners refrain from applying them near fishable waters, drinking-water reservoirs, playgrounds, schools, parks or homes — a recommendation running counter to some of the upscale Chicago uses Kawa observed. Perhaps effluence cannot be so readily absorbed and transmuted by affluence after all.

The review closes with Kawa's own attempt to heal what Marxian scholars called the "metabolic rift" between man and nature: for sixteen months he skipped the family bathroom for a toilet-seat-over-a-bucket setup in his basement, keeping a diary — "Wow, I guess I'm just going for it. . . . You don't realize how much water helps to minimize smell by enveloping it in a liquid medium" — adding peat moss for odor and composting, producing two full buckets a month, "the same rate as books I read in my free time," which fertilized zinnias and sunflowers in his back yard. He also meets the Reverend Moule's spiritual descendants, like Joe Jenkins, a Pennsylvania roofer who has composted his family's excretions for decades and wrote "The Humanure Handbook"; his compost pile contains raccoons and possums he shot from his bedroom window after they raided his chicken coop — "The best way to cover up that smell? Humanure." And Sarah Nahar, an eco-theologian who coined "defecatory justice" to discuss unequal access to safe toilets, reminds him that around two in five people globally have "no place to take a dignified poop in peace," and describes bucket-composting programs in Kenya and Haiti that provide toilet security and end up as fertilizer or heating briquettes. Kawa calls for more mindfulness about defecation and its afterlife — even if he, like so many, cannot resist the distraction of Wordle while on the can. Mead concludes he might be onto something: there is more shit consciousness today than ever, from fecal-transplant treatments to "Everyone Poops" selling over a million and a half copies to gut-health influencers guiding viewers through the Bristol Stool Chart with candy bars as fecal stand-ins. We have learned to eat mindfully, even — like the reformed gourmand Pete Wells, once a Times restaurant critic — to spend twenty-five minutes savoring a single raisin. "We are surely due for a movement that brings a comparable measure of self-awareness to the other end of the operation."

articles.title: North Korea has stopped sending troops and missiles to Russia, Ukrainian intelligence says
articles.description: Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) said on November 27 that North Korea has suspended military cooperation with Russia, halting troop deployments and shipments of ballistic missiles and artillery ammunition. The rupture reportedly followed Russian remarks about easing tensions with South Korea, which Pyongyang saw as a betrayal of the alliance. North Korea has also barred Russian military transport planes from its airspace. If it holds, the break would cut off a major source of manpower and munitions for Moscow.
articles.body: Ukraine's military intelligence directorate (HUR) said on November 27 that military cooperation between Russia and North Korea has been suspended. The rupture followed a statement by Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Rudenko, who said Moscow would work to ease tensions between South Korea and North Korea, according to the HUR. North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui reportedly said the remarks were inconsistent with the two countries' alliance commitments and demanded that Russia clarify its policy toward Seoul, adding that military cooperation had been temporarily suspended. Pyongyang has barred Russian military transport planes from using its airspace and suspended shipments of ballistic missiles and artillery ammunition to Russia, the HUR said. North Korean authorities have also delayed sending Russia the additional troop contingent Moscow had requested. Official sources make no mention of any disagreement: North Korea's KCNA has reported on delegation visits in both directions, and Russia's TASS news agency quoted Rudenko as saying a visit by Kim Jong Un to Russia 'is constantly on the agenda.' Russia and North Korea signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty in September 2024, which became the basis for sending North Korean troops to fight in the war against Ukraine. If the suspension holds, it would cut off a significant source of manpower and munitions for Moscow at a moment when Russia is preparing new large-scale strikes.

articles.title: Overnight Russian attack kills six and leaves six regions without power — an update to the morning's toll
articles.description: Russian attacks over the past day killed six people and injured 25 across Ukraine, officials said on November 27 — an update to the morning's toll of two killed and 23 injured. The Air Force said Russia launched 155 drones overnight, including 83 jet-powered ones, with 110 downed. Strikes hit railway stations, two coal mines and substations across nine regions, leaving consumers in six regions without power, worst in Dnipropetrovsk and Kherson, where emergency blackouts were imposed.
articles.body: Russian attacks killed six people across Ukraine over the past day and cut electricity to consumers in six regions, Ukrainian officials said on November 27, updating the morning's figures of two killed and 23 injured. The Air Force said Russia launched 155 drones overnight, including 83 jet-powered aircraft, plus Gerbera drones and Parodiya decoys, with air defences downing or suppressing 110 by 8 a.m. local time. Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi said strikes hit nine regions in total, targeting railway stations in Kryvyi Rih and Kamianske, two coal mines in Dnipropetrovsk region, electrical substations in Vinnytsia and Kirovohrad regions — including ones that power the railways — and civilian businesses in Zaporizhzhia, Kyiv and Mykolaiv regions. In Izyum, Kharkiv region, a drone attack set fire to an apartment building and injured five people, while a private house was damaged in Odesa region and a dormitory and residential building in Sumy region. Deaths were reported in Kharkiv, Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Odesa regions, with 25 people injured. First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said the power situation was hardest in Dnipropetrovsk and Kherson regions, where emergency blackouts were imposed after equipment damage and a voltage drop in the high-voltage grid. Hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 queues are in effect in most regions throughout November 27, while repair crews work where it is safe to do so.

articles.title: Nine Ukrainian children and one adult returned from Russia and occupied territory
articles.description: Nine Ukrainian children and one adult resident of a care home were returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory from Russia and occupied areas on November 27. Among them was an eight-year-old boy who had not seen his mother since 2022. The return came through a humanitarian initiative linked to Melania Trump, bringing the total number of children brought home via her mission to 43.
articles.body: Nine children and one adult resident of a care home were returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory from Russia and occupied areas on November 27, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Among those brought home was an eight-year-old boy who had not seen his mother since 2022, when the full-scale invasion separated them. The tenth returnee is an adult resident of the Oleshky boarding school in occupied Kherson region. The return took place through a humanitarian initiative linked to Melania Trump, and brings the total number of children returned via her mission to 43. Ukraine says Russia has deported or forcibly transferred tens of thousands of Ukrainian children since 2022, and their return remains one of Kyiv's most sensitive demands in any peace talks. Each return involves months of negotiation, verification and logistics, often through third countries and intermediaries, because there is no direct channel between Kyiv and Moscow on the issue. The children are now undergoing medical checks and reunification with their families, with psychological support arranged by the state. While the numbers are small next to the scale of deportations, each return is treated in Kyiv as a significant humanitarian success.

articles.title: Silksong's Sea of Sorrow expansion is free and out December 11 — plus Team Cherry will now publish other indies
articles.description: Team Cherry's first 'Cherry Time!' showcase on Friday finally dated Hollow Knight: Silksong's Sea of Sorrow expansion: it launches free for all players on December 11, just two weeks away. The nautical expansion adds new ocean areas, bosses, a new crest and even fishing. Team Cherry also unveiled a new publishing label, Team Cherry Presents, with three indie games.
articles.body: Team Cherry ended nearly a year of silence in its first-ever 'Cherry Time!' presentation on Friday, announcing that Hollow Knight: Silksong's first expansion, Sea of Sorrow, will launch free for all players on December 11, 2026 — just two weeks after the reveal. The nautical-themed expansion sends Hornet voyaging above and beneath Pharloom's forgotten ocean, across islands, through forts and into deep caverns beneath the waves, with new areas, characters, tools, bosses and a new crest, plus a fishing minigame spotted at the end of the launch trailer. Christopher Larkin returns to score the expansion, and Team Cherry calls it an adventure 'unlike anything we've done before', describing it as Silksong's 'first major content update' — a wording that hints more could follow. The DLC was first teased in December 2025 with only a vague 2026 window, and fans had begun to doubt it would make the year after months without news. The presentation also unveiled a surprise new venture: a Team Cherry Presents publishing label, with three indie games from close friends of the studio, including Blokkan: Secret of the Walking City, a robot-detective game based on a comic book, and Radio Rain, a 2D pixel-art side-scroller. Silksong itself launched in September 2025 after more than six years of waiting, and the expansion will be free on every platform, including for Game Pass subscribers.

articles.title: Middle East attacks send oil prices rising again
articles.description: A fresh wave of Middle East attacks has pushed Brent crude to around $96 a barrel, its highest since the midterm-election week and on track for its first weekly gain this month. The flare-up follows a suspected Iranian drone strike in Kuwait that killed two Italians and Houthi strikes on two Saudi refineries. Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz are running at just 55% of pre-war levels.
articles.body: Brent crude, the global benchmark, climbed to around $96 a barrel on Friday after settling Thursday at its highest since the week of the midterm elections, putting it on track for a roughly 3.5% weekly gain — its first weekly rise this month after a slide driven by oversupply fears. US-traded West Texas Intermediate also rose about 1% to around $84.50. The trigger is a fresh wave of attacks: on Thursday a suspected Iranian drone strike on a Kuwaiti military site killed two Italian nationals, according to Italy's foreign minister Antonio Tajani, while Yemen's Houthis struck two Saudi oil refineries back-to-back this week, including the kingdom's biggest refinery at Ras Tanura on Wednesday. A Riyadh skyscraper housing Saudi Arabia's trillion-dollar sovereign wealth fund was also hit for a second time in days, wounding 11 people, and Iran has kept striking tankers in the Strait of Hormuz — around two dozen attacks reported in November, nearing October's record of 30, according to a CNN analysis of UK Maritime Trade Operations data. Oil flows through the strait ran at just 55% of their pre-war level in the week to November 25, preliminary Kpler data showed. The OPEC+ group meets on Sunday, and analysts warn a sustained price rise could take the shine off the AI-led stock rally, even as US stock futures rose Friday morning with Nasdaq-100 contracts up more than 2%.

articles.title: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani heads for the operating room after a soccer injury
articles.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani was expected to have surgery on Friday to repair the Achilles tendon he tore earlier this month playing soccer against the City Hall press corps. He scored a goal, then tore the tendon — 'I forgot that I was 35,' he said. He will miss the postponed Macy's parade on Saturday and is due back at work on Monday.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani was expected to undergo surgery on Friday to repair the Achilles tendon he tore earlier this month while playing soccer with a group of reporters. The friendly match between Mamdani — a self-described rabid soccer fan — and the City Hall press corps was originally meant to be off the record, but the mayor had to disclose the injury last week when he hobbled into a news conference on crutches and wearing an orthopedic walking boot. 'I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch, and I forgot that I was 35,' Mamdani said at the November 20 news conference in City Hall's rotunda, adding that he tore his Achilles soon after — though not before his team beat the press corps 10-5. A City Hall spokesperson said Mamdani was expected to be in the hospital until at least 2 p.m. on Friday and to spend the rest of the day recovering. While he recovers, First Deputy Mayor Dean Fuleihan will fill in, followed by Julia Kerson, the deputy mayor for operations. The timing means Mamdani will miss the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, which was postponed to Saturday because of the weather, and he is not expected to attend any events over the weekend, with a return to work planned for Monday.

articles.title: UPDATE: New storms threaten post-Thanksgiving travel as 500,000 still lack power
articles.description: Fresh storms are set to slow post-Thanksgiving travel this weekend, with rain and snow building Saturday and a stronger system hitting Sunday — the year's busiest travel day. It follows the Thanksgiving nor'easter that knocked out power to 900,000 customers at its peak; more than 500,000 are still without power. At least 30 spots in the Mid-Atlantic saw major flooding, some beating Superstorm Sandy records.
articles.body: Another round of storms could slow the trip home from Thanksgiving for millions of Americans this weekend and into early next week, just as the region is still recovering from the nor'easter that battered the East Coast on the holiday itself. The messy weather ramps up on Saturday and carries into Sunday, typically the busiest travel day of the year. The first storm will bring snow and strong winds to the Rockies on Friday night before spreading soaking rain across the Plains on Saturday, then intensifying on Sunday morning with potentially heavy rain and gusty winds from the Louisiana Gulf Coast to southern Michigan before reaching the Northeast by Sunday evening. A second storm moves into the Pacific Northwest on Sunday and could affect West Coast travel as the work week starts. Forecasters do not expect the weekend storms to match the Thanksgiving system, which stretched from Missouri to Massachusetts, knocked out power to 900,000 customers at its peak, and set off major coastal flooding along the Mid-Atlantic. More than 500,000 homes and businesses were still without power on Friday afternoon, with Pennsylvania and New Jersey accounting for about 245,000 combined outages. Thursday saw 462 flight cancellations and more than 2,500 delays, wind gusts topped 70 mph in the Northeast, and at least 30 locations across Virginia, Maryland, Delaware and New Jersey saw major flooding, some topping Superstorm Sandy levels by 1.5 feet or more. The Commodore Barry Bridge between Pennsylvania and New Jersey is expected to stay shut until at least Saturday.

articles.title: The Chicks join Jason Isbell's class action against Suno as amended complaint adds 16 plaintiffs and targets v6
articles.description: The Chicks have joined Jason Isbell's proposed class action against AI music generator Suno, in an amended complaint filed in Boston federal court on November 24. The filing adds 16 new plaintiffs — including Dirty Projectors' David Longstreth, Carl Craig and the estates of Willie Colón and Sam Moore — and takes aim at Suno's newer v6 models. It matters because the case, which accuses Suno of encoding artists' identities into its models without consent, is now far broader and directly challenges Suno's claim that v6 was trained only on licensed music.
articles.body: An amended complaint filed in Boston federal court on Tuesday, November 24, has widened Jason Isbell's proposed class action against Suno, adding 16 new plaintiffs led by The Chicks (Martie Maguire, Natalie Maines and Emily Strayer). The new names also include Dirty Projectors founder David Longstreth, Detroit techno producer Carl Craig, Mount Eerie's Phil Elverum, Ezra Furman and the surviving spouses of salsa bandleader Willie Colón and Sam & Dave singer Sam Moore. Isbell filed the original suit on August 31 alongside David Lowery, Guy Forsyth and Eduardo Calle, and the amendment arrived 21 days after Suno asked the court to dismiss the case — the last day the plaintiffs could amend without permission. The case contains no copyright claims: instead it accuses Suno of encoding musicians' identities into its AI models and answering their names with songs, text and cover images that evoke them, without consent, under right-of-publicity laws in 14 US states and Puerto Rico plus Illinois' biometric privacy law. Crucially, the filing adds demonstrations using Suno's v6 models, launched in September, which Suno says were trained from scratch on licensed music from Warner, BMG and Believe — a claim the plaintiffs dispute, citing a prompt for Franz Nicolay that produced theatrical folk-punk songs despite him giving no consent. The amended complaint keeps the original 17 counts and seeks an injunction, statutory and liquidated damages, restitution, disgorgement of profits and punitive damages. Suno continues to face litigation on several fronts, including a second UMG/Sony suit filed in September covering 60,202 further recordings.

articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dead at 65
articles.description: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of Duran Duran, has died at 65 after a years-long battle with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer. His death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement on social media and the band's website. Taylor, who died peacefully at home on Monday, November 23, surrounded by his family, was behind the riffs on hits like 'Rio' and 'Hungry Like the Wolf'.
articles.body: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of Duran Duran, has died at 65. His death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and the band's website. Taylor died peacefully at home on Monday, November 23, surrounded by his family, after a long battle with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer, which he first revealed publicly in 2022 when he bowed out of the band's Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction. He had been diagnosed in 2018. Taylor was the guitarist behind the riffs on Duran Duran's biggest hits, including 'Rio', 'Hungry Like the Wolf' and 'The Reflex', and the band's rise was inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, making them icons of the 1980s. His bandmates said his no-nonsense, unsentimental outlook kept them grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed. Simon Le Bon spoke of a massive Andy Taylor-shaped hole in his heart. Beyond Duran Duran, Taylor was also known for his work with the supergroup Power Station. Billboard marked his passing with a rundown of Duran Duran's biggest chart hits — the band scored 15 top-40 Hot 100 hits between 1983 and 1993 — while Nile Rodgers paid tribute, calling the band true family. Taylor's death is one of three major losses in British music this week, alongside Buzzcocks drummer Phil Barker, also 65, and King Crimson co-founder Michael Giles, 84.

articles.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' soundtrack drives to No. 1 on ARIA chart
articles.description: The 'Grand Theft Auto VI' soundtrack has driven to No. 1 on Australia's ARIA chart. The achievement is a fresh chart milestone for the game, whose deluxe album edition added 23 new songs this week. It underlines how the GTA VI rollout has become one of the biggest music events of the year, with the soundtrack — and Carly Rae Jepsen's 'Run Away With Me', up 288% in streams — dominating the conversation.
articles.body: The 'Grand Theft Auto VI' soundtrack has driven to No. 1 on Australia's ARIA chart, Billboard reports. The chart-topping debut is a fresh milestone for the game, whose deluxe album edition added 23 new songs this week and has dominated music coverage since its release. The soundtrack's success underlines how the GTA VI rollout has become one of the biggest music events of the year, blurring the line between gaming and the charts in a way few releases ever have. The album's momentum is already visible across the streaming landscape: Carly Rae Jepsen's 'Run Away With Me' saw a 288% streaming bump thanks to its inclusion in GTA VI, and the deluxe edition's 23 new songs have kept the conversation going all week. Australia's ARIA chart No. 1 is the latest in a string of chart achievements for the soundtrack, which is performing like a major album release rather than a game tie-in. For the Australian market, the No. 1 caps a week in which the game has been everywhere — in playlists, on social media and in the charts. The GTA VI phenomenon shows how a game's soundtrack can now compete with, and beat, traditional album releases, and it raises the stakes for every future blockbuster game launch. Rockstar's rollout has turned the soundtrack into a cultural event in its own right, with artists across genres benefiting from the exposure.

articles.title: At least 87 members of Russia's most secretive special forces unit have died in Ukraine, investigation finds
articles.description: At least 87 members of Russia's Special Operations Forces, its most secretive special forces unit, have died since the full-scale invasion began, an iStories investigation of leaked Rosstat death records found. At least 54 died in Ukraine and three more of wounds in Russian hospitals. The finding comes from the same leaked database behind Meduza and Mediazona's estimate of at least 490,000 Russian war dead by late September 2026 — 700,000 including the missing.
articles.body: At least 87 members of Russia's Special Operations Forces (SSO) have died since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, the independent Russian investigative outlet iStories found after examining a leaked Rosstat database of death records. The data show that at least 54 SSO operatives died in Ukraine and three more died of wounds in Russian hospitals, with the rest dying in other circumstances linked to the war. The SSO is Russia's most secretive special forces unit, and its losses are rarely disclosed, making the figure a rare window into the cost of the war for elite units. Journalists gained access to the Russian death data after a hack of the state statistics agency Rosstat that the hacker groups Cyber Partisans of Belarus and Silent Crow reported on November 1. Based on that leak, Meduza and the independent outlet Mediazona updated their estimate of Russian military losses: at least 490,000 Russians had died in the war by the end of September 2026, and the toll reaches 700,000 when including those listed as missing. The Kremlin has dismissed that estimate, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov telling the public to trust Defence Ministry numbers instead. The SSO figure underscores that even Russia's best-trained units have suffered heavy, sustained losses nearly five years into the war.

articles.title: Russia's pro-war bloggers slam proposed prison sentences for sharing photos of Ukrainian strikes
articles.description: Prominent pro-war Russian military bloggers have turned on a bill introduced in the State Duma on November 26 that would jail people for up to five years for sharing photos or videos of the aftermath of Ukrainian strikes on Russia. The bloggers argue the ban would hide attacks from the public and damage volunteer fundraising and air-raid warning networks. The backlash is notable because it comes from the Kremlin's own supporters, and it follows a separate FSB order expanding the list of information deemed a security risk.
articles.body: Russia's pro-war military bloggers have sharply criticised a bill introduced in the State Duma on November 26 that would impose prison sentences of up to five years for sharing photos or videos of the aftermath of Ukrainian drone and missile strikes, acts of sabotage and other attacks on Russian territory. The bloggers, who are normally among the Kremlin's most loyal cheerleaders, argue the ban would leave Russians in the dark about attacks on their own cities and undermine the volunteer networks that raise funds for the front and warn civilians about incoming drones. Their backlash is striking because it pits the pro-war community against a measure its own senators proposed, with one widely shared refrain amounting to 'no reports, no strikes' — the idea that hiding the consequences of attacks does nothing to stop them. The bill was submitted by a group of Russian senators and would criminalise the unlawful dissemination of information about the aftermath of attacks on sites in Russia. The backlash follows a separate FSB order expanding the list of non-classified information deemed a security risk, including military and defence industry salaries and data on prisoners recruited for the war. Together, the moves point to a widening crackdown on open discussion of the war inside Russia, even among its supporters. Whether the Duma presses ahead with the bill despite the outcry from its own base will be a test of how far the authorities are willing to go to control the narrative.

articles.title: Russia to impose 35% duties on seafood from 'unfriendly' countries
articles.description: Russia plans to raise import duties on seafood from countries it calls 'unfriendly' to 35%, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov told the Federation Council on November 27. The ministry has drafted the decree and it is now being coordinated with other agencies; currently there is no duty at all on these products. The figure is well above the 15% rate the ministry had floated earlier, and follows calls to scrap tax breaks on delicacy foods. Imported fish and seafood are likely to get more expensive for Russian shoppers.
articles.body: Russia will raise import duties on seafood from countries it has designated 'unfriendly' to 35%, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov told the Federation Council, the upper house of parliament, on November 27. Siluanov said the Finance Ministry has drafted a government decree setting the new rate and that it is currently being coordinated with other agencies; at present there is no duty on these products at all. The proposal is a sharp escalation from earlier plans: the ministry had previously spoken of a 15% duty on delicacies from 'unfriendly' countries, a list that includes every country that has imposed sanctions on Russia. In early October, Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matviyenko called for scrapping the reduced VAT rate on delicacy products such as oysters and lobsters. The move fits a broader push to squeeze imports from sanctioning states while raising revenue for regional budgets, which Siluanov also addressed in his appearance before the upper house. For Russian consumers, the 35% duty is likely to push up prices for imported fish and seafood or push suppliers toward domestic and 'friendly'-country alternatives. The decree has not yet been signed, so the timing of when the new rate takes effect remains unclear.

articles.title: AI could replace 13% of Russian workers, Sberbank study finds
articles.description: Artificial intelligence could fully replace 13% of Russian workers and change how another 38% do their jobs, according to a joint study by Sberbank and the All-Russian Research Institute of Labor — 51% of the workforce affected in total. Office and retail workers are the most exposed, while managers are expected to become more productive. The findings came out of this week's Sberbank AI conference in Moscow, where Putin said the leader in AI will become 'the ruler of the world.'
articles.body: Artificial intelligence could fully replace 13% of Russian workers and change how another 38% do their jobs, according to a joint study by Sberbank analysts and the All-Russian Research Institute of Labor. In total, AI could affect 51% of working Russians, the study found, with office and retail workers the most exposed to being cut as businesses automate routine tasks. The researchers argue that companies adopting AI will be able to save on wages while making their managers more productive, as the technology takes over paperwork, customer service and other repetitive work. The findings were presented against the backdrop of the Sberbank AI conference in Moscow this week, where Vladimir Putin told participants that the leader in AI will become 'the ruler of the world' and warned that AI must never be used against Russia. The study lands as Russia's labour market is already strained by the war, with hundreds of thousands of men at the front or dead and employers complaining of shortages in many sectors. For workers, the message is double-edged: AI may ease some shortages, but it also threatens the jobs of millions of office and shop staff. The researchers do not say over what timeframe the displacement would happen, leaving open whether the shift will be gradual or abrupt.

articles.title: Patriarch Kirill says God will task Christians with taming AI — and Russia has a special role to play
articles.description: Russian Orthodox Patriarch Kirill told a plenary session of the World Russian People's Council that God will task Christians with 'taming' artificial intelligence, and that Russia has a special role thanks to its 'advanced technology and deep faith.' He warned that AI claims the right to decide for people and erodes human responsibility, but argued that will and morality — preserved through faith — can keep it under control. His remarks echoed Putin's warning at the Sberbank AI conference that AI must never be used against Russia.
articles.body: Russian Orthodox Patriarch Kirill said Christians have a duty to 'tame' artificial intelligence, arguing that people must retain moral judgement and the will to make decisions as the technology grows more powerful. Speaking at a plenary session of the World Russian People's Council, Kirill said AI can bring both benefits and harm: it claims the right to make decisions for people, freeing them from the need to take responsibility and think, and some already treat its advice as truth while others fear it will take over every process. Orthodox Christians should not give in to despair, he said, because God will charge them with the mission of taming this new force — and Russia has a special role to play thanks to its 'advanced technology and deep faith.' Kirill argued that although AI is already stronger than humans in many respects, people retain two advantages, will and morality, and only faith in God offers the chance to keep the technology under human control. His remarks come as Kirill turns 80, with Meduza retracing how he went from backing Ukrainian self-determination to defending Moscow's full-scale invasion. The speech also dovetailed with Vladimir Putin's remarks at this week's Sberbank AI conference, where the president said AI must never be used against Russia and warned that models trained on foreign values could imperceptibly shape the consciousness of millions. Together, the two speeches show how Russia's political and religious leadership are framing AI as a spiritual and civilisational contest, not just a technological one.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones strike St. Petersburg and three Russian regions, injuring three and disrupting flights
articles.description: Ukrainian drones struck St. Petersburg and three Russian regions overnight, injuring three people in Novorossiysk, Krasnodar Krai, and disrupting flights, Meduza reported on November 27. Drone-danger warnings were declared in St. Petersburg and Leningrad region, where officials said 44 drones were shot down. The raid is part of Ukraine's near-nightly long-range drone campaign against targets deep inside Russia, and comes as Kyiv braces for a feared new massive Russian strike on energy and logistics.
articles.body: Ukrainian drones struck St. Petersburg and three Russian regions overnight, injuring three people and disrupting air travel, Meduza reported on November 27. Authorities in St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad region declared a drone-attack danger warning, and residents were told to take shelter as air defences engaged incoming drones. Three people were injured in Novorossiysk, in Krasnodar Krai, according to the regional emergency response headquarters, and flights were disrupted as airports in the affected areas restricted operations. Russian officials reported dozens of drones intercepted over the course of the night, including 44 over Leningrad region alone. The raid follows a pattern of Ukrainian long-range drone strikes reaching deep into Russian territory, including repeated attacks on refineries, ports and military infrastructure far from the front line. It also comes as Ukraine braces for what President Zelensky has warned could be a new massive Russian strike on energy and logistics targets. The overnight exchange shows the drone war escalating on both sides at once, with Ukrainian strikes on Russian cities now a near-nightly occurrence and Russian retaliation expected within days.

articles.title: How Russian soldiers are escaping Putin's war: five deserters recount their journeys
articles.description: Meduza published a feature on November 27 in which five Russian deserters recount how they escaped the war — fleeing the front, crossing borders illegally, trekking through forests with bears, and in one case crossing the English Channel. Their accounts describe smugglers, volunteer networks, days without food or shelter, and the fear of capture, which can mean prison or being sent back to the front. The stories offer a human face to the war's toll as Russia's manpower strain deepens.
articles.body: Meduza published a feature on November 27 telling the stories of five Russian soldiers who deserted and fled the country, recounting journeys across borders, through forests with bears, and over the English Channel. It is well known that some Russians manage to desert successfully — slipping away from the front and then illegally crossing the border — but the men's accounts give a rare, detailed picture of how they did it and what it cost them.
