Masked gunmen swept through American neighborhoods, foreigners stayed away from American airports, international students began disappearing from universities, and after Charlie Kirk's murder the White House set out to purge his detractors while Stephen Miller warned the enemies of goodness that they had awakened a dragon. In red towns critics lowered their voices; in blue cities families talked seriously about moving abroad; some people Packer knew tried to parlay a deceased grandparent into a foreign passport. The spirit of the moment was captured in a recent translation of The Oppermanns, Lion Feuchtwanger's 1933 novel about a German Jewish family that flees as soon as Hitler takes power. Freedom House gave the United States its lowest democracy score ever in 2025 — on par with South Africa and below Panama.

Then a free election delivered an overwhelming rebuke to Trump and his rule. "What kind of fascist allows that to happen?" Packer asks. His summary of his own error is blunt: "I overrated Trump's competence as a dictator, and I underrated the resilience of American democracy." Lawrence Norden, an election-security expert at the Brennan Center for Justice, tells him, "I don't think that people were wrong to be worried, and I don't think the threat is over. I do think maybe some people underestimated the ability to fight back."

Packer argues Trump wants to rule as a fascist — cult of the leader, nationalist and xenophobic rhetoric, glorification of the "real" people, demonization of opponents, a blizzard of propaganda — and at what was probably the peak of his power, after the raid on Venezuela, declared that only "my own morality, my own mind" could stop him from doing anything he wanted. But Trump is, in Packer's phrase, a failed fascist: too shallow, undisciplined and selfish to lead a movement with a vision that outlives him, distracted by vanity construction projects and self-enrichment, his attraction to crassly beautiful women become, in his less priapic ninth decade, an attraction to crassly rich men — Elon Musk, Larry Ellison, Jensen Huang. A competent dictator would not lose touch with the people whose voice he claims to be, or keep harping on his new ballroom while health premiums and gas prices spike.

The fears about the midterms themselves were not fever dreams, Packer concedes: Trump tried to change voting rules, disqualify registered voters, intimidate election officials with threats of criminal charges, and mobilize the Justice Department to challenge results. But when courts struck down his executive orders he did not defy them; when people in Minneapolis protested armed agents terrorizing their neighbors, he backed off. Two institutions made sure the public would have a say: the federal courts and the state and local election system, with a decentralized structure that, as Norden puts it, let states and civil society "take advantage of that to be ready for the assault." The midterms showed democracy still matters to most Americans — not as abstract concepts like separation of powers, but as a visceral sense of fairness: Americans who voted for Trump three times were still capable of turning against him when his spectacular corruption affronted people who believe they are their own masters in a self-governing republic. Packer closes with a caution against the opposite error: "It was better to exaggerate than underrate Trump's ability to bring 250 years of democracy to an end" — vigilance, he writes, should be our constant state, because 250 years have left expectations and habits in American minds that, though they might disappear for a time, are not easily killed.

articles.title: The 200 Best Songs of the 1990s
articles.author: Rob Sheffield
articles.description: Rolling Stone's big year-end canon exercise, published November 23: 200 songs, one per artist, spanning hip-hop, Britpop, country and teen pop — with Nirvana on top for the second time in a decade.
articles.body:
Rolling Stone published its ranking of the 200 best songs of the 1990s on November 23, 2026, written by Rob Sheffield, with one song allowed per artist and a short write-up for each entry. At number one, for the second time in a decade — Sheffield also crowned it in his 2016 list of the 50 best songs of the decade — is Nirvana's "Smells Like Teen Spirit." Sheffield calls it "the song that blew up the world," the song "that defied all rules about how music worked and how much raw emotion you could cram into three cheap chords and a crummy guitar solo," the rebel-punk anthem that killed off 1980s schlock rock overnight and "kicked off a new decade of wide-open possibilities." It still hits home, he writes, because Kurt Cobain "is making the ultimate challenge — he's daring you to dream bigger, demand more, fight harder."

The rest of the top ten shows the list's range: Blackstreet's "No Diggity" at number two, praised as a utopian blend of doo-wop, R&B and hip-hop; the Notorious B.I.G.'s "Juicy" at three, described as both a memoir of his childhood and a history of hip-hop culture; Bikini Kill's "Rebel Girl" at four, the Riot Grrrl anthem produced by Joan Jett that was first released as a seven-inch single; Missy Elliott's "The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)" at five; Pavement's "Gold Soundz" at six; Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg's "Nuthin' But a 'G' Thang" at seven; Liz Phair's "Fuck and Run" at eight; Aaliyah's "Are You That Somebody?" at nine; and Pulp's "Common People" at ten.

Further down, the list moves freely across genres and eras of the decade: 2Pac's "California Love" at 72, Pearl Jam's "Daughter" at 61, Green Day's "Basket Case" at 112, TLC's "No Scrubs" at 17, Alanis Morissette's "You Oughta Know" at 24, Britney Spears' "...Baby One More Time" at 33, Cher's "Believe" at 120, Tori Amos' "Cornflake Girl" at 167, and Digital Underground's "The Humpty Dance" kicking things off at 200. The harder-rock entries include Rage Against the Machine's "Killing in the Name" at 46, Nine Inch Nails' "Closer" at 52, the Foo Fighters' "Everlong" at 65, Soundgarden's "Black Hole Sun" at 98, Metallica's "Enter Sandman" at 149, and Hole's "Doll Parts" at 18. The list's breadth — hip-hop, Britpop, country, teen pop, grunge, R&B and electronic music side by side — is the point: a decade when the charts and the underground kept colliding, ranked by a critic who has spent ten years arguing about it.

articles.title: MAHA champions promote dubious products, Post investigation finds
articles.description: A 41-minute Washington Post investigation into the business behind the Make America Healthy Again movement: how its fastest-growing influencers turned distrust of medicine into a flood of supplements, detoxes and enema kits — some of them flagged as unsafe.
articles.body:
The Washington Post's investigation, published November 22, 2026, examines the retail arm of the Make America Healthy Again movement — the wellness influencers who championed Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s agenda and built businesses that could outlast the political moment. To map it, the Post identified more than 80 podcasters, wellness gurus and other personalities who described themselves as MAHA supporters and had at least 100,000 followers on a single social network, then narrowed the group to the 18 whose Instagram followings climbed by 50 percent or more between August 2024 and June 2026. Reporters examined more than 37,000 social media posts, podcasts and newsletters since January 2024, reviewed regulatory filings, nutritional labels, lawsuits and customer complaints, and interviewed more than a dozen public health experts, scientists and former regulators.

The commercialization is the story. All but one of the 18 promoted products, and the flood grew fast: promotions of products or brands rose from 257 in the first half of 2024 to 795 over the same period this year. Alex Clark, the "Culture Apothecary" podcaster for Turning Point USA, advertised "Microplastic Daily Detox" supplements at $39.95 a capsule, saying they stopped her feeling like she was "turning into a human plastic bag"; she posted 352 promotions for brands or products in the first half of this year, nearly three times as many as in the first half of 2024. Carly Brown marketed Happy Bum Co.'s $74.95 silicone enema kits, saying coffee enemas were part of her cancer "healing journey" and gave skin a "radiant glow," and said on Instagram in May that she had built a "million-dollar online business" earning $10,000 a month from brand partnerships alone. Joel "Dr. Gator" Warsh touted bottles of drinkable silver for children's immune systems — doctors warn colloidal silver can turn skin bluish gray and damage kidneys, liver and nerves — and runs a $34.97-a-month Substack with more than 150,000 free and paid subscribers offering one-on-one "Vaccine Coaching" sessions to VIP members paying $499 a year.

The piece follows the money through the movement's biggest names: Del Bigtree, communications director for Kennedy's 2024 presidential campaign, who said "I don't sell products, I sell the truth" but later acknowledged paid promotions including a parasite cleanse; Nicole Shanahan, Kennedy's vice-presidential running mate; and Casey Means, Trump's second nominee for surgeon general, who a previous Post investigation found was paid more than half a million dollars for partnerships and sponsorships with companies selling "diagnostic testing," "herbal remedies and wellness products" and "teas, supplements, and elixirs." Courtney Swan, creator of the Realfoodology podcast, went from promoting 25 products in the first half of 2024 to 137 this year, including a covid-shot "detox" from The Wellness Company — a month's supply costs $89.99 — and promoted Serenity Kids toddler formula as one of the "cleanest options out there," though the company later faced allegations its children's-food pouches carried lead levels warranting disclosure under California law.

The Post tested the products against independent standards. At least 14 of the brands promoted by the fastest-growing influencers offer products that environmental watchdogs say contain lead at levels high enough to warrant special labeling under California's Proposition 65, which requires disclosure above 0.5 micrograms of exposure. At least 15 of the products would likely fail the Defense Department's Operation Supplement Safety scorecard — a seven-question test asking whether a supplement is third-party certified, has fewer than six pronounceable ingredients, and stays under 200 milligrams of caffeine per serving. The FTC fined one promoted company, TruHeight, which had claimed its supplements could make children taller: a $4 million judgment in April, later reduced to $750,000 on inability to pay, after the agency found its claims rested on a single company-sponsored study of 32 people that "showed no meaningful differences" and thousands of glowing reviews written by employees or bots. Warsh has promoted TruHeight at least 12 times since the judgment. Primally Pure, a skincare brand Clark advertised more than 50 times in under two years, was referred to the FTC in September 2025 for failing to substantiate claims its sunscreen was "better and safer" than conventional ones; its terms of service warn that "any reliance on the material on this site is at your own risk."

The investigation also documents the darker edge: Brown promoted Hope4Cancer, an alternative-treatment operator in Mexico whose centers faced since-settled lawsuits from the estates of two patients who died within months of starting treatment, and who says she ignored her doctors' advice for surgery and radiation in favor of colonics and "spiritual healing." Studies in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute and the Journal of Gastrointestinal Surgery found patients who relied on alternative cancer treatments had lower survival rates than those who pursued conventional care. Moms Across America promoted "vaccine detox" herbal extracts and an acupuncturist who warned women were having "menstrual abnormalities" from walking near covid-vaccinated people — the CDC calls that a myth. The Department of Health and Human Services said Kennedy's leadership "should not be interpreted as a blanket endorsement of every influencer, commercial partnership, or product." But as Peter Lurie of the Center for Science in the Public Interest puts it, the influencers are looking to "capitalize on ... very misleading beliefs" they perpetuate, and bioethicist Arthur Caplan calls the trade "completely dishonest, unethical ripoff profiteering."

articles.title: Is the Populist Moment Over?
articles.author: David Brooks with Fareed Zakaria
articles.description: David Brooks and Fareed Zakaria use the Democrats' midterm sweep to ask the biggest question of the moment: have we passed peak populism — and can liberal elites rebuild the trust they lost?
articles.body:
In this episode of The Atlantic's podcast The Permanent Questions, published November 22, 2026, host David Brooks asks Fareed Zakaria whether the midterm results signal the end of the Trump era — and with it, the beginning of the end of the populist moment. Brooks opens with what he calls a permanent problem: great nations fall when elites get too distanced from the masses and lose popular legitimacy, and the people rebel. The rise of Donald Trump as a political force more than a decade ago was part of a global wave of that anti-elite sentiment. But populists, Brooks argues, turn out to be guilty of all the sins people associate with the old elite — and can be more corrupt, more incompetent, more morally bankrupt and more out of touch than the people they promised to replace. When that happens, voters want to throw the populists out too, and Brooks believes that is what happened in the American election of 2026.

Zakaria — host of CNN's Fareed Zakaria GPS, a Washington Post columnist, and author of Age of Revolutions: Progress and Backlash From 1600 to the Present — agrees the moment is historic, but places it in a longer pattern. In every one of the liberal experiments he traces in his book, he says, a backlash eventually arrives when people decide the change has gone too far. The current backlash is against 30 or 40 years of globalization, massive economic and technological change, and enormous cultural change — the rise of women, the rise of minorities, immigration as its symbolic flashpoint. What is new, in his view, is that Trump 2.0 was a much purer implementation of right-wing populism than Trump 1.0, and that its failure was correspondingly clearer. His conclusion is cautiously optimistic: the election was so big that, in the United States at least, "not only is Trumpism over, but we've passed peak populism."

The conversation then turns to the harder question: what comes next. Both men argue that the decline of populist movements is an opening to rebuild liberal legitimacy, but only if elites change — addressing the profound disconnect with the public, and the loss of cultural dignity that drives populist anger more than economic data does. Zakaria stresses that liberal societies must embrace their pluralistic, crossroads character to keep innovating, while cultivating a leadership class that values wisdom and social responsibility over insular credentialism. Technology makes this rebuilding different from past cycles, they agree: it has enabled a radical individualism and fragmented the common culture and shared moral order that institutions once rested on. The episode ends where it began — with the open question of whether either party can craft a compelling vision that addresses the underlying problems rather than merely exploiting the rejection of populism, and whether a new historical era, and a restored popular legitimacy, is actually possible.

articles.title: The Outages Are Just Getting Started
articles.author: Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess
articles.description: WIRED's Kernel Panic newsletter on the week everything broke at once — Microsoft 365, Apple, the banks, United, even the NSA — and why AI is turning routine patches into a years-long outage risk.
articles.body:
Over one week in mid-November, Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess write in WIRED's Kernel Panic newsletter (November 21, 2026), a disruptive streak of technical outages hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA's classified network. There is no evidence these were cyberattacks, they stress — the incidents were "definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree" and taken individually they all seem to have routine explanations. Microsoft's massive 365 outage was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure, exacerbated by other network failures; officials said the NSA's internal communications outage was due to botched patching following October's critical PHP updates; Apple said its problems related to an internal update. Senator Mark Warner, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said on November 17 that "at this point, there is no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort."

But the routine explanations are not the whole story, the piece argues. As AI reshapes digital defense, researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs: the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 has surpassed 100,000, compared with around 25,000 in 2022, the last full year before large language models went mainstream — more than double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025. In October alone the database logged more than 17,000 new flaws, up from fewer than 5,000 in October 2025. Researchers recently disclosed AI-found critical bugs in PHP (for the second time), the NGINX web server software, and Java; Forbes reported 35 vulnerabilities across Apple products discovered by researchers using AI; Microsoft alone patched 3,554 flaws in the two and a half months before its November outage.

Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to patch quickly — and the patching itself is where systems break. The median time from a flaw's disclosure to its exploitation has fallen from 120 days to 80, according to VulnCheck, with some flaws exploited within hours, and Microsoft chief Satya Nadella has said patches must now go "instantly from being available to being patched in production." The chain, as WIRED lays it out, has five steps: AI finds flaws faster, attackers exploit them faster, vendors and IT teams feel pressure to patch at once, they push updates onto systems that were not built for that pace, and some of those systems fail. Senator Warner said AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are "putting tremendous strain on systems that weren't built to handle that pace of change." Cloudflare chief executive Matthew Prince predicts "it's going to feel like the sky is falling for two years."

The piece keeps the scale in perspective: only about 300 vulnerabilities have been added this year to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's catalog of flaws known to be exploited, and VulnCheck counts roughly 1,500 known-exploited flaws so far in 2026 — just 1.5 percent of the bugs discovered. As one researcher puts it, "the number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant. The caveat is that the pace at which they're being used or weaponized has increased dramatically." The warning is not that AI is attacking the internet, but that it is accelerating everything around it — discovery, exploitation, and the rushed fixes — faster than the systems built to absorb them can handle. "Welcome to internet outage hell."

articles.title: Lukashenko offers to fly Zelensky to Moscow for peace talks with Putin
articles.description: Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko has offered to fly Volodymyr Zelensky to Moscow for peace talks with Vladimir Putin. The offer comes as negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. prepare to meet in Abu Dhabi, with Washington pushing for a deal by January.
articles.body: Alexander Lukashenko, the Belarusian leader and Putin's closest ally, says he is ready to fly Volodymyr Zelensky to Moscow for direct peace talks with Vladimir Putin. The offer is striking because Belarus has been a launchpad for Russia's invasion and Lukashenko has long acted as Moscow's intermediary, not as a neutral broker — which raises obvious questions about whether Kyiv would ever accept a trip arranged by him. It comes at a moment of intense diplomacy: negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the United States are preparing to meet in Abu Dhabi, Zelensky has said Washington wants a deal by January, and Trump's envoy Jared Kushner has been praising Putin in public. No response from Kyiv has been reported, and a Zelensky–Putin meeting has been floated and dropped many times before without happening. The proposal may be less a practical plan than a signal — Lukashenko positioning himself, and Moscow, as open to talks while Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure ahead of the negotiations.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones strike Russia's Samara region, killing one and setting two Rosneft oil refineries ablaze
articles.description: Ukrainian drones struck Russia's Samara region, killing one person and setting two Rosneft oil refineries on fire, the regional governor said. The attack is part of Ukraine's sustained campaign against Russian oil infrastructure, which Kyiv says funds the war.
articles.body: Ukrainian drones attacked Russia's Samara region, killing one person and setting two Rosneft oil refineries ablaze, Samara Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. The strike fits Ukraine's months-long campaign against Russian refineries, which has repeatedly disrupted fuel production and forced Moscow to restrict petrol exports. Kyiv has been explicit that oil infrastructure is a legitimate target because it bankrolls the war, and the Samara attack shows the campaign reaching deep into Russia's industrial heartland, hundreds of kilometres from the front. For Russia, each refinery fire is both an economic hit and a humiliation for air defences that have struggled to stop drone swarms. The attack also comes as Zelensky warns that Moscow is preparing a new massive strike on Ukrainian energy and logistics, and as the U.S. pushes both sides toward talks in Abu Dhabi — a reminder that the fighting, and the long-range strikes, are escalating even as diplomacy accelerates.

articles.title: Zelensky: Russia is finishing preparations for a new massive strike on energy and logistics
articles.description: Volodymyr Zelensky says Russia is finishing preparations for a new massive strike, with energy, logistics and life-support facilities in cities and towns as the targets again, according to intelligence. He said Ukraine is preparing new sanctions against Russian ballistic-missile production and awaiting a foreign-ministry report on air-defence supplies.
articles.body: President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned that Russia is finishing preparations for a new massive strike, and that intelligence points to energy, logistics and life-support facilities in cities and communities as the targets once again. The warning comes after a night in which Russia attacked water supplies, heating networks, shopping centres and residential buildings in Kyiv and seven regions, leaving at least ten people injured, according to Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi. The energy situation is especially difficult in Dnipro, the Dniprovskyi district and Pavlohrad, Zelensky said, thanking repair crews and utilities workers restoring power after the strikes. He also said Ukraine is preparing new sanctions against Russian companies and individuals involved in producing ballistic missiles, and is awaiting a report from the Foreign Ministry on talks with partners about air-defence deliveries. In a separate development, Koretskyi said Russian forces attacked two foreign civilian ships near Odesa carrying more than 100,000 tonnes of grain. The warning underlines that Moscow's campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure is not letting up even as U.S.-brokered talks approach — and that Kyiv expects the next wave to be aimed squarely at keeping Ukrainians cold and in the dark.

articles.title: Ubisoft reportedly requires all employees to use generative AI — and justify it if they don't
articles.description: Ubisoft has reportedly told all of its employees they must use generative AI, with developers required to justify it if they choose not to. The mandate, described by one report as a company 'gripped by psychosis', is the most aggressive AI push yet from a major publisher.
articles.body: Ubisoft has reportedly required all of its employees to use generative AI, with developers expected to justify themselves if they choose not to use it, according to media reports. The mandate is the most aggressive AI push yet from a major publisher, and it comes as the games industry argues bitterly over what generative AI is for: a tool that speeds up routine work, or a replacement for the artists, writers and designers who make games. Ubisoft, which has faced years of financial pressure and restructuring, appears to be betting that AI can cut costs and speed up production across its studios. For its developers, the requirement to justify not using AI flips the usual logic — the burden is now on the human to explain why a machine should not be involved. The report's description of a company 'gripped by psychosis' captures the mood inside an industry where AI mandates are landing on top of layoffs, and where the people being told to use the tools are often the same ones whose jobs the tools are meant to replace.

articles.title: Thanksgiving storm leaves roads flooded and more than 800,000 without power in eastern US
articles.description: The Thanksgiving nor'easter has left roads flooded and more than 800,000 people without power across the eastern US, shutting down some East Coast bridges and roadways as the storm pushes north. The same storm forced the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday — the first postponement in its history.
articles.body: The nor'easter raking the East Coast on Thanksgiving Day has left roads flooded and more than 800,000 people without power across the eastern United States, with some bridges and roadways shut down as the storm continues its push north. The storm brought the ingredients forecasters warned about all week: heavy rain — up to seven inches in eastern North Carolina — wind gusts topping 60 mph along the coast, and coastal flooding near record levels at Ocean City, Maryland, and the highest since 2016 at Cape May, New Jersey. Inland, the same system dropped heavy snow across the mid-Mississippi Valley, with more than seven inches in St. Louis and up to ten near Perryville, Missouri, and even tornado warnings in Virginia Beach. The storm is also the reason the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed to Saturday for the first time in its 100-year history, and it has snarled holiday travel on the roads and in the air. Power crews are working through the holiday to restore service, but with the storm still moving north into New England, the outages — and the flooding — are not over yet.

articles.title: Houthis strike Saudi oil export hub, putting global energy markets on edge
articles.description: A Houthi drone attack has hit a Saudi oil facility in Yanbu, striking a key oil export hub and putting global energy markets on edge. The attack is a reminder of how exposed the world's energy infrastructure is to the region's conflicts.
articles.body: A Houthi drone attack has hit a Saudi oil facility in Yanbu, striking a key oil export hub and putting global energy markets on edge. The attack on one of Saudi Arabia's main export terminals is a reminder of how vulnerable the world's energy infrastructure is to the region's conflicts — and how quickly a single drone can rattle oil prices. The Houthis, who have repeatedly targeted shipping and energy infrastructure in the Red Sea region, have shown they can reach deep into Saudi territory, and each successful strike raises the risk premium on oil. For Saudi Arabia, the attack is both a security failure and a diplomatic headache, coming as the kingdom tries to balance its relationships with Washington, Tehran and its Gulf neighbours. For energy markets, the question is whether this is a one-off or the start of a new campaign — and whether the world's spare oil capacity is enough to absorb the shock if the attacks continue.

articles.title: LiveOne is paying its Global Music Rights licensing fees in stock — if they aren't covered in 90 days, GMR can terminate the license
articles.description: LiveOne is paying licensing fees owed to Global Music Rights in stock, agreeing to issue 40,000 shares worth about $104,000. The deal comes with a 90-day deadline: if the fees aren't covered by then, GMR can terminate the licence — a stark sign of the streaming company's cash strain.
articles.body: Nasdaq-listed LiveOne, owner of streaming service Slacker, is paying licensing fees owed to performance rights organisation Global Music Rights in stock, agreeing to issue 40,000 shares to GMR, according to SEC filings from last Friday. The shares serve as payment for outstanding fees under the companies' performance licence and as a prepayment of part of the fees owed through June 2027 — but the arrangement comes with a 90-day deadline from issuance. If a certain amount of the fees hasn't been covered in that window, via share sales or cash, and LiveOne doesn't make up the balance, GMR will have the right to terminate the licence. The shares carry an assumed price of $2.60 each, LiveOne's closing price on November 4, valuing the issuance at about $104,000 — less than 0.3% of the company's shares outstanding. The underlying licence dates to June 2020 and now runs through June 2027. The filings also repeat LiveOne's disclosure of 'substantial doubt' about its ability to continue as a going concern, and note an October 29 forbearance agreement with senior debenture holders. It is a vivid snapshot of a small streamer paying for music rights with equity because cash is short.

articles.title: Tidal bans fully AI-generated music from its platform
articles.description: Tidal is banning wholly AI-generated music, saying it will reject and remove any fully AI-generated track submitted to the platform from December 9. The service says 43% of all tracks distributed to it over the past 90 days were detected as entirely AI-made.
articles.body: Tidal is banning wholly AI-generated music from its platform, saying it will reject and remove 'any wholly AI-generated track that's submitted to Tidal' starting on December 9. The Block-owned streaming service says 43% of all tracks distributed to it over the past 90 days were detected as wholly AI-generated — a flood that helps explain why it is acting now. Tidal has named Ircam Amplify, the commercial arm of the French audio research institute IRCAM, as the technology partner behind its AI detection. The policy was announced on X on Tuesday by Tidal and by Robert Andersen, Tidal Lead at Block. The figure is close to what Deezer has reported, suggesting the AI deluge is industry-wide rather than a Tidal problem alone. Tidal is not the first to draw the line: in January, Bandcamp banned music and audio created 'wholly or in substantial part by AI'. But as the first major streaming service to ban fully AI-generated tracks outright, Tidal's move puts pressure on Spotify, Apple Music and the rest to say where they stand — and it lands in the same week the Suno lawsuits keep widening.

articles.title: Pearl Jam rage against 'unconscionable' ICE arrests at Seattle airport
articles.description: Pearl Jam have condemned the 'unconscionable' ICE arrests at Seattle airport, joining a wave of artists speaking out against the immigration enforcement operation. The band, long outspoken on politics, called the arrests at their hometown airport unacceptable.
articles.body: Pearl Jam have spoken out against the ICE arrests at Seattle airport, calling them 'unconscionable' in a statement that puts one of rock's biggest bands squarely against the immigration enforcement operation. The arrests at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport have drawn condemnation from across the music world, with the Seattle band — hometown heroes who have never shied from politics — among the loudest voices. The band's intervention matters because Pearl Jam rarely lend their name to a fast-moving news story unless they feel strongly, and because their Seattle roots make the airport arrests personal: this is their city, their airport, their neighbours being detained. The arrests have become a flashpoint in the wider debate over immigration enforcement under the current administration, with artists using their platforms to amplify what might otherwise be a local story. Pearl Jam's statement is short and furious, and it sets the tone for a growing chorus of musicians who are no longer content to stay out of the fight.

articles.title: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' spends 29th week atop Hot 100 and ties 50-week country record
articles.description: 'Choosin' Texas' by Ella Langley continues for a record-extending 29th week atop the Billboard Hot 100, and ties Bebe Rexha and Florida Georgia Line's 'Meant To Be' for the longest command ever — 50 weeks — on the Hot Country Songs chart. The song's run is now one of the longest in chart history.
articles.body: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' continues for a record-extending 29th week atop the Billboard Hot 100, and ties Bebe Rexha and Florida Georgia Line's 'Meant To Be' for the longest command ever — 50 weeks — on the Hot Country Songs chart. The run has made Langley one of the defining chart stories of the year: a country song that has held the biggest chart in American music for more than half a year, with a substantial margin over the rest of the top 10. Behind her, the chart is in transition, with holiday songs already climbing and the rest of the top 10 jostling for position. Langley's achievement is also a country music story: 'Meant To Be' was a crossover phenomenon, and matching its 50-week country reign puts 'Choosin' Texas' in rare company. With holiday music about to flood the charts, the question is how much longer the run can last — but for now, Langley owns the Hot 100 in a way few artists ever have.

articles.title: UPDATE: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have died in Ukraine, Meduza estimates
articles.description: Meduza has published its estimate that more than 700,000 Russian soldiers have died in Ukraine over nearly five years of full-scale war — more than the United States lost in World War II, and more than the number of boys born in Russia in a single year. The Kremlin dismissed the figure earlier today and told the public to trust Defense Ministry numbers instead.
articles.body: Meduza's investigation puts the Russian military death toll in Ukraine at more than 700,000 over nearly five years of full-scale war, a scale the outlet compares to the United States' total World War II losses and to the number of boys born in Russia in a single year. The estimate lands the same day the Kremlin publicly dismissed Meduza's figure of 720,000 war dead, telling Russians to trust the Defense Ministry's numbers instead — a rare direct response that underlines how sensitive the casualty count has become. The toll reflects a war of attrition in which Russia has kept up offensives despite enormous losses, and it frames the backdrop to the U.S.-brokered talks, with Washington pushing for a peace deal by January. For Ukraine, the figure is a measure of what the invasion has cost Russia; for Moscow, it is a number it refuses to acknowledge, even as recruitment bonuses and payments to soldiers' families keep rising. The estimate is based on open-source records, obituaries and statistical modelling, the method Meduza has used with independent researchers to track Russian losses since 2022.

articles.title: Kushner calls Putin a 'historic figure' and 'grandmaster of politics', says he showed 'restraint' and promised no nuclear weapons
articles.description: Trump envoy Jared Kushner has lavished praise on Vladimir Putin, calling him a 'historic figure' and a 'grandmaster of politics' with a 'deep understanding of the issues', and saying Putin has shown 'restraint' in Ukraine and promised not to use nuclear weapons. The remarks come as Kushner helps steer the U.S.-brokered peace talks.
articles.body: Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and a key envoy in the Ukraine peace effort, has publicly praised Vladimir Putin as a 'historic figure' and a 'grandmaster of politics', crediting him with a 'deep understanding of the issues'. Kushner also said Putin has shown 'restraint' in Ukraine and promised not to use nuclear weapons — a striking characterisation given the daily missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities, which have killed civilians and wrecked energy infrastructure this week alone. The comments land as negotiators prepare to meet in Abu Dhabi and Washington pushes for a deal by January, and they fit the administration's reported shift back to a 'land for peace' formula. For Kyiv, the praise is alarming: an envoy publicly vouching for Putin's restraint while Russia intensifies its attacks, and while Zelensky accuses Moscow of treating diplomacy 'as a subtype of expansion'. Kushner's role makes the words more than flattery — they signal how the U.S. side is framing the talks, and how far its view of Putin has moved from the language of previous administrations.

articles.title: Russian lawmakers propose up to five years in prison for sharing photos and videos of drone strike aftermath
articles.description: Russian lawmakers have proposed up to five years in prison for sharing photos and videos of the aftermath of drone strikes. The bill would criminalise publishing images of damage from Ukrainian attacks, tightening the information blackout around the war's impact inside Russia.
articles.body: Russian lawmakers have proposed prison terms of up to five years for sharing photos and videos showing the aftermath of drone strikes, in a new escalation of wartime censorship. The bill would make it a crime to publish images of damage from Ukrainian attacks — the kind of footage that has spread widely on social media after refinery fires and strikes on military sites. It comes as Ukrainian drones hit targets deep inside Russia with growing frequency, including the Samara refineries this week, and as Moscow tries to control the narrative about the war's cost at home. The proposal follows years of laws punishing 'discrediting' the army and spreading 'fake' war news, but a five-year sentence for a photo would be among the harshest measures yet aimed at ordinary people rather than journalists. If passed, it would push evidence of the war's impact on Russian territory further underground, leaving the public dependent on official accounts that routinely minimise damage.

articles.title: Russian lawmakers advance bill to automatically transfer 6.6 trillion rubles in pension savings to long-term savings program
articles.description: Russia's State Duma has approved in a first reading a bill that would automatically transfer 6.6 trillion rubles of pension savings into the long-term savings program. The move would sweep the funded portion of Russians' pensions into a state-backed scheme as the government hunts for money.
articles.body: Lawmakers in Russia's State Duma have approved in a first reading a bill that would automatically transfer the funded portion of Russians' pensions — some 6.6 trillion rubles — into the long-term savings program known as PDS. The money, built up in individual pension accounts, would move into the state-backed scheme without account holders having to opt in. The government presents the program as a way to encourage long-term saving, but the scale of the transfer, and its timing, point to a state hunting for funds as war spending strains the budget and regional governments cut costs. For millions of Russians, the funded pension was supposed to be a personal pot on top of the state pension; moving it automatically into a new vehicle raises questions about access, returns and who ultimately controls the cash. The bill still needs further readings, but first-reading approval in the Duma usually signals it will pass — and it adds a domestic financial story to a day dominated by war and diplomacy.

articles.title: Moscow court closes trial of Novaya Gazeta journalist Oleg Roldugin to public and press
articles.description: A Moscow court has begun hearing the criminal case against Novaya Gazeta journalist Oleg Roldugin behind closed doors, barring the press and public. Roldugin is accused of illegally using personal data — a charge rights groups see as part of the pressure on Russia's last independent media.
articles.body: The Nikulinsky District Court in Moscow began hearing the criminal case against Oleg Roldugin, a journalist at the independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, on November 26 — and immediately closed the proceedings to the press and public. Roldugin is accused of illegally using personal data under Part 3 of Article 272.1 of Russia's Criminal Code. At the start of the hearing the prosecutor asked Judge Konstantin Dubkov to close the trial, citing the disclosure of state secrets and officials' personal data; the judge agreed, and the case will now be heard without spectators or journalists present. The closure means the public will not hear the evidence against a reporter from one of the few independent outlets still operating in Russia. It comes weeks after Novaya Gazeta announced it was closing at the end of October, a further blow to independent journalism in a country where reporting on the war and on officials already carries severe legal risk.

articles.title: Deputy commander of Russia's Aerospace Forces arrested on bribery charges amid crackdown on senior officers
articles.description: The deputy commander of Russia's Aerospace Forces has been arrested on bribery charges, the latest senior military official caught up in an ongoing anti-corruption crackdown. The arrest adds to a string of high-profile cases against generals since the war began.
articles.body: The deputy commander of Russia's Aerospace Forces has been arrested on bribery charges, in the latest case in an ongoing crackdown on senior military officials. The arrest continues a pattern that has seen a series of generals and top defence officials detained on corruption charges since the full-scale invasion began — a purge that has swept through the Defence Ministry and the armed forces' upper ranks. For the Kremlin, the cases serve a double purpose: they let the leadership blame corruption for military failures while also removing officials who have built independent power bases. For the military, the steady drumbeat of arrests is a reminder that no rank is safe, even as the war grinds on and the Aerospace Forces play a central role in the daily missile and drone strikes on Ukraine. Details of the charges against the deputy commander have not been made public beyond the bribery allegation, and it is not clear whether the case is connected to procurement or to other offences.

articles.title: Pentagon says it is ramping up production of Patriot missiles
articles.description: The Pentagon says it is ramping up production of Patriot missiles, the air-defence system Ukraine relies on to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. The increase matters because Ukraine's interceptors are being burned through in nightly attacks.
articles.body: The Pentagon says it is increasing production of Patriot missiles, the backbone of the air-defence system Ukraine depends on to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles. The announcement comes as Russia steps up its strikes on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, firing Iskanders, Zircons, S-400s and more than a hundred attack drones in a single night this week. Ukraine's Patriot batteries have been the main shield against ballistic threats, but every interception costs an interceptor — and Kyiv has repeatedly told allies that supplies, not willpower, are the constraint. More production would ease that bottleneck, though missiles take time to build and deliver, and Ukraine's needs compete with orders from other allies. The ramp-up also signals that Washington expects the air war to continue even as it pushes for a peace deal by January, with diplomats and generals preparing for both a negotiated end and a winter of continued strikes.

articles.title: Romanian president: shooting down targets over Ukraine would mean NATO joining the war
articles.description: Romania's president has said that shooting down targets over Ukraine would amount to NATO taking part in the war — pushing back against Poland's proposal that the alliance consider intercepting Russian missiles headed toward its territory. The split shows the limits of the idea inside NATO.
articles.body: Romania's president has said that shooting down targets over Ukraine would mean NATO participating in the war, pushing back against a proposal from Poland that the alliance consider intercepting Russian missiles over Ukrainian territory when they are headed toward alliance territory. Poland floated the idea this week, according to Bloomberg, arguing that NATO should act when a missile's trajectory threatens a member state. Bucharest's response exposes the fault line inside the alliance: some members want a more forward posture against Russian strikes that have repeatedly crossed or neared NATO borders, while others fear that firing on Russian weapons over Ukraine would be a direct step into the war. The debate is not abstract — Russian drones and missiles have strayed into Poland and Romania before, and the question of what NATO does next time is unresolved. For Kyiv, which has long asked allies to help shoot down missiles over its territory, the Romanian position is a reminder that even sympathetic neighbours draw the line at actions they see as direct participation.

articles.title: Armenia plans to end Russian border guards' activities on its territory
articles.description: Armenia plans to end the activities of Russian border guards on its territory, in another step away from Moscow's orbit. The move follows years of fraying ties since Russia failed to back Armenia in its conflict with Azerbaijan.
articles.body: Armenia plans to stop Russian border guards from operating on its territory, in the latest sign of Yerevan drifting away from Moscow. Russian border guards have long been stationed in Armenia, a legacy of the Soviet era and of Armenia's membership in the Russian-led CSTO alliance. But relations have frayed badly since Russia failed to come to Armenia's aid in its conflict with Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh, and Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has since frozen Armenia's participation in the CSTO and courted closer ties with the West. Ending the border guards' presence would be a concrete break, not just rhetoric — removing a visible symbol of Russian influence from Armenian soil. Moscow has watched Armenia's pivot with growing irritation, and the decision adds to a pattern of former Soviet states quietly reducing their dependence on Russia while it is bogged down in Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian drone hits educational institution in Kharkiv, killing one and injuring another
articles.description: A Russian drone struck an educational institution in Kharkiv, killing one person and injuring another. The attack is the latest in a wave of strikes on the city, which was also hit overnight by ballistic missiles and more than a hundred drones.
articles.body: A Russian drone has hit an educational institution in Kharkiv, killing one person and injuring another, in the latest strike on Ukraine's second city. The attack follows the overnight barrage in which Russia fired ballistic missiles and 113 drones at Kyiv, Kharkiv and other regions, killing two people in a Kharkiv apartment strike and injuring seven in Kyiv. Kharkiv, close to the Russian border, has been under near-constant attack for months, with drones and missiles hitting homes, hospitals and schools as well as military targets. The strike on a place of learning underlines the indiscriminate character of the campaign, which has repeatedly hit civilian infrastructure even as Moscow claims to target only military sites. Air defences shot down 87 of the 113 drones overnight, but the ones that got through were enough to kill and maim — and to keep the city's residents living under nightly alerts.

articles.title: Russians attack post office in Donetsk region, killing a woman and injuring three
articles.description: Russian forces attacked a post office in the Donetsk region, killing a woman and injuring three people. The strike hit a civilian facility in a frontline area where post offices are often the only link to pensions, parcels and outside help.
articles.body: Russian forces have attacked a post office in the Donetsk region, killing a woman and injuring three people. The strike hit a civilian facility in an area where the front line is never far away, and where post offices do far more than deliver mail — they are where residents collect pensions, receive parcels and stay connected to the rest of the country. The attack is part of the daily toll of strikes on the Donetsk region, which has been under sustained bombardment as Russian forces push toward Kostiantynivka and other towns in the east. It also fits a pattern of Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure that Ukraine has documented throughout the war, from hospitals and schools to energy substations. For the people still living in frontline towns, the loss of a post office is not just a building destroyed; it is one more service gone in places where almost nothing still works.

articles.title: General Staff: Ukrainian forces destroyed over 50,000 occupiers for a second month running
articles.description: Ukraine's General Staff says its forces destroyed more than 50,000 Russian occupiers for a second consecutive month, with over 2,000 eliminated in the past day alone. The figures point to the grinding attrition on the front, where around 150 battles were fought since the start of the day.
articles.body: Ukraine's General Staff says its defence forces destroyed more than 50,000 Russian occupiers for a second month in a row, with over 2,000 Russian soldiers eliminated in the past day alone. The figures describe a front where the fighting has not eased despite the diplomatic push: around 150 battles took place since the start of the day, with the heaviest pressure around Kostiantynivka in the Donetsk region, according to the commander-in-chief's report to the president. The numbers are Ukraine's own count and cannot be independently verified, but they track with the scale of losses Meduza separately estimated this week at more than 700,000 Russian dead since the full-scale invasion. For Kyiv, the attrition figures are evidence that Russia is paying an enormous price for incremental gains. For Moscow, the willingness to absorb such losses — and to keep recruiting — is the other side of a war it still believes it can win by endurance.

articles.title: Four police officers killed in Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia region
articles.description: Four police officers have been killed in a Russian strike on the Zaporizhzhia region, where the injured toll from this week's attacks has climbed to 50, including children. The region has been hit repeatedly, with homes, cars and infrastructure damaged.
articles.body: Four police officers have been killed in a Russian strike on the Zaporizhzhia region, adding to a mounting casualty list from this week's attacks on the area. The number of people injured in the Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia has risen to 50, including children, after strikes that damaged homes, cars and infrastructure and left three people injured in one attack alone. Zaporizhzhia, a major city close to the front, has been hit again and again by missiles and drones, and its police and emergency services are often among the first on the scene — and among the casualties when follow-up strikes hit. The deaths underline the human cost of a campaign that has targeted the region's cities relentlessly, even as the diplomatic focus shifts to Abu Dhabi and the January deadline Washington has set for a deal.

articles.title: CD Projekt Red: The Witcher 4 will launch on Xbox on day one despite Sony agreement
articles.description: CD Projekt Red has reassured fans that The Witcher 4 will launch on Xbox on day one, despite the studio's agreement with Sony. The message — 'no one gets left behind' — is meant to calm fears of a PlayStation-first release.
articles.body: CD Projekt Red has moved to reassure fans that The Witcher 4 will launch on Xbox on day one, despite the studio's agreement with Sony. The message, summed up as 'no one gets left behind', is aimed at Xbox players who feared the next Witcher might arrive first — or only — on PlayStation, after reports of a deal between CD Projekt and Sony. The Witcher 4 is one of the most anticipated games in development, the next chapter in a series that sold tens of millions of copies and defined a generation of role-playing games. For CD Projekt, which is also growing its Cyberpunk 2 team to nearly 200 people, the reassurance is good business: the Witcher audience is spread across every platform, and the studio cannot afford to alienate any of them. For players, it is a promise that will be tested only when the game finally has a release date — but for now, Xbox fans can breathe easier.

articles.title: Microsoft will push Xbox harder in 2027, from Call of Duty to Diablo and The Elder Scrolls
articles.description: Microsoft will promote Xbox more actively in 2027, leaning on its own franchises — from Call of Duty to Diablo and The Elder Scrolls — to sell the platform. The push follows years in which Xbox's identity has blurred between console, PC and cloud.
articles.body: Microsoft will promote Xbox more actively in 2027, leaning on its own franchises — from Call of Duty to Diablo and The Elder Scrolls — to sell the platform. The plan is a recognition that Xbox now owns some of the biggest names in gaming, after the Activision Blizzard and Bethesda acquisitions, and that it has not yet turned that catalogue into a clear reason to choose Xbox. Call of Duty, Diablo and The Elder Scrolls are among the most valuable franchises in the industry, and putting them at the front of Xbox's marketing would be the most direct statement yet that Microsoft intends to compete on games, not just on services. The push comes as the console market shifts: PlayStation dominates hardware sales, Nintendo's Switch 2 is selling fast, and Xbox has increasingly pitched itself as a platform that lives on PC, cloud and console alike. For players, the promise is more of the games they already love, marketed harder — and for Microsoft's rivals, it is a warning that the Xbox catalogue is about to get louder.

articles.title: GTA VI posts the biggest launch of the generation in the UK physical sales chart
articles.description: Grand Theft Auto VI has posted the biggest launch of the generation in the UK physical retail chart, underlining the scale of a release that is dominating games, music and culture at once. The game's soundtrack alone has sent older songs surging on streaming.
articles.body: Grand Theft Auto VI has posted the biggest launch of the generation in the UK physical retail chart, a measure of a release that is dominating not just gaming but music and culture at once. The physical chart matters because it captures the players who still buy discs — and GTA VI has outsold every other launch of the generation on that measure, in a market where physical sales have been shrinking for years. The scale of the launch is matched by its cultural footprint: the game's soundtrack rollout has sent songs like Carly Rae Jepsen's 'Run Away With Me' up 288 percent on streaming, Take-Two's chief executive is talking about his 'responsibility to society', and a Miami music event tied to the game features Travis Scott and Cardi B. For Rockstar, the numbers confirm what the hype promised. For the industry, GTA VI is a reminder that a single game can still move the whole market — and that the biggest launches are now cultural events, not just retail ones.

articles.title: Remedy: the fate of Quantum Break 2 depends on Microsoft
articles.description: Remedy Entertainment says the fate of a Quantum Break sequel depends on Microsoft, which owns the IP — though journalist Jez Corden thinks a return could fit Xbox's strategy. The studio is meanwhile progressing well on its Max Payne remakes with Rockstar.
articles.body: Remedy Entertainment has said the fate of a Quantum Break 2 depends on Microsoft, which owns the rights to the time-bending action game. The original Quantum Break, released in 2016, was a Microsoft-published Xbox exclusive that blended a TV show with a shooter, and its sequel has been a long-standing 'what if' for fans. Remedy's comment makes the situation plain: the studio would like to return to the series, but the decision is Microsoft's, not theirs. Journalist Jez Corden has suggested a return could fit Xbox's current strategy, as Microsoft leans harder on its own franchises. The news lands as Remedy reports its Max Payne remakes, made in partnership with Rockstar, are progressing well — so the studio is busy either way. For fans, the Quantum Break update is a flicker of hope, not a promise: the game exists only if Microsoft wants it to.

articles.title: Nvidia cut RTX 50 graphics card production by up to a third, report says
articles.description: Nvidia has cut production of its RTX 50 graphics cards by 20 to 30 percent, according to Commercial Times, citing Taiwanese IT partners. The cut could tighten supply — and prices — for PC gamers heading into the holidays.
articles.body: Nvidia has cut production and supply of its RTX 50 graphics cards by 20 to 30 percent, according to Commercial Times, citing Taiwanese IT partners. The cut, if it holds, could tighten supply for PC gamers heading into the holiday season, when graphics cards are among the most sought-after upgrades. The RTX 50 series is Nvidia's current flagship line, and any reduction in output tends to show up quickly in prices, with retailers and resellers passing scarcity on to buyers. The report's headline — 'the jacket demands sacrifices', a nod to chief executive Jensen Huang's signature leather jacket — captures the wry mood around a company that dominates the GPU market and the AI boom alike. For gamers, the timing is unwelcome: the cards are already expensive, and a production cut would make them harder to find. For Nvidia, which is also navigating the AI trade's volatility and Huang's own dramatic reinstatement as chief executive, the GPU business is a reminder that its oldest customers still matter.

articles.title: HONOR Watch 6 review: up to 35 days of battery life
articles.description: GameMAG's hands-on review of the HONOR Watch 6 promises up to 35 days of battery life and rich functionality, in a smartwatch that aims to outlast its rivals by weeks rather than days. Battery life is the headline feature.
articles.body: GameMAG has published a hands-on review of the HONOR Watch 6, the new smartwatch that promises up to 35 days of battery life and rich functionality. The battery claim is the headline: most smartwatches need charging every day or two, so a watch that can run for a month would be a genuine change in how the device is used — no nightly charging, no dead watch on a trip. The review describes a 'solid recovery' for the line, with the new generation offering more features alongside the endurance, from health tracking to notifications and workouts. For buyers, the trade-off is the usual one for long-battery watches: whether the software and sensors match the stamina. For the market, the HONOR Watch 6 is part of a wider push by Chinese brands to compete on battery life and value, in a category Apple and Samsung have long dominated. If the 35-day claim holds up in real use, it is the kind of number that makes people pay attention.

articles.title: Settlers torched his home. Then came the bulldozer.
articles.description: A developing story from the Jordan Valley: settlers torched a Palestinian home, and then a bulldozer came to demolish what was left. The report, posted this afternoon, is the latest account of settler violence in the West Bank.
articles.body: A developing story from the Jordan Valley in the West Bank: settlers torched a Palestinian home, and then a bulldozer arrived to demolish what remained. The report, posted on CNN's homepage this afternoon, is the latest account of settler violence in the occupied West Bank, where attacks on Palestinian homes, land and livelihoods have surged. Details are still emerging about the family involved and the circumstances of the attack, but the sequence — a home set on fire, then levelled by a bulldozer — captures the pattern of violence and demolition that Palestinians in the Jordan Valley have faced for years. The story lands in a week when the world's attention has been on Ukraine and on Thanksgiving at home, but the West Bank's slow-burning crisis continues, with settler attacks rarely punished and demolitions carried out under military orders. CNN's report is a reminder that the conflict's daily toll extends far beyond Gaza's headlines.

articles.title: Two Italians killed in alleged Iranian drone attack on Kuwait; Tehran denies involvement
articles.description: Two Italian nationals have been killed in an alleged Iranian drone attack on Kuwait, which Tehran denies being behind. The incident adds a dangerous new flashpoint to the region's already volatile mix.
articles.body: Two Italian nationals have been killed in an alleged Iranian drone attack on Kuwait, in an incident Tehran denies being behind. The attack, if confirmed as Iranian, would mark a sharp escalation: a drone strike on a Gulf Arab state that killed European citizens, at a moment when the region is already on edge over the war in Gaza, the Houthi attacks on shipping and the standoff over Iran's nuclear programme. Tehran's denial leaves the attribution contested, and it is not yet clear what evidence links the drones to Iran or what the target was. For Italy, the deaths of two of its nationals abroad will demand a response, and Rome will be pressing for clarity on who was responsible. For the Gulf states, the incident is a reminder of how exposed they are to drone warfare — and how quickly a regional shadow war can claim lives far from any battlefield.

articles.title: The US has authorized SpaceX to launch up to 1 million satellites
articles.description: The United States has authorized SpaceX to launch up to one million satellites, a staggering expansion of its Starlink fleet that would rival the entire satellite industry combined. The scale of the plan has raised concerns about orbital crowding and astronomy.
articles.body: The United States has authorized SpaceX to launch up to one million satellites, a staggering expansion of its Starlink constellation that would rival the entire satellite industry combined. The authorisation, from the Federal Communications Commission, would let SpaceX grow a fleet that already numbers in the thousands into something on a wholly different scale — a mesh of satellites beaming internet to every corner of the planet. The scale has raised concerns among astronomers, who warn that so many satellites will crowd the night sky and interfere with telescopes, and among space-safety experts, who worry about collisions and debris in already busy orbits. Supporters say the expansion would bring connectivity to places terrestrial networks will never reach, and that SpaceX's satellites are designed to deorbit safely. The authorisation does not mean a million satellites will launch tomorrow — building and launching them would take years and billions of dollars — but it removes the regulatory ceiling on the most ambitious space project ever attempted.

articles.title: The head of the company behind GTA VI says he has a 'responsibility to society'
articles.description: Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick says he has a 'responsibility to society' as the company behind Grand Theft Auto VI, the most anticipated game in history, prepares for release. The comments come as the game's launch dominates the charts and the culture.
articles.body: Strauss Zelnick, the chief executive of Take-Two Interactive, the company behind Grand Theft Auto VI, says he has a 'responsibility to society' as the most anticipated game in history heads for release. The comment is striking from the head of a company whose flagship franchise is built on crime, violence and satire — and it shows how seriously Take-Two is taking the cultural weight of a launch that is already dominating the charts and the conversation. GTA VI has posted the biggest launch of the generation in the UK physical sales chart, and its soundtrack rollout has sent songs like Carly Rae Jepsen's 'Run Away With Me' surging on streaming. Zelnick's remarks suggest Take-Two knows the game will be judged not just as entertainment but as a cultural event, with politicians, parents and pundits all watching. Whether the industry's biggest launch can also be its most responsible is a question the game itself will have to answer.

articles.title: Alleged Russia-directed sabotage incidents are spreading across Europe
articles.description: Alleged Russia-directed sabotage incidents are spreading across Europe, with investigators hunting for the network behind a spate of attacks in the UK, Denmark and beyond. The campaign is part of the shadow war running alongside the fighting in Ukraine.
articles.body: Alleged Russia-directed sabotage incidents are spreading across Europe, with investigators hunting for the network behind a spate of attacks in the UK, Denmark and beyond. The incidents — fires, damaged infrastructure and other covert attacks — are part of a shadow war that has run alongside the fighting in Ukraine, and European intelligence agencies have increasingly blamed Moscow for orchestrating them through proxies and recruited operatives. The spread of the incidents shows the campaign is not confined to one country or one target: it is a pattern, and European governments are now treating it as a sustained effort to destabilise the continent and punish support for Ukraine. Attribution is difficult by design — the attacks are meant to be deniable — but the accumulation of cases has hardened the consensus in European capitals that Russia is behind them. For the public, the sabotage campaign is a reminder that the war in Ukraine has a European front that is quieter but very real, fought in warehouses, rail yards and undersea cables.

articles.title: UPDATE: Donations pour in so marching band can still play Saturday's postponed Macy's parade
articles.description: UPDATE: The director of a band that was set to play in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade says a slew of donations will allow them to perform on Saturday, after the parade was postponed for the first time in its history. The outpouring followed the storm-forced move.
articles.body: UPDATE: The director of a marching band that was set to play in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade says a slew of donations will allow the band to perform on Saturday, after the parade was postponed for the first time in its history. The postponement — forced by the nor'easter's heavy rain and strong winds — left bands, dancers and performers who had travelled to New York facing the prospect of missing their moment entirely, with hotels, travel and rehearsal costs already sunk. The donations, which poured in after the postponement was announced, will cover the extra day's costs and let the band take its place in Saturday's rescheduled parade, which now starts at 8:30 a.m. ET. It is a small, warm story inside a grim weather day: a community rallying so that teenagers who practised for months still get to march down Sixth Avenue. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani will not attend Saturday's parade because of scheduled foot surgery, but for the band, the show — a day late — will go on.

articles.title: ATC Music Group to acquire UK's One Media IP for $20M, secures conditional facility of up to $133M to buy more music rights
articles.description: ATC Music Group is acquiring the UK's One Media IP for $20 million and has secured a conditional facility of up to $133 million from Corrum Capital to buy more music rights. The deal is the latest in a busy year of music-rights consolidation.
articles.body: ATC Music Group is acquiring the UK's One Media IP for $20 million, and has secured a conditional facility of up to $133 million from Corrum Capital to fund further purchases of music rights. The deal pairs a straightforward catalogue acquisition with a much larger war chest, signalling that ATC intends to keep buying. One Media IP holds a catalogue of music rights, and the acquisition gives ATC more repertoire to work with across its artist services and rights businesses. The Corrum Capital facility, conditional on further deals, is the kind of debt financing that has powered the music-rights gold rush of recent years, as buyers bet that proven catalogues generate steady returns. For the industry, the announcement is a reminder that consolidation has not slowed: even in a year dominated by AI lawsuits and streaming economics, money is still flowing into owning the rights themselves.

articles.title: Israeli producer sues Travis Scott, Don Toliver and Sony Music over 2019 JackBoys track 'What To Do?'
articles.description: Israeli producer Niv Kalisky, who records as Early Yellow, is suing Travis Scott, Don Toliver and Sony Music over the 2019 JackBoys track 'What To Do?', claiming it was built on his recording 'Moazin99bpm' and that he has not been paid any master royalties in nearly seven years.
articles.body: Israeli producer Niv Kalisky, who works as Early Yellow, is suing Travis Scott, Don Toliver and Sony Music over the 2019 JackBoys track 'What To Do?'. Kalisky claims the track was built on a recording of his called 'Moazin99bpm', and that he has not been paid any master royalties for its use in the nearly seven years since 'What To Do?' was released. The suit is the latest in a long line of sampling disputes in hip-hop, where a beat or loop can travel from an obscure producer's hard drive onto a hit record without credit or payment. For Kalisky, the case is about seven years of missing royalties on a track that has streamed for years as part of the JackBoys project. For the industry, it is another reminder of how murky clearance can be when music moves fast and globally — and how producers with no leverage can wait years before taking a claim to court.

articles.title: Disney sued by NFL agent Zac Hiller's LAA Music over alleged use of unlicensed music in promos
articles.description: Disney is being sued by NFL agent Zac Hiller's LAA Music, which alleges the company used unlicensed music in ESPN, Hulu, Disney Parks and FX social media promos. The complaint says all seven videos came down after notices were sent, and that Disney blamed an unnamed 'Dutch company' for two of them.
articles.body: Disney is being sued by LAA Music, the company of NFL agent Zac Hiller, over the alleged use of unlicensed music in social media promos for ESPN, Hulu, Disney Parks and FX. The complaint says all seven videos at issue were taken down after the plaintiffs sent notices, and that Disney blamed an unnamed 'Dutch company' for two of them. The case is a classic sync-licensing dispute: music used in promotional videos needs a licence, and when the licence is missing the rights holder can sue even a company as big as Disney. For Disney, the embarrassment is compounded by the takedowns themselves, which amount to an admission that the videos should not have been up. For the wider industry, the suit is part of a wave of litigation over unlicensed music use — from Coachella suing Walmart over festival merch to Baltimore suing Vivid Seats over ticket pricing — in which rights holders are increasingly willing to take big names to court.

articles.title: With friends like these: Suno and MiniMax team up
articles.description: Suno and MiniMax are teaming up, in a partnership between two AI music companies that have both faced the music industry's wrath. The alliance, examined in a new MBW op-ed, comes as Suno faces a widening wave of copyright lawsuits.
articles.body: Suno and MiniMax have teamed up, in a partnership between two AI companies that sit at the centre of the music industry's fight over generative AI. The alliance is examined in a new MBW op-ed by Victoria Furniss, chief executive of the Alliance for Responsible Innovation in the Arts and Media, who frames it as a moment of consolidation among the companies the industry is suing. Suno is facing a growing stack of copyright cases — from the majors, and now from a widening class action led by Jason Isbell that this week added The Chicks and 16 more plaintiffs and took aim at Suno's v6 model. MiniMax, the Chinese AI firm behind the Hailuo music tools, has drawn its own criticism from rights holders. For the two companies, joining forces is a way to pool technology and present a united front. For the industry, it is a sign that the AI music firms are not retreating under legal pressure — they are organising, and the fight over training data, licensing and artist consent is set to run for years.

articles.title: UMG and Sony end court fight to make DistroKid hand over data on its AI-detection tool in Suno lawsuit
articles.description: Universal Music Group and Sony Music are ending their court fight to force DistroKid to hand over data on its AI-detection tool for their copyright lawsuit against Suno, after the distributor produced the material. The majors told a Manhattan federal court they are withdrawing the motion.
articles.body: Universal Music Group and Sony Music Entertainment are ending their court fight to make DistroKid hand over data on its AI-detection tool, after the distributor produced the material for their copyright lawsuit against Suno. The two majors told a federal court in Manhattan on November 16 that they are withdrawing their motion because DistroKid has now handed over documents covering the two requests still in dispute, weeks after refusing to produce them. The dispute was a sideshow to the main event — the majors' lawsuit accusing Suno of training its AI on copyrighted recordings without permission — but it mattered because DistroKid's AI-detection tool is one of the ways the industry tries to tell human music from machine-made tracks. With the documents now in hand, the majors can get on with building their case against Suno itself, which has only grown since: a separate class action led by Jason Isbell has added The Chicks and 16 more plaintiffs and now targets Suno's v6 model. The DistroKid episode shows how the AI lawsuits are pulling in companies across the music supply chain, not just the AI firms themselves.

articles.title: Brandi Carlile says the 'horror' of ICE arrests at Seattle airport 'cannot be overstated'
articles.description: Brandi Carlile has said the 'horror' of the ICE arrests at Seattle airport 'cannot be overstated', adding her voice to the artists condemning the operation. The Washington-raised singer is the second major Seattle-area artist to speak out in a day.
articles.body: Brandi Carlile has said the 'horror' of the ICE arrests at Seattle airport 'cannot be overstated', in a statement that makes her the second major Seattle-area artist to condemn the operation in a day. Carlile, raised in Washington state and one of the most respected voices in Americana, did not mince words: the arrests at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, she said, are horrifying in a way that is hard to overstate. Her statement follows Pearl Jam's condemnation of the same arrests as 'unconscionable', and together the two interventions turn a local enforcement story into a national one. Carlile has a long record of speaking out on social issues, from LGBTQ+ rights to refugee support, and her voice carries weight with an audience that spans country, folk and pop. The twin statements from Pearl Jam and Carlile show how quickly artists are now willing to mobilise — and how the immigration debate has moved from the political pages onto the music pages.

articles.title: Seal returns favor, covers Tame Impala's 'New Person, Same Old Mistakes'
articles.description: Seal has covered Tame Impala's 'New Person, Same Old Mistakes', returning the favour after years of mutual admiration between the British soul star and Kevin Parker's band. The cover reworks the Currents standout in Seal's unmistakable voice.
articles.body: Seal has released a cover of Tame Impala's 'New Person, Same Old Mistakes', returning the favour in a long-running mutual admiration between the British soul star and Kevin Parker's band. The track, a standout from Tame Impala's 2015 album Currents, is a slow-burning psychedelic soul song that has always sounded like it was waiting for a voice like Seal's — and his version leans into the song's warmth and ache. The cover is the kind of cross-generational collaboration that thrives on streaming: an established star reinterpreting a modern classic, introducing it to his audience while giving Tame Impala's fans a new way into a song they already love. It also lands in a week when Tame Impala are everywhere in the charts conversation, with JENNIE's 'Dracula' collaboration holding at No. 3 on the Hot 100. For Seal, whose career has spanned soul, pop and electronic music, the cover is a reminder of a voice that still stops a room.

articles.title: Thomas Markle indicted on charges of having child sex abuse material
articles.description: Thomas Markle, the father of the Duchess of Sussex, has been indicted on charges of having child sex abuse material. The indictment is a shocking turn for a man who has been a tabloid fixture since his daughter's marriage into the royal family.
articles.body: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been indicted on charges of having child sex abuse material. The indictment marks a grave and shocking turn for a man who has been a tabloid fixture since his daughter married Prince Harry, giving interviews and making headlines for years. Details of the charges beyond the indictment itself have not been widely reported, and it is not yet clear where the case was brought or what the next steps will be. The news will inevitably be read through the prism of the royal family's long and fractious relationship with Markle, who was estranged from his daughter before the wedding and has remained a source of public embarrassment for the Sussexes. But the charges, if proven, would stand on their own as a serious criminal matter, far removed from the family drama that has defined his public image.

articles.title: Carly Rae Jepsen's 'Run Away With Me' sees 288 percent streaming bump thanks to 'GTA VI'
