articles.body: The Mechanical Licensing Collective has now distributed more than $4.4 billion in total royalties to songwriters, music publishers and other rightsholders since launching in January 2021, and its membership has passed 110,000, CEO Kris Ahrend tells Music Business Worldwide in a new interview. The MLC collects mechanical royalties from streaming and download services in the US under a blanket license created by the Music Modernization Act of 2018. At its annual membership meeting in September, the MLC announced it will begin distributing its remaining unclaimed accrued royalties on a market-share basis in April 2027, the first time it will use the payout mechanism written into the Act. The royalties are ones the MLC collected but could not match to a song, or for which not every ownership share has been claimed; the Act requires holding them for at least three years. It will start with January 2021 usage, which had just over $6 million remaining as of September, then work through the rest of 2021 one month at a time. Ahrend says tens of thousands of rightsholders who previously were not collecting their digital mechanical royalties in the US are now doing so, and the MLC has added more than 36,000 members so far this year. His priorities for the next five years include deeper engagement with members and songwriters through better tools, including a planned feature letting writers flag data problems directly to their publishers, and using AI to tackle longstanding structural issues in music publishing. He also wants distributors and other upstream actors to do far more to check the recordings and data they put into the market, to ease royalty processing and help prevent fraud. The MLC remains in litigation with Spotify over the streamer's 2024 decision to reclassify Premium subscriptions as bundles with audiobooks; a judge sided with Spotify on the bundling question in January 2025, but the MLC's amended suit continues, and Spotify estimates it could owe around $619 million for March 2024 to September 2026 if the MLC prevails on appeal. The MLC also works with more than 100 collecting societies worldwide, distributing royalties to songwriters in more than 125 countries.

articles.title: Mary Bono asks appeals court to overturn Cher's win in Sonny Bono song royalties fight, arguing Cher already received nearly fifty years of royalties
articles.description: Mary Bono, the widow of Sonny Bono, has asked an appeals court to overturn Cher's win in the long-running fight over royalties from Sonny Bono's songs. She argues Cher has already received nearly fifty years of royalties, and that Sonny could not sign away rights that did not exist during his lifetime. The filing cites Cher's own testimony: I should get what I've always gotten.
articles.body: Mary Bono, the widow of Sonny Bono, has asked an appeals court to overturn Cher's victory in the long-running dispute over royalties from Sonny Bono's songs, arguing that Cher has already received nearly fifty years of royalties. Mary Bono's case is that Sonny could not sign away rights that did not exist in his lifetime, so the royalties at issue should not flow to Cher under the terms she claims. The filing also cites Cher's own testimony in the case, in which she said: I should get what I've always gotten. The appeal is the latest turn in a dispute over the song catalog of Sonny Bono, the singer-songwriter and former husband and musical partner of Cher, whose songs include some of the duo's best-known work. The fight turns on how publishing and royalty rights in those songs were divided, and on whether later changes to copyright law created rights that could be claimed decades after the original agreements. Cher had won the earlier round of the royalties fight, and Mary Bono is now asking the appeals court to reverse that outcome. The case is being watched in the music business as a test of how far legacy royalty arrangements stretch when copyright law changes after an artist's death, and of how courts weigh decades of payments already made against claims for more.

articles.title: Rolling Stone names the 200 best songs of the 1990s, with Nirvana's 'Smells Like Teen Spirit' at No. 1
articles.description: Rolling Stone has published its ranking of the 200 best songs of the 1990s, topped by Nirvana's Smells Like Teen Spirit. The list allows only one song per artist, and runs from Digital Underground's The Humpty Dance at No. 200 to the Notorious B.I.G.'s Juicy at No. 3 and Missy Elliott's The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly) at No. 5. Rob Sheffield called the No. 1 pick the song that blew up the world.
articles.body: Rolling Stone has published its list of the 200 best songs of the 1990s, with Nirvana's Smells Like Teen Spirit taking the top spot. The ranking allows just one song per artist, which forced some hard choices across a decade packed with era-defining hits. The Notorious B.I.G.'s Juicy came in at No. 3, followed by Missy Elliott's The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly) at No. 5, while TLC's No Scrubs placed at No. 17, Alanis Morissette's You Oughta Know at No. 24 and Britney Spears' ...Baby One More Time at No. 33. Further down the list, 2Pac's California Love landed at No. 72, Pearl Jam's Daughter at No. 61, Green Day's Basket Case at No. 112, Cher's Believe at No. 120 and Tori Amos' Cornflake Girl at No. 167, with Digital Underground's The Humpty Dance closing the countdown at No. 200. Writing about the No. 1 pick, Rob Sheffield called Smells Like Teen Spirit the song that blew up the world, the song that defied all rules about how music worked and how much raw emotion you could cram into three cheap chords and a crummy guitar solo. He described it as the rebel-punk anthem that killed off Eighties schlock rock overnight and kicked off a decade of wide-open possibilities, arguing it still hits home because Kurt Cobain is daring listeners to dream bigger, demand more and fight harder. The list arrives as Rolling Stone continues its run of decade rankings and canon lists, which reliably spark debate among readers over omissions and ordering.

articles.title: U2 will bring their 'Greatest Show on Earth' stadium tour to North America in 2027
articles.description: U2 have announced the North American leg of their Carnaval De Luz Presents: The Greatest Show On Earth world tour, a 15-night stadium run from August 13 in Miami to October 18 in Vancouver. It is the band's first major tour since the Joshua Tree anniversary tour ended in 2019, and includes two nights at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, on August 26 and 28. General sale starts December 4 via Ticketmaster.
articles.body: U2 will bring their Greatest Show on Earth stadium tour to North America in 2027, the band announced, marking their first worldwide tour in eight years and their first major tour since the Joshua Tree anniversary tour ended in 2019. The 15-night North American run opens August 13 at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami and closes October 18 at BC Place in Vancouver, with stops in Atlanta, Baltimore, Chicago, Toronto, Foxborough, Arlington, Los Angeles, Las Vegas and Santa Clara. The routing includes two nights apiece at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, on August 26 and 28, Rogers Stadium in Toronto on September 7 and 9, and SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles on October 1 and 2. The War on Drugs and Stephen Wilson Jr. will split opening duties. The tour supports Carnaval De Luz, U2's 16th studio album and their first new material since 2017's Songs of Experience, which was released on November 13 and debuted at No. 4 on the Billboard 200. The band has shared a first look at the stage production, featuring an enormous red curtain, two walkways extending into the audience and giant depictions of the sun and moon. Drummer Larry Mullen Jr. returns to touring with the band after undergoing surgery. Subscriber presale launches November 30 at 10 a.m. local time at U2.com, followed by a Visa cardholder presale on December 2 and an artist presale on December 3, with registration for the artist presale open through November 29 at 9 p.m. ET. General sale begins December 4 at 10 a.m. local time through Ticketmaster. The North American dates follow shows in Mexico City, Sao Paulo and Buenos Aires in February and March, and an extensive UK and European stadium tour including four sold-out nights at London's Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in June.

articles.title: Brandi Carlile and Pearl Jam condemn ICE arrests at Seattle airport
articles.description: Brandi Carlile and Pearl Jam have condemned the detention of a father and daughter by masked ICE officers at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Sunday, November 22. Carlile posted a letter to her 1.5 million Instagram followers calling the video horrific and urging donations to immigrant-support groups, while Pearl Jam called the arrests unconscionable and the product of a system driven by cold cruelty.
articles.body: Brandi Carlile and Pearl Jam have publicly condemned the detention of a father and daughter by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Sunday, November 22. The two, identified as Sofia Hernandez Meija and her father Ricardo Larrondo Mendo, both Mexican nationals, were arrested as they boarded a flight, allegedly for overstaying their visas, and video of the detention spread widely. On Tuesday, Carlile posted a letter to her 1.5 million Instagram followers, writing that she had seen the horrific video of a father and daughter being violently detained, and that the horror and heartache she felt watching it, hearing their cries of desperation and fear, cannot be overstated. The Washington-born singer-songwriter noted that many people will be travelling across the US for the Thanksgiving holiday, and urged followers to channel their distress into action by donating to her Looking Out Foundation and other organizations working to protect immigrants, or by calling their representatives and asking them to abolish ICE. Earlier in the week, Seattle-founded Pearl Jam issued a statement saying it is heartbreaking and infuriating to watch the human toll of a system driven by cold cruelty, and describing a family torn apart and dragged off a jetway in their own airport by masked individuals as unconscionable. The band said it stands firmly against this kind of inhumane treatment. The arrests have renewed outrage and protests against ICE, and the musicians' interventions add two of the Pacific Northwest's biggest acts to the public criticism of the enforcement operation.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo shares heartache for the holidays with 'Miss This Christmas' live debut
articles.description: Olivia Rodrigo performed her new sad Christmas song miss this christmas live for the first time on Monday, November 23, at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville. The track is the B-side of the vinyl version of her first holiday single, take me home (4 christmas), and has not yet been released digitally. Produced by Dan Nigro with the MUSYCA Children's Choir, it is the melancholy counterpart to the upbeat A-side.
articles.body: Olivia Rodrigo gave her new holiday song miss this christmas its live debut on Monday night, November 23, at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, the first of two shows in the city on her Unraveled Tour. The track is the B-side of the 7-inch vinyl edition of take me home (4 christmas), her first original holiday single, released on November 5, and it has not yet had a wide digital release. Introducing the song, Rodrigo told the crowd she had written a really happy A-side about her fantasy of having a boyfriend who takes her to his parents' house for the holidays, and a really sad Christmas song to go on the B-side, which nobody had really heard before. Produced by longtime collaborator Dan Nigro and featuring the MUSYCA Children's Choir, miss this christmas is a melancholy portrait of spending the holidays without someone who once made the season feel different. The Nashville set drew 12 songs from her third album, you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love, along with five each from GUTS and SOUR, with Devon Again opening the show. Rodrigo's Nashville visit also included two intimate live-to-acetate sets at Jack White's Third Man Records Blue Room on Sunday, November 22, where she recorded a cover of the White Stripes' Dead Leaves and the Dirty Ground. She returns to Bridgestone Arena for a second Nashville concert on Tuesday, before heading to Vancouver for two nights on December 1 and 2 and then down the West Coast. The debut gives fans a first live hearing of a song that, for now, exists only on the physical release of her holiday single.

articles.title: Nick Carter loses bid to dismiss sexual battery claim from Melissa Schuman
articles.description: A Los Angeles County judge has rejected Backstreet Boys singer Nick Carter's bid to dismiss a sexual battery claim brought by singer and former Dream member Melissa Schuman. Judge Lisa K. Sepe-Wiesenfeld ruled the claim can proceed under a California law that took effect January 1, opening a two-year revival window for otherwise time-barred adult sexual abuse claims. A trial is set for May 10, 2027.
articles.body: A Los Angeles County judge has rejected Backstreet Boys singer Nick Carter's bid to dismiss a sexual battery claim brought by singer and actress Melissa Schuman, clearing the way for the case to head to trial. In a ruling issued Monday and obtained by Rolling Stone, Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Lisa K. Sepe-Wiesenfeld said the claim could proceed under a California law that took effect January 1, opening a two-year revival window for otherwise time-barred claims of adult sexual abuse against individual perpetrators. Unlike the law in effect when Schuman first sued Carter, the new statute allows lawsuits against individuals without requiring plaintiffs to establish a cover-up or name a business as a defendant. The judge wrote that the individual claim against Carter for sexual battery is proper irrespective of the existence of a cover-up, and that there is a conflict in the evidence presented as to whether a sexual assault occurred, meaning a triable issue of material fact is present. Schuman first sued Carter in April 2023, alleging he raped her at his Santa Monica home in 2003, when she was 18 and he was 23. Carter denies the allegations and maintains their relationship was consensual, and he has filed a $2.5 million cross-complaint against Schuman. Carter had sought to dismiss the claim by attacking the alleged cover-up in her complaint, arguing at a November 6 hearing that her only proof of a cover-up came from Shannon Ruth, who alleges Carter sexually assaulted her on a tour bus outside the Tacoma Dome in Washington in 2001. After taking two weeks to consider the arguments, the judge ruled in Schuman's favor. Schuman's lawyers, Guinness Costello and Jamie Majerus, praised the decision, saying she first stepped forward in 2017 and has waited almost a decade to put her case before a jury. The ruling does not decide whether the allegations are true, only that the claim can be tested in court, with trial set for May 10, 2027.

articles.title: Bob Seger and the Silver Bullet Band bassist Chris Campbell dead at 78
articles.description: Chris Campbell, the longtime bassist for Bob Seger and the Silver Bullet Band, has died at 78. His wife Courtney confirmed to Rolling Stone that he died of natural causes on Sunday, November 22. Campbell joined Seger in 1969 as a fill-in and stayed through the farewell tour in 2019, playing on hits including Night Moves, Against the Wind and Turn the Page.
articles.body: Chris Campbell, the longtime bassist for Bob Seger and the Silver Bullet Band, has died at the age of 78. His death was announced by former bandmate Jim Moose Brown on Sunday, November 22, and his wife Courtney later confirmed to Rolling Stone that he died of natural causes. Campbell's career with Seger began in 1969, when he was hired as what he thought was a temporary fill-in bassist after Bob Seger System bassist Dan Honaker broke his wrist in a motorcycle accident just before the Mongrel tour. He was recalled when Seger put the Silver Bullet Band together in the early 1970s and remained a core member for five decades, through Seger's farewell tour in 2019. Fans can hear his playing on timeless hits including Turn the Page, Night Moves, Rock and Roll Never Forgets, Still the Same, Hollywood Nights and Against the Wind, and on classic albums such as Stranger in Town from 1978 and Against the Wind from 1980. In a 2011 interview with Rolling Stone he said of his life in the band: This is my life, and I'm very happy with it. He added that the group were all friends, that Seger was their rock and patriarch, and that he was easy to work with. Two years after the farewell tour, Campbell sued Seger and longtime manager Punch Andrews over royalties he said he was owed, and lost his claims over recording royalties. Silver Bullet Band vocalist Shaun Murphy paid tribute, writing that she was grieving the loss of her longtime friend and bandmate and offering prayers to his wife and three daughters. Campbell was born in Detroit and raised in nearby Plymouth, Michigan, and his half-century run with Seger made him one of the most durable sidemen in American rock.

articles.title: Karol G returns to No. 1 on the Global 200 for a seventh week
articles.description: Karol G is back at No. 1 on the Billboard Global 200 with BbY WOW, her collaboration with Judeline and Rusowsky, marking the song's seventh nonconsecutive week at the top. Tate McRae's Housewife, which held No. 1 for four weeks, falls to No. 3. Holiday classics are also climbing the global charts as the season approaches.
articles.body: Karol G has returned to No. 1 on the Billboard Global 200 with BbY WOW, her collaboration with Judeline and Rusowsky, marking the song's seventh nonconsecutive week at the top of the worldwide chart. According to Billboard's latest chart update, published November 25, the track reclaims the leading position as Tate McRae's Housewife moves down to No. 3 after four weeks at No. 1. The Global 200 ranks songs based on streaming activity and digital sales across international markets, giving a snapshot of music consumption worldwide. Karol G's return to the summit underlines the staying power of BbY WOW, which has now spent seven weeks at No. 1 across separate runs, a rare feat on a chart where turnover at the top is usually fast. The change at the top also ends McRae's four-week run with Housewife, which had been one of the defining global hits of the autumn. Meanwhile, holiday classics are gaining momentum across the global charts, with Wham!'s Last Christmas and Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You climbing as listeners return to their favorite seasonal songs ahead of the holidays. The festive surge mirrors the US charts, where the same songs are storming the Hot 100's top 10. Karol G's chart-topping return caps a strong year for Latin music on the global charts, with the Colombian star remaining one of the most consistent hitmakers in the format.

articles.title: UPDATE: Holiday songs storm the Hot 100 top 10 as Ella Langley extends her record run to 29 weeks
articles.description: Three holiday songs have surged into the Hot 100's top 10 on the chart dated November 28: Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You jumps 18-4, Wham!'s Last Christmas climbs 14-5 and Bobby Helms' Jingle Bell Rock rises 28-9. Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas still leads for a record-extending 29th week, tying Drake for the most weeks at No. 1 by an artist in a single year, and its 50th week atop Hot Country Songs ties the all-time record.
articles.body: The holiday season has arrived early on the Billboard Hot 100, with three Christmas songs surging into the top 10 on the chart dated November 28. Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You jumps 18-4, the earliest point in November the perennial smash has ever cracked the chart's top five, followed by Wham!'s Last Christmas climbing 14-5 and Bobby Helms' Jingle Bell Rock rising 28-9. Carey totaled 13.5 million streams in the tracking week, and the carol is the No. 1 hit on Billboard's Greatest of All Time Holiday 100 Songs retrospective. Still, Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas continues to lead the Hot 100 for a record-extending 29th week, boosted by the 60th Annual Country Music Association Awards on November 18, where Langley won six trophies, the most in a single night. The smash totaled 16.9 million official streams, 45.5 million radio airplay audience impressions and 6,000 sold in the US in the week of November 13-19, and it holds atop both Streaming Songs and Digital Song Sales for a record-extending 28th and 22nd week respectively. Langley's 29 weeks at No. 1 in 2026 tie her with Drake for the most by an artist in a single year. The song also claims a 50th week at No. 1 on the Hot Country Songs chart, tying the all-time mark set by Bebe Rexha and Florida Georgia Line's Meant to Be. The chart's longest-leading hits since 1958 now read: 29 weeks for Choosin' Texas, 22 for All I Want for Christmas Is You, and 19 each for Shaboozey's A Bar Song (Tipsy) and Lil Nas X's Old Town Road. With three holiday songs in the top 10 before December, the festive takeover is running weeks ahead of its usual pace.

articles.title: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping soundtrack debuts at No. 1 on the Soundtracks chart
articles.description: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (The Album) debuts at No. 1 on Billboard's Soundtracks chart, the franchise's third chart-topping soundtrack after the 2012 and 2013 albums. The 29-track set, released November 13 via MCA and executive produced by Dave Cobb, also enters the Billboard 200 at No. 13. It features Noah Kahan, the Smashing Pumpkins, Stevie Nicks, Kacey Musgraves, Ella Langley and Jennifer Lawrence.
articles.body: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (The Album) has debuted at No. 1 on Billboard's Soundtracks chart, the franchise's third leader on the list after The Hunger Games: Songs From District 12 and Beyond in 2012 and The Hunger Games: Catching Fire in 2013. The set also enters the Billboard 200 at No. 13. Released on November 13 via MCA, a week before the film reached theaters on November 20, the 29-track album is executive produced by Grammy-winning producer Dave Cobb, who told Billboard the through line of all of it is honesty. The lineup runs from Noah Kahan's lead single Draw You Out, co-written with Aaron Dessner, to the Smashing Pumpkins' Black Stars, Gigi Perez's Favor and Lizzy McAlpine's The Wheel, alongside contributions from Stevie Nicks, Kacey Musgraves, Ella Langley with Here Then We're Gone, Noah Cyrus, Stephen Wilson Jr. and Violet Grohl. The film's stars also feature: Whitney Peak opens the album with The Raven I, McKenna Grace contributes Half Alive, and Jennifer Lawrence returns with a new version of Deep in the Meadow, first featured on the Mockingjay Part 2 soundtrack. The Cure close the set with a live version of Alone, recorded in Berlin in 2022. The album mixes country, Americana, indie and rock, continuing the franchise's habit of pairing Panem with the music of its moment, and its chart-topping debut shows the series' soundtracks remain a commercial force more than a decade after the first film.

articles.title: Robert Glasper on the state of R&B, Kendrick Lamar's 'To Pimp a Butterfly' and why AI can't copy this
articles.description: Five-time Grammy winner Robert Glasper has spoken to Billboard about genre boundaries, Kendrick Lamar's landmark 2015 album To Pimp a Butterfly and artificial intelligence. He says the industry is catching up on letting artists blend genres, recalls recording piano for eight songs on the Lamar album in less than an hour, and argues AI cannot reproduce the human mistakes that make music feel real.
articles.body: Five-time Grammy winner Robert Glasper has opened up to Billboard about the changing musical landscape, the importance of originality and why he believes AI cannot copy what makes human music special. Glasper, whose career as a pianist has bridged jazz, hip-hop, R&B and soul, says the industry is becoming more open to artists embracing multiple influences, even if the evolution is unfinished. I feel like it's catching up, he said. We're not all the way there, but I think that door is open to where people are more open to exploring different genres of music and artists not feeling like they have to be a monolithic thing. He drew a line between great musicians and the rarer artists who redirect the culture, naming Erykah Badu and Kendrick Lamar as people who moved the needle by arriving with a different sound and a different outlook that changed generations. His connection to Lamar's work is personal: he contributed piano to the critically acclaimed 2015 album To Pimp a Butterfly, recording parts for eight songs in less than an hour, with Lamar giving him the freedom to listen to each track and play whatever he felt was right. He also explained why Lamar chose not to feature mainstream pop stars on the album after the success of Good Kid, M.A.A.D City, instead inviting what Glasper calls the heroes, respected musicians such as Bilal and Lalah Hathaway. On AI, Glasper said he is not worried about what the technology means for his craft: AI can't make mistakes, and I think that's what makes humans human. The imperfection is what makes humans human, and the imperfections are the things I feel are the sweet spots in music in general. He also discussed upcoming film-scoring projects, including Miles and Juliet and Don't Ever Wonder 2, and praised H.E.R. as an artist who excites him, while noting that much modern R&B can sound the same and the industry often values what is easiest to market over musicianship.

articles.title: Metallica wrap their 2026 touring year with first Connecticut show in 28 years
articles.description: Metallica wrapped up their 2026 touring year on Saturday at Mohegan Sun Arena in Connecticut, their first show in the state in 28 years. The band return to the Sphere in Las Vegas in January before a final North American tour leg in May.
articles.body: Metallica have wrapped up their 2026 touring year, closing the run on Saturday at Mohegan Sun Arena in Connecticut, their first show in the state in 28 years. The Connecticut date marked the end of a year on the road for the metal giants, who have spent much of 2026 touring behind their current live cycle. The band are not standing still for long: they return to the Sphere in Las Vegas in January, resuming their residency-style run at the venue, before a final North American tour leg in May. The Sphere shows have become a major draw for the band, pairing their arena-scale production with the venue's immersive visuals, while the May leg will close out the current touring chapter in North America. The Mohegan Sun finale also underlined the band's enduring drawing power more than four decades into their career, with the Connecticut return itself a notable event for fans in a state the band had not played in nearly three decades. Details of the January Sphere dates and the May leg are expected to be confirmed as the band's touring plans firm up.

articles.title: This week's other Billboard chart leaders: Latto and Doja Cat, almost monday, Grupo Firme and DJ Mau P
articles.description: Beyond the Hot 100 and Billboard 200, this week's Billboard charts dated November 28 bring fresh No. 1s across the formats: Latto and Doja Cat top Rhythmic Airplay with Okayyy, almost monday lead Alternative Airplay with No More Regrets, Grupo Firme collect a 14th Regional Mexican Airplay crown, DJ Mau P pick up a fourth Dance Airplay No. 1, and Bruno Mars earn a third Adult Contemporary leader with I Just Might. Michelle Branch and New Radicals also push their updated The Game of Love into the Adult Pop Airplay top 10.
articles.body: Billboard's charts dated November 28, reflecting the November 13-19 tracking week, brought a crop of new No. 1s across the radio formats. Latto and Doja Cat claim the Rhythmic Airplay crown with their collaboration Okayyy, while almost monday secure an Alternative Airplay leader with No More Regrets. Grupo Firme collect their 14th Regional Mexican Airplay No. 1 with Al Final del Día, extending one of the most consistent runs in the format, and DJ Mau P picks up his fourth Dance Airplay No. 1. Bruno Mars lands his third Adult Contemporary leader with I Just Might, adding another format No. 1 to a career built on crossing radio boundaries. Elsewhere, Michelle Branch and New Radicals push their updated collaboration of The Game of Love into the top 10 on Adult Pop Airplay, revisiting the 2003 hit more than two decades on. The format charts matter because they show where radio programmers are placing their bets week to week, and this week's spread, from Latin regional to dance to adult contemporary, captures how fragmented the current hit landscape is. Taken together with the album and singles charts, the week underlines a market in which established stars, Latin acts and left-field collaborations are all finding room at the top of their respective formats.

articles.title: What If We Told You She's a Mastermind? A Tale of Pop Stardom
articles.author: May Jeong
articles.description: The most talked-about magazine profile of the week: Vanity Fair spent a year and spoke to more than 100 people to tell two opposite versions of the Taylor Swift story — and never once prints her name. Whatever you think of Swift, the reporting, the structure and the backlash are a pop-culture event in themselves.
articles.body:
The piece is built like a record, with two sides telling the same life in opposite keys. On the A side, a child is born in 1989 and grows up on a Christmas tree farm south of Reading, Pennsylvania, destined for the stage. She plays Sandy in Grease, Kim in Bye Bye Birdie and Maria in The Sound of Music. A computer repairman teaches her guitar and she plays until her twelve-year-old fingers bleed. At fifteen she signs with a newly opened Nashville label, and it is soon clear she is a generational talent. Her name even seems to foretell her fate: the Latin root of celebrity is celere, meaning rapid, fast, swift. She has romances with celebrities, some of whom treat her badly, including a boy-band member who ends things in a twenty-seven-second phone call. Fame, remarkably, does not warp her the way it warps nearly everyone else. She doesn't even have a manager — what she has are many great friends. At twenty-nine, the Nashville record company betrays her by selling her life's work to her archnemesis's manager. She would have bought the rights to her own songs, only she was never given the chance. She appeals to her fans, who defend her, and with their support she wins her music back. By then she has met her shining knight, and after a happy and very public courtship, her English and gym teachers wed. When the curtain falls on humanity, the piece says, they will say that for a time she defined American sonic life — that her music owned the 2010s and the long 2020s.

The B side tells the same story with the gloss stripped off. The child grows up on an eleven-acre Christmas tree farm that her third-generation banker father bought from a client at Merrill Lynch, where he is a vice president managing a portfolio of around $270 million. When she is ten, the family moves to a 3,560-square-foot, five-bedroom Georgian Colonial in Wyomissing, Pennsylvania, which a visitor calls a six-star hotel. Her mother is, in the words of Sandy Carbone — whose son directed the young star in her school musicals — definitely a theater mom, very aggressive. Carbone's other son, computer repairman Ronnie Cremer, is asked to teach the girl a twelve-string guitar. She complains that the chords hurt her hands, and when Cremer passes this on, the parents reply: just keep working her, she needs this to get better. Once, during a lesson, the mother comes home with Taco Bell, but salad is the girl's lot — nobody wants to see a fat pop star, Cremer recalls the mother saying. Her father's connections get her singing the national anthem before a minor-league baseball game, which he videotapes and sends to a marketing manager for the Philadelphia 76ers, which is how she ends up singing the anthem for them. Four months into her guitar-playing career, her father is driving her to gigs, giving tickets away to business associates and asking them to cheer loudly so she always seems to be playing to a full house, taping the performances to send to Nashville before moving the family there. By 2006, the father has a stake in the Nashville record company after a reported $500,000 investment, according to Music Business Worldwide, and makes $15 million when it sells. In 2023 she becomes a billionaire on account of her tour, the highest-grossing of all time. Her fans do not mind. Of all the billionaires, one fan says, she is my favorite billionaire.

Across twelve eras and interviews with more than a hundred people — people who worked with her, who work with her, confidants, contemporaries, scholars, critics, rivals, neighbors, classmates, teachers and a lover — the piece argues that what emerges as the star's most enduring identity is not musician, not artist, not celebrity, but a combination of victim and victimizer. The dissenting chorus has its own folklore: that she often seems to present herself as persecuted even as she sits on a throne of gold and diamonds, that she has been known to crucify those who cross her, that she weaponizes her sense of victimhood. She is punitive, says a music-industry professional the piece calls The Exec. She loves to smack people in the head, figuratively, says a person familiar with the matter who used to be close to the star — a way of feeling like she can discipline people. The reporting itself becomes part of the story: a lawyer with knowledge of the star declined to be interviewed on their own phone and spoke through an intermediary; a manager asked for correspondence to be deleted; a pastor from her childhood church said they could not speak without express permission from the star's family; people who did speak of her in public did so softly, using initials. A Washington Post reporter who recently wrote a book about the star has noted that countless sources refused to go on the record even to say nice things. Someone who previously collaborated with the star advised the writer to turn down the assignment — did they think the star would read the article? Oh yes. The star's Manichaean notion of the world, according to a musician who toured with her and spoke from behind a nondisclosure agreement, means that if you are in the circle, she takes amazing care of you, and if you are not, you face social censure.

The profile then tests the star's own origin story. In a 2009 interview with Katie Couric, she said that when she was about twelve, a group of friends decided they didn't want to hang out with her anymore, and that when she sat down at the lunch table they would get up and move their trays to another table. That wasn't true, says Sharon Luyben, her music teacher for thirty-four years at Wyomissing Area Junior/Senior High: we had assigned seating in junior high. Chanice Skinner, who sat next to the star in Luyben's class, remembers her as always part of the popular crowd, among preppy kids who wore Ralph Lauren shirts with the collars popped. If you weren't part of her friend group, Skinner says, you didn't exist to her. Years later, watching a Target commercial in which the star talked about being bullied, Skinner thought: you were part of that — if anything, you were one of the bullies. Arielle Peppers, a year behind the star and on the other side of Skinner in class, remembers the star coming to school in Ugg boots — she had the brown one, the black one, the blue one. Peppers had transferred from nearby Reading after her neighbor was stabbed in the neck, and when she asked her mother for a pair of the same boots, her mother asked: do you know how much they cost? A pair of Uggs amounted to half her single mother's paycheck, earned variously at a bakery, a dairy mill and as a caretaker. The star's one teasing at school, Peppers recalls, came at a talent show, when she sang about her crush on a classmate called Corey — and won.

The B side then runs through the feuds. The masters saga: the label boss, called The Machine, tells the star he will part with her master recordings — accounting for fifty to eighty percent of the label's revenue — only if she agrees to make new music in exchange for old, the same bad deal that stymied Prince and Janet Jackson. A high-profile manager representing top talent hears the news and calls The Machine. On June 28, 2019, the board approves a sale giving the manager control of the masters, and two days later the star takes to Tumblr, accusing him of incessant, manipulative bullying. The manager says he met the star only three times. Her fans send him death threats; he relays this to her team and hears nothing back. She begins rerecording her old albums, depreciating the value of the originals enough to buy them all back eventually — a hitherto unprecedented feat, declared a victory for the people, and certainly a victory to the star, who, in making herself a metonym for all women, successfully equates criticism against her as criticism against womenkind. There is the pop star the piece calls The Brat, who opened for the star in 2018 and was platonically courted into her inner circle, then released a 2024 song about her insecurities around the world's biggest pop star — I couldn't even be her if I tried — and the star's apparent 2025 clapback accusing The Brat of consuming illegal substances. There is The Protégé, affiliated with the star until 2021, when she sent her debut album to the wife of the star's archnemesis, and later released a 2023 song that appeared to intimate a falling-out: trust that you betrayed, confusion that still lingers, took everything I loved and crushed it in between your fingers. There is The California Girl — an adult pretending to be a child, the piece says, while the star might be a child pretending to be an adult — and the Kardashian affair, whose details the piece says it is excluding. It's truly Regina George, The Exec says. There once lived a music critic who dared pan the star; after her negative review ran, her friends — professional musicians who had previously credited the critic for their early success — shunned her, and her roommate asked her to move out of their shared duplex. Nobody is beyond reproach with her, says The Person Familiar: if you don't see it her way, she comes after you. Even a sometimes close and dear friend, after their private correspondence spilled across the tabloids as part of a public lawsuit, was not seen at the star's wedding.

The piece closes with the wedding and a theory of stardom. The star's latest beau — regretfully called Redwood — brought a new intensity, a golden light, as they courted at a stadium show, a podcast interview, more shows, in Instagram posts. They have so much in common, the star points out: they both perform at stadiums. He practices; she rehearses. He plays games, she plays shows. Ahead of the wedding, the couple donates $26 million to local charities. Since then the star has released four new songs, launched an Oscar campaign and got a haircut. In the B-side telling, the world's most famous sexy baby — who insists she is really a monster on a hill — chooses as the site of her nuptials midtown Manhattan during a heat wave, her guests nibbling buffet food as thousands of New Yorkers lose power. The $26 million giveaway, apart from being a tax write-off, is akin to a person making $81,228 — the median household income in New York City — giving away $1,055. In fall 2025, when the article was commissioned, the star was worth $1.6 billion; by the time the issue goes to press she will be worth over $2 billion, or the GDP of Eritrea. Beyond need lies want, the piece concludes, quoting the star's ex Matty Healy on the deadening effects of modern wealth: beyond want, greed. And beyond greed was a tricked-out walled garden for the enchanted, her betrothed, and a thousand of their family and friends. Love may be free, the piece says, but the performance of it is not: it requires crates, trucks, officers on overtime, private jets, SUVs, HVACs, all the queen's horses, all the queen's men, a Jumbotron. The article ends by asking where the star might have learned to be so punitive — why, us, of course. Stars function, as the cultural theorist Stuart Hall observed, as a mirror. I want you to know I'm a mirrorball, the star sang in a 2020 hit: I'll show you every version of yourself tonight. If churches were once society's primary source of community, identity and meaning, the piece argues, in these secular times we turn instead to celebrities — and we look, especially, to singers, because who among us is immune to music? The piece is also laced with a hidden joke of its own: bolded capital letters scattered through the text spell out the title of her 2017 hit, Look What You Made Me Do, and it closes with the line: The Star's version was used in the making of this article.

articles.title: Inside Google's Failure to Make Google Maps Work for Palestinians
articles.author: Elena DeBre, Paresh Dave, Lama Rabah
articles.description: A joint investigation by WIRED, Lighthouse Reports, ARIJ and the Palestine Reporting Lab into how the world's most-used navigation app fails Palestinians in the West Bank — and the Google product manager who spent six years trying to fix it, only to watch the company undo his work.
articles.body:
One product manager made it his mission to accurately map Israeli checkpoints in the West Bank on the world's most popular navigation app. Then the company undid his work. That is the story WIRED tells in this investigation, reported with Lighthouse Reports, ARIJ and the Palestine Reporting Lab: a six-year effort inside Google to make Google Maps work for Palestinians, and the decision to roll it back.

The stakes are not abstract. Palestinian drivers in the West Bank face more than 900 Israeli military checkpoints, many of them guarded with lethal force, and for them navigation is a life-or-death issue: a wrong turn can mean being routed toward a checkpoint, a closed road, a wall, or a restricted area where they may face a dangerous encounter with Israeli authorities. Residents have long complained that missing and outdated data on Google Maps — including accurate information about road restrictions and street regulations — make the app unreliable and sometimes difficult to use, and the start of the war in Gaza in October 2025 made the problems worse. WIRED spoke with drivers who say the app sometimes leads users into traffic jams, walls and onto restricted roads, and in an earlier investigation in December 2024 the magazine documented users being directed toward the separation barrier, closed gates and roads they could not safely or practically use, with some trips between Palestinian cities returning no route at all.

At the center of the new investigation is Rubén Lozano, a former Google product manager who spent six years pushing for better maps. He built a prototype that mapped Israeli- and Palestinian-controlled areas and flagged checkpoints, using infrastructure Google had developed during Covid. Google eventually launched the update in late 2025, and the Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that Israeli drivers were being alerted when crossing into Area C. But weeks later, the company largely retracted it. By December 2025, Google confirmed to WIRED that it had pulled back important parts of the update. Interviews with current and former employees allege internal tensions and that Google abandoned the effort, leaving a map that harms Palestinians. Dozens of employees inside Google had been urging company leaders over the past year to make improvements to Google Maps that would benefit Palestinians, according to three current and former staffers involved in the advocacy or on the maps product team, who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Google's position, as stated to WIRED, is that it does not differentiate between Israeli and Palestinian roads, because doing so would require determining users' citizenship status. A Google spokesperson, Caroline Bourdeau, said that any claims of Google Maps showing bias in the region are false, and that the company has updated thousands of roads, street names, place names and postal codes in the West Bank and Gaza, adding about 5,000 miles of roads in the West Bank and Gaza since 2021, and launching an update in November 2024 intended to make West Bank addresses easier to find. She describes the region as complex to map because conditions change constantly and available data is inconsistent and ill-defined, and says Google Maps stays neutral on geopolitical issues. She also says traffic jams caused by checkpoints are reflected in Google's routing and estimated arrival times. But the users WIRED spoke to say that showing congestion does not tell a driver whether a road is actually available to them — a checkpoint can add unpredictable delays or prevent passage altogether — and one current Google employee alleges, based on internal data they have seen, that users in the West Bank have largely abandoned Google Maps for navigation. The investigation leaves a hard question hanging: when a mapmaker insists on neutrality in a place where the roads themselves are not neutral, who pays the price?

articles.title: The remarkable recovery of a National Guardsman shot near the White House
articles.description: The Washington Post's front-page feature for Monday: a year after Staff Sgt. Andrew Wolfe was shot in the head while on patrol near the White House, his recovery has been called miraculous by the surgeon who saved him — but the piece is really about what 'recovery' costs, and how badly Wolfe wants an ordinary life back.
articles.body:
Inside the childhood bedroom he moved out of long ago, and aches to move out of again one day, Andy Wolfe is surrounded by reminders of the worst day of his life. On one wall hangs a framed Purple Heart, awarded for injuries received in the line of duty. A shelf nearby holds dozens of challenge coins — small, custom medallions given to him over the months by military leaders, including President Donald Trump. His closet door is lined with an impressive collection of hats he wears to cover his still-healing skull, and his dresser and closet brim with other mementos: a Distinguished Service Medal from the West Virginia National Guard, a signed baseball bat from the FBI director, a hometown heroes award from a U.S. attorney's office, a plaque from the Trump administration's Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force recognizing his exceptional service and sacrifice. Almost a year after a gunshot to the head while deployed to his own nation's capital very nearly ended Wolfe's life, the staff sergeant has made, by almost any measure, an astounding leap toward healing his mind and body. He is reclaiming the language and cognition that the shooting impaired, beginning to drive again, to play golf, to hone his once-sharp cornhole skills. He can wrestle again with his dogs, Bailey and Charlie. It is a miraculous degree of recovery, and one that I would never have anticipated, having seen the degree of carnage, said Jeffrey Mai, the Washington neurosurgeon who saved his life the night of the shooting, and still texts with his family. But that remarkable comeback is only part of a more complicated, arduous story that has unfolded largely outside the public eye.

Wolfe still grapples with aphasia, a disorder that disrupts the ability to communicate and can make it difficult to find words and understand speech. He sometimes relies on his family to interpret his halting sentences, and struggles to articulate the conflicting realities of his new life: how grateful he feels to have survived the attack that killed a fellow service member, and how he longs to move on from constant reminders of the shooting; how much he appreciates the fierce love of parents who have been with him every step of a grueling and disorienting year, even as he yearns to live on his own again; how much he appreciates the many recognitions he has received, and how he would trade them all to return to the comfortable existence he once knew — his own apartment, a job he loved as a lineman for a communications company, weekends snowboarding or hunting. I just want to get back to normal, Wolfe says, again and again. It is the mantra he utters to his family almost daily, an answer he gives to strangers and well-wishers who ask how he is doing, a wish he speaks aloud, almost like a prayer.

Wolfe had multiple chances to return home to West Virginia before the shooting last November 26. Twice, he agreed to extend his deployment to Washington with the West Virginia Air National Guard's 167th Airlift Wing. He had joined the Guard in 2019 during his senior year of high school but had never deployed. He was sent to D.C. in the early days of Trump's decision to summon National Guard units to the nation's capital and other cities, a move that brought vehement opposition, not to mention legal action. But for a 24-year-old airman, orders were orders, and his family worried little about the assignment. It wasn't like a combat zone, his mother, Melody Wolfe, recalled. It wasn't like we were sending him overseas. Wolfe remembers how he liked patrolling the city, from the National Mall to neighborhoods such as Foggy Bottom and U Street. Off duty, he and members of his unit would explore the city — Rocket Bar in Chinatown, with its pool tables and arcade games, was one favorite stop. It was actually pretty normal most days, Wolfe said. On the day before Thanksgiving, he and about a half dozen other troops were patrolling an area not far from the White House. West Virginia Army National Guard Specialist Sarah Beckstrom, 20, was among them. Wolfe had worked with her on occasion and the two were friendly, but didn't know each other well. Wolfe says he doesn't remember much about the day, other than how he and the others had stopped briefly near Farragut Square to get food and use the bathroom. He and Beckstrom were standing just outside the Farragut West Metro entrance, waiting on the rest of their group. That's when, prosecutors say, Rahmanullah Lakanwal, a 30-year-old Afghan national who had worked with the U.S. government as a partner in Afghanistan, ambushed Wolfe and Beckstrom just after 2 p.m. In a flash, both lay on a D.C. sidewalk, each shot in the head with a .357 Smith & Wesson revolver.

Across town, Mai assessed Wolfe after the airman arrived at MedStar Washington Hospital Center. Emergency workers had intubated him and given him a blood transfusion. Still, he was bleeding heavily from the wound in the back of his skull. He wasn't following commands and couldn't move his right leg. A scan showed that a bullet fragment had carved a path of destruction from his left temporal lobe to his frontal lobe — through an area that plays a critical role in managing language and memory — before lodging between the two halves of his brain. This all portends a very, very poor outcome, Mai said. He had an absolutely devastating injury. Mai decided there was still a chance of survival, but the clock had started. Over the following several hours, he performed surgery to remove a large part of Wolfe's skull to relieve pressure and allow the brain to swell, while also working to stanch the bleeding. Sixty miles away, Wolfe's family was preparing for Thanksgiving. Melody Wolfe had been slicing apples for a pie. His father, a sergeant with the Berkeley County Sheriff's Office and a Marine veteran, had just returned from a deer hunting trip. They saw reports on television that two National Guard members had been shot in Washington, but initially tried not to worry. Melody Wolfe checked her son's location and saw that his phone was near the site of the incident. He wasn't returning their calls or texts. An hour and a half after the shooting, but before Wolfe's family knew he was involved, West Virginia Governor Patrick Morrisey tweeted: It is with great sorrow that we can confirm both members of the West Virginia National Guard who were shot earlier today in Washington, DC have passed away from their injuries. Twenty minutes later, the governor walked back the announcement, saying there were conflicting reports. Sometime around 6 p.m., Jason Wolfe saw headlights in the quiet cul-de-sac where the family lives outside Martinsburg. Three Air National Guard members in uniform came to the door. Just tell me my son is alive, he told them. They handed him a phone, and on the other end was a colonel who said Andy was in surgery. I made it to D.C. in an hour and 15 minutes, Jason Wolfe recalled of a drive that often can take two hours. At the hospital, Mai told Wolfe's parents that their son had come through surgery, but to brace for the worst. A minute by minute thing, Melody Wolfe, 47, remembers hearing. That night, she told anyone who would listen — her son's doctors and fellow Guard members, Trump when he called, her own family — that Andy would somehow be okay. That really struck me, Mai recalls even now. She was unwavering. Doctors declared Beckstrom dead the following day, with her parents by her side. At one point, the Wolfes met with Beckstrom's parents in a room at the hospital. One couple, grieving an unfathomable loss. The other, wondering whether they would soon face the same fate. I hugged her mom, Melody Wolfe recalled. And we both just wept. There really wasn't much to say. We just cried.

He spent sixteen days in the ICU, followed by a week in Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, and then four intense months at a polytrauma rehabilitation center in Richmond, where Wolfe learned to reuse the right side of his body, to eat normally again after weeks with a feeding tube, to regain speech and cognitive abilities affected by his head wound, and to take the first steps toward relearning skills he would need to work and live on his own again. His progress was undeniable, but so was his discontent. He adored his therapists, his family recalls, but bristled against the fact he was stuck. Day after day, he would tell his mother, who had quit her job as a second-grade teacher to stay by his side: I just want to go home. I hated it so much, Wolfe said. I'm not gonna lie, I was just miserable. The family opened Christmas presents at the rehab center, rang in the New Year there, and marked Andy's 25th birthday there in early February. One of his few escapes came February 24, when he attended the State of the Union address on Capitol Hill with his mother. Andy sat in a brown suit and tie, a ball cap covering his head where part of his skull was still missing, a quiet smile concealing the deer-in-headlights feeling he had most of the night. An hour into his speech, Trump recognized Beckstrom's parents, who were seated nearby, calling their daughter a true American patriot. Then he turned to the Wolfes. No one thought he could possibly make it, he said of Wolfe. With God's help, Andrew has battled back from the edge of death — and we're talking about the edge of death — on his way to a miraculous recovery. In April, he finally returned home to West Virginia. But even then, the shooting has loomed over his days: ongoing speech and occupational therapy sessions, relearning to drive, write, comprehend words on a page and manage a bank account. In early September, he headed back to Walter Reed to undergo his third surgery, to repair and reshape part of his skull that doctors had to remove in the perilous hours after the shooting. Doctors had tried the surgery, known as a cranioplasty, in early March, only to discover an infection once the procedure began. That meant waiting six months and taking antibiotics. Now, military neurosurgeon Melissa Meister used plates and screws to attach a piece of 3D-printed material to the spot where Wolfe's skull once was. For many patients, she said, the procedure can be a key part of the journey toward feeling normal again: it's this step where it brings them back to looking like themselves. When Meister saw him again a month later, she was struck by the leap he had made in his speech and cognition. It was a huge difference between the first time I saw him, she said. Wolfe still faces the risk of infection, but so far, Meister said, he has beaten so many odds. A lot of people don't necessarily make that recovery, she said.

What he seems to long for most these days, beyond physical recovery, is anonymity. But even in his hometown, that has proven hard to come by. At a diner in Martinsburg, customers one table over seemed to recognize who he is and couldn't help but stare. After dinner, the family headed to a nearby Trunk or Treat event in the parking lot of a shopping center, where hundreds of children had turned out under a glorious autumn sunset and a C-17 from the nearby Air National Guard base circled overhead. Wolfe seemed at ease as he navigated the scene in a ball cap and green hoodie, enjoying a piece of Airheads candy that Violet, his niece in her butterfly costume, shared with him. He has a lot of good days now, his father, Jason, noted as he walked a few steps behind his son. More good days than bad. Later that night, Andy drove through the falling darkness in his GMC Denali truck — the one big purchase he has made since the shooting, and a sliver of the normalcy he craves — steering along the country roads he has known all his life, past the airfield where he once trained, his father reminding him to use his turn signals and mind the speed limit. Once home, the Wolfes reflected on the support that helped them through the past twelve months: the vigils full of well-wishers, the neighbors who lit their front porch lights red for months in a sign of solidarity, friends and colleagues who offered constant help, thousands of people who have written cards and letters of encouragement. We've been blessed beyond measure, Jason Wolfe said. That night, outside of earshot of Andy, they talked again of the hurdles that remain — the lingering risk of seizures, the slow work of overcoming the language-processing disorder, the need to make sure he can safely live and work on his own again. But this much is clear: they want for Andy what he wants for himself — something resembling a normal 25-year-old's life — and they refuse to accept that any of that is out of reach. The man charged with killing Beckstrom and almost ending Wolfe's life has pleaded not guilty and remains in federal custody awaiting trial. Thousands of National Guard members continue to patrol the streets of Washington. But all that seemed far away on a recent fall morning, as Melody and Andy made the familiar half-hour drive to a medical center in Winchester, Virginia, for yet another round of speech therapy. After the appointment, Melody drove Andy to a nearby golf course to meet his father and brother for a round together. His disposition changed the moment he took his first swing on the driving range. Soon, the three Wolfe men were out on the course, surrounded by the oaks and maples and poplars at the peak of their fall colors. They laughed at particularly terrible shots. They trash talked one another. Trust me, I'm grateful to be alive, Wolfe said at one point, driving the cart in between holes. But, he added, grasping for the right words, it's just weird to constantly be reminded of the shooting. Out here, no one brings it up. No one tries to shake his hand or present him with a medal. No one mentions the next medical appointment. There is only the fresh fall air, the backdrop of the Shenandoah Valley and a momentary sense of normalcy. On the eighth hole of the day, a par five, Andy launched a shot from the fairway with a 3-wood high into the sky. The ball settled softly on the green, 253 yards away. Easily the best shot of the day. Just beautiful, he said to no one in particular, smiling the smile of a man who, for the moment, was exactly where he wanted to be.

articles.title: What It's Like to Go Birding in Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: The most charming piece of the week: inside the most violent video game ever made, players are quietly stopping to watch the birds. Sixty species, a logbook, binoculars — and a meditation on why a game built for car chases keeps rewarding people for paying attention.
articles.body:
Whooping cranes, the tallest birds in North America, have elegant black wing tips that can only be seen when they prepare to take flight. When startled, they emit a brief call that sounds like a croaking bugle. The species is exceedingly rare, and, for birders, spotting one is a prize. On my second day playing Grand Theft Auto VI, one of the most anticipated video games of all time, I saw a whooping crane in the wild, sitting by a marsh. I was steering my character off the highway, and pulled over sharply. My car was lightly smoking from a series of earlier collisions. I spent a long moment admiring the bird through a pair of in-game binoculars. Then a police siren began to whirr, and a voice said over a loudspeaker that I needed to move my car.

Whooping cranes like to engage in what birders call probing — gently pushing their bills into soil or water to see what might be hiding there. I had been doing some probing, too. Traditionally, the Grand Theft Auto games revolve around violence, theft, sex, and car chases, but lately video games have become obsessed with immersion. G.T.A. features a sprawling, realistic world, and I wanted to know what else I could find. The latest installment has at least sixty species of bird that players can track in a logbook. I was delighted to find that the main menu opens with four options: STATS, VEHICLES, WEAPONS, and ANIMALS. Joey Cruz, a birder who has also been playing G.T.A., told me that he spent six minutes watching a bald eagle. His character had recently broken into a police impound lot to steal back a car that belonged to his boss, a local crime lord. At one point, I think I saw a hummingbird, but I'm not too sure, he added. Another birder, who goes by Wren online, streams videos of herself playing games, and specializes in analyzing the birds in them. I found a new bird in the middle of a cocaine quest, she told me. It was an anhinga, a long-necked waterbird that expertly spears fish with its beak.

I began playing G.T.A. VI as soon as it was released, at midnight on Thursday. I had to sit through a long intro before I could get to the wildlife. A series of tutorials showed me how to aim a gun so that I could rob a bank, and how to drive a speedboat so that I could retrieve packages of cocaine. Finally, I learned how to equip a pair of binoculars so that I could spy on an unfolding drug deal. This was good practice for the birds. After the drug deal deteriorated into a shoot-out, a pop-up screen informed me that I could incapacitate targets with nonlethal shots. Sadly, I had already killed a few of them. Developers spent hours achieving bird realism. Feather types were a huge focus, Michael Kane, the game's vice-president of dynamic art, said in an e-mail. Red Dead Redemption 2, a previous game made by the same studio, also featured birding, but, since then, designers made advances in extreme poses, such as folded wings, Cecilio Cardenete Burgos, a lead technical artist, added. Birds have a patagium tendon that runs along the wing web, and that helps enable flight. G.T.A. VI's birds have digital skeletons with a dynamically simulated patagium tendon.

Why are there even birds in the game? For a long time, video games were split into a foreground, where the action was, and a more or less decorative background. As games began to offer open worlds that could be explored, however, the background increasingly became the point. In G.T.A. VI, you can go to the gym. There is a thriving public-transit system. One night, I found a button that let me renovate my staircase. Games are calibrated to hold your attention, and one could see this abundance of detail, uncharitably, as addictive: immersion means you spend more time playing the product. More charitably, it can be fun. G.T.A. has always been a sandbox for the id. Sometimes the id wants birds. Early in the game, on my way to a gun store, I stepped outside and got a first glimpse of my character's house, a shack on stilts that backed onto a glittering marina. I heard squawks, flaps, and the soft lapping of water. Through my binoculars, I spotted a fat, squat pelican sitting on the edge of a dock. Its mate lay resting. Then it stretched its patagium tendon, plumped its beak, and flew lazily off. Later, I spotted a roseate spoonbill, digging by some reeds. Even though there's this crime going on, it's still very beautiful and peaceful, River Sanchez-Dudik, another birder and gamer, said. On a website built to track bird sightings in the game, I saw a screenshot of two great blue herons mating.

My own journey in birding began with an owl called Flaco, who escaped from the Central Park Zoo, lived in the park for a while, and ultimately died after flying into a building. As I logged birds in G.T.A. VI, I wondered if the game could prompt players to care about the non-virtual environment. I texted my question to a birder I'd met on the Flaco trail. You're asking me if a violent game will encourage people to be interested in real-life bird conservation? the birder texted back. I don't play games that glorify violence, birds or no birds. Then they told me never to contact them again. Gaming, like birding, is about noticing the little things, Wren told me. A quest can be enlightening even if the outcome doesn't really matter. Aristotle was a birder; Salman Rushdie was addicted to Super Mario World. In birding and in gaming, you devote intense focus to something that is fleeting and often beyond your control. Wren said that, a few years ago, birds helped her through the lowest point in her life. She had moved across the country, away from her family, and was feeling lonely. Her new house had sliding glass doors that looked into the back yard, and, one day, she noticed that sparrows were bathing in a puddle in the grass. She decided to build them a fountain. That's what life is about, she told me. Stopping for a second and paying attention.

articles.title: Putin threatens new strikes on Ukraine's energy grid in retaliation for refinery attacks
articles.description: President Vladimir Putin said on November 24 that Russian retaliation against Ukraine's energy infrastructure is "inevitable" in response to Kyiv's continuing strikes on Russian oil refineries. Speaking at a meeting of the commission on fuel and energy strategy, he accused Ukraine of ignoring a direct request from Donald Trump to stop attacking refineries. The threat lands as Russia's energy war on Ukraine is already at full intensity, with five major thermal power plants damaged in recent weeks.
articles.body: President Vladimir Putin warned on Tuesday, November 24, that Russia's retaliatory strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure are "inevitable" in response to Kyiv's continuing attacks on Russian oil refineries. Speaking at a meeting of the Commission on Fuel and Energy Complex Development Strategy and Environmental Safety, Putin said: "We see that the Kyiv regime continues its attacks on our processing facilities, despite the call and direct request of the US president to refrain from these attacks. But the Kyiv authorities are not heeding such advice. Everything continues as if nothing happened. In this connection I would like to point out: retaliatory actions on our part are inevitable. Everyone should know this." He also said the escalation Ukraine began in early June — publicly described as a 40-day plan — could not inflict critical damage on Russia, and he warned European countries that attempts to limit Russian fuel exports would backfire on them. At the same time Putin acknowledged that Russia's own fuel market remains difficult, though he claimed petrol prices had stabilised after peaking in early October, and he proposed discussing extra protection for refineries and their workers. The threat is not abstract: Russia has already knocked out five major Ukrainian thermal power plants in recent weeks — in Kharkiv, Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Ivano-Frankivsk and Dnipropetrovsk regions — and Odesa faces the prospect of weeks without power. On November 2 Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow stopped attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, an offer Putin's statement effectively rejects. For Ukrainians facing winter blackouts, the message is that the energy war will escalate further.

articles.title: Russian strike hits 12-storey apartment block in Dnipro, six injured
articles.description: Russian forces struck a 12-storey residential building in Dnipro's Shevchenkivskyi district on November 24, injuring six people and destroying several flats. At least seven neighbouring buildings were damaged and a school's canteen had its windows blown out. Russian forces attacked Dnipropetrovsk region almost 30 times during the day with drones and artillery.
articles.body: Russian forces struck a 12-storey residential building in Dnipro's Shevchenkivskyi district on Tuesday, November 24, injuring six people, regional military administration head Oleksandr Hanzha reported. The strike destroyed several flats and damaged the building's upper floors, and the blast wave damaged at least seven neighbouring buildings, shattering hundreds of windows and wrecking balconies, according to Dnipro mayor Borys Filatov. A nearby lyceum was also hit, with windows smashed in its school canteen. The casualty count rose through the day, from four injured in the first hours to six as medics updated their figures; all the injured were receiving medical care. The Dnipro strike was part of a wider day of attacks: Russian forces hit Dnipropetrovsk region almost 30 times with drones and artillery on November 24, and two men aged 29 and 36 were injured overnight in Pavlohrad. A Russian FPV drone also hit a DTEK repair crew's service vehicle near a frontline village, though the energy workers were at a safe distance and no one was hurt. Dnipro, a major industrial city that has been repeatedly targeted, sits within range of Russian drones and missiles, and the attack on a residential block in daylight underlines how the war keeps reaching civilian life far from the front. Emergency services, charities and district officials worked at the scene, and a warming tent was set up for residents left without intact homes.

articles.title: Ukraine and Norway unveil DESNA, a new anti-drone air-defence system already in use
articles.description: Ukraine and Norway have jointly developed a new air-defence system called DESNA, designed to shoot down Russian drones with cheap, mass-producible Ukrainian missiles linked to Norwegian Kongsberg fire-control systems. The system is already in use in Ukraine, including against jet-powered drones, and Norway has bought and delivered several units in recent months. The two countries' defence ministers met in Oslo on November 24 to discuss expanding it to cover more of Ukraine.
articles.body: Ukraine and Norway have jointly developed a new air-defence system called DESNA, designed to protect civilians and critical infrastructure from Russian drones, the Norwegian Defence Ministry announced on November 24. The system pairs Ukrainian-made air-defence missiles and launchers with fire-control systems from Norway's Kongsberg, and is named after Ukraine's Desna River. Its key advantage, according to Norwegian Defence Minister Tore Sandvik, is cost: the Ukrainian missiles are cheap and can be produced in large quantities, which matters at a moment when air-defence missiles are in short supply globally and Russia is launching hundreds of drones a night. DESNA is already in use in Ukraine and has shown results against drones, including jet-powered ones, Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara said, and Norway has purchased and delivered several systems in recent months. The two ministers met in Oslo on November 24 to discuss expanding the system to protect more of Ukraine, and also signed a letter of intent allowing Norway's armed forces to test Ukraine's DELTA battlefield-management system. Kongsberg says DESNA complements NASAMS, the Norwegian system Ukraine has used since 2022, and the two countries are also working on Project Freyja, intended as a cheaper alternative to American Patriot systems. Norway plans to provide Ukraine with at least $7 billion in aid in 2027. For Kyiv, DESNA is part of a wider shift toward home-grown, affordable air defence as the drone war escalates and Western interceptor stocks run thin.

articles.title: UPDATE: GTA VI sold an estimated 44.9 million copies in four days — three in four on PlayStation
articles.description: New estimates from Alinea Analytics put Grand Theft Auto VI at 44.9 million copies sold through by the end of its opening weekend, grossing more than $4 billion in four days. Three in four copies sold on PlayStation 5, and 40.8 million people played on Sunday alone. Pre-orders alone were worth $2.36 billion, according to Sensor Tower — a record for the industry.
articles.body: Grand Theft Auto VI sold an estimated 44.9 million copies by the end of its opening weekend, generating more than $4 billion in gross revenue in four days, according to market research firm Alinea Analytics, whose head of market analysis Rhys Elliott shared the figures on X on November 23. The platform split is stark: 33.7 million copies, or 75.1 percent, sold on PlayStation 5, and 11.2 million, or 24.9 percent, on Xbox Series X|S, with Alinea estimating the game reached about 30 percent of the install base on both platforms. Around 40.8 million people logged in to play on Sunday, November 22, about 76 percent of them on PS5. The launch also drained rival games: Alinea estimates daily player counts fell 42 percent for Call of Duty and 28 percent for Fortnite as GTA VI launched. Separate Sensor Tower data published November 24 shows pre-orders alone brought in $2.36 billion from 24.5 million copies — the biggest pre-order result in gaming history, nearly three times the previous record held by Call of Duty: Modern Warfare II — with 82 percent of buyers choosing the $100 Ultimate Edition. Take-Two's own official figures remain more conservative: $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales and 32.5 million copies sold before release, and the company has not confirmed any post-launch total, so the Alinea and Sensor Tower numbers are estimates, not official results. Even so, the scale is now clear: GTA VI is the biggest entertainment launch ever, and PlayStation is where most of it happened.

articles.title: Jensen Huang apologizes to employees and says he's in therapy in first meeting since his return
articles.description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees in an hour-long company-wide meeting on Tuesday, his first since being reinstated, and said he is in therapy, according to a source familiar with the matter. The apology comes a day after his return ended an 11-day boardroom crisis that wiped $1.5 trillion from Nvidia's market value and drew direct intervention from President Trump.
articles.body: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang apologized to employees in an hour-long company-wide meeting on Tuesday and said he is in therapy, according to a source familiar with the matter, in his first all-hands address since being reinstated as CEO. The apology comes a day after Nvidia's board voted to bring Huang back, just 11 days after accepting his resignation, ending a boardroom crisis that wiped about $1.5 trillion from the company's market value and prompted an unprecedented pressure campaign from President Trump, who said he spoke to the board directly and indirectly. Huang resigned under pressure amid allegations he had an affair with a major customer executive, former Megaspeed head Alice Huang, and was reportedly in a relationship with an employee; US officials have said they cannot draw firm conclusions about claims that Alice Huang was in contact with Chinese intelligence, and Trump has publicly defended Jensen Huang. The board said Monday that US government officials assured directors that rehiring Huang posed no national security risk, though a board-ordered investigation into whether he was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort" continues. Huang's return supercharged a market rally on Monday, with the Nasdaq Composite surging 6.5 percent, its best day in 19 months, and shares in Nvidia-backed "neoclouds" such as CoreWeave jumping 22 percent. But the circumstances of his exit and return have left governance questions hanging over the world's most critical chipmaker, and on Tuesday Republican lawmakers began breaking publicly from Trump over the reinstatement. The apology and the therapy disclosure suggest Huang is trying to reset the relationship with his own workforce before he turns to the investors and partners who demanded him back.

articles.title: Shanghai party chief Chen Jining placed under corruption probe as Xi's purge escalates
articles.description: Chen Jining, the Communist Party chief of Shanghai and a politician widely seen as a potential heir to Xi Jinping, has been placed under investigation for suspected "serious violations of discipline," state media Xinhua said on Tuesday evening. The probe marks a sharp escalation of Xi's anti-corruption purge, which has already ensnared a large swath of China's top talent — and it hits the leader of the country's largest city and financial centre.
articles.body: The Communist Party chief of Shanghai, Chen Jining, has been placed under investigation on a corruption charge, marking an escalation of an anti-corruption purge that has already ensnared a large swath of China's top talent. Chen, 62, who has run China's largest city and financial centre since October 2022, is suspected of "serious violations of discipline," state media Xinhua said on Tuesday evening. Chen was considered one of the potential heirs to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and his fall is the most significant yet in a purge that has steadily moved up the ranks of the party, the military and state-owned industry. Shanghai is not just China's biggest city but its financial capital, home to its stock exchange and the headquarters of its largest banks and companies, so an investigation into its party chief sends a shock through the business community as well as the political system. The announcement comes days after the trilateral summit in Shenzhen at which Trump, Putin and Xi signed a joint declaration, and it underlines how Xi's domestic power consolidation continues even as he engages in high-profile diplomacy abroad. Xinhua gave no further details of the allegations against Chen, and it is not clear what specific conduct is under investigation or how long the probe will take. In China's system, a corruption investigation by the party's disciplinary body is usually the first step toward expulsion from the party and criminal prosecution. For Xi, the probe is both a demonstration of control and a reminder that no figure, however senior or however close to the top, is untouchable.

articles.title: LISA's 'Leave With Me' wins Billboard poll with over 84% of votes
