articles.description: LISA of BLACKPINK has won Billboard's weekly new music poll with her solo single "Leave With Me," taking more than 84% of the vote. Billboard posted the poll on November 20 and it closed on November 22. The win follows her EP "PRESS PLAY," released October 23.
articles.body: LISA of BLACKPINK has won this week's Billboard new music poll with her solo single "Leave With Me," pulling in more than 84% of the vote, according to Billboard. The poll, posted on November 20, asked fans to pick their favourite new release from a list of fresh songs and albums, and closed on November 22 — and LISA's share of the vote was a landslide by the poll's usual standards. The win follows her EP "PRESS PLAY," released October 23, which has kept her solo momentum going after a year in which BLACKPINK's members have each built substantial solo careers alongside the group's work. LISA is one of K-pop's biggest global stars, and her solo releases consistently draw enormous fan engagement, which is exactly what a fan-voted poll measures. The weekly poll has become a reliable barometer of which new releases have the most energised fanbases, and an 84%-plus share signals a fanbase voting as a bloc rather than a close contest. For LISA, the result is another marker of her standing as a solo artist in her own right, not just as a member of one of the world's biggest groups. It also shows how much of the week's new-music conversation belonged to K-pop, with ATEEZ topping the Billboard 200 the same week — though that chart story was already covered in the morning digest.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says he'll ask new US Congress to tighten sanctions if Trump fails to secure peace by year's end
articles.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Bloomberg he will ask the new US Congress to increase pressure on Russia if Donald Trump fails to get Vladimir Putin to end the war on terms acceptable to Kyiv by the end of the year. The interview sets a deadline on the current diplomacy and signals Kyiv's plan B if the talks stall. It comes as Washington pushes for a deal by December or January while Putin says he has no interest in a ceasefire.
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Bloomberg he will ask the new US Congress to tighten sanctions on Russia if Donald Trump fails to secure a peace deal by the end of the year, Meduza reported on November 24. The statement sets an explicit deadline on the diplomacy now under way and lays out Kyiv's fallback if the talks fail: take the case to a Congress that is expected to be more pro-Ukrainian once Democrats take control, when everything from funding to Elon Musk's role in the war effort falls under scrutiny. The interview lands at a sensitive moment. Trump, Putin and Xi have just signed a joint declaration in Shenzhen from which the Ukraine clause was dropped, Putin has said Russia has no interest in negotiating a ceasefire, and partners are pushing for four-party talks before Christmas, with Europeans insisting on a four-party format in Abu Dhabi. Zelenskyy also said the US wants to wrap up a deal by December or January, but that Ukraine will not accept peace at the cost of its independence or territory, and that Putin expects to break Ukraine over the winter. He urged partners to speed up deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles — a plea sharpened by the Financial Times report, covered in the morning digest, that the Pentagon has not approved the transfer of about 60 interceptors already allocated to Kyiv. The Bloomberg interview is Zelenskyy's clearest signal yet that he is preparing to outlast the current negotiating round and shift his appeal to Washington's next legislature if Trump cannot deliver.

articles.title: UPDATE: Chibis spent seven years consolidating power in Russia's Arctic — now the Kremlin loyalist is in police custody
articles.description: Meduza published a profile on November 24 of Murmansk Governor Andrey Chibis, detained a day earlier as he stepped off a plane at Moscow's Sheremetyevo Airport, tracing how he spent seven years consolidating power in Russia's Arctic region. Investigators allege the theft of more than 39 million rubles from the regional construction ministry and the misappropriation of over 1 billion rubles allocated to rebuild the Apatity–Kirovsk road. The case is the latest in a series of corruption prosecutions against Russian regional governors.
articles.body: Meduza published a profile on November 24 of Andrey Chibis, the governor of Russia's Arctic Murmansk region, a day after police detained him as he stepped off a plane at Moscow's Sheremetyevo Airport. The piece traces how Chibis spent seven years consolidating power in the region he has governed since 2019, building a reputation as a Kremlin loyalist, before being taken into custody on charges of funnelling public money abroad. Investigators allege the theft of more than 39 million rubles (about $478,000) in budget funds from the regional construction ministry and the misappropriation of over 1 billion rubles allocated by the regional transport ministry for the reconstruction of the Apatity–Kirovsk road. Other suspects face charges of fraud, embezzlement and illegal currency operations involving forged documents. The detention followed a confused day of reporting on November 23, when the Mash Telegram channel first reported Chibis had been stopped at the plane's steps, while the region's information minister initially denied the detention, saying he was in Moscow on a planned work trip. Chibis's arrest is the latest in a series of corruption cases against Russian regional governors, and comes as the Kremlin continues to use anti-corruption prosecutions to discipline regional elites during the war. The profile asks what changed: a loyalist who had survived seven years in one of Russia's toughest postings is now accused of the same kind of graft the system has long tolerated in its own.

articles.title: Ukraine invokes UN Charter in defence of its strike on Russian warship in Libya
articles.description: Kyiv says its strike on the Russian corvette Merkuriy off the coast of Libya was not an expansion of the war's geography but an exercise of Ukraine's lawful right to self-defence under the UN Charter. Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi said Ukraine "is not dragging anyone in and is not moving the war anywhere." Ukrainian naval drones hit the corvette in the Libyan port of Benghazi on the morning of November 22.
articles.body: Ukraine has invoked the UN Charter in defence of its strike on the Russian corvette Merkuriy off the coast of Libya, Meduza reported on November 24. Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi said the attack was not an expansion of the war's geographic scope but an exercise of Ukraine's lawful right to self-defence. "Ukraine is not dragging anyone in and is not moving the war anywhere," Tykhyi said. Ukrainian naval drones attacked the corvette in the port of the Libyan city of Benghazi on the morning of November 22, and Al Jazeera reported that Russian and Libyan citizens were killed in the strike. The Merkuriy was one of Russia's newest warships, and the attack destroyed a Ka-27 combat helicopter on board, according to earlier reporting. Kyiv's legal framing matters because the strike took place far from the Black Sea, in a port where Russia maintains a naval presence, and Moscow has accused Ukraine of escalating the war by hitting its ships in the Mediterranean. The defence comes days after Zelenskyy confirmed Ukraine was behind a separate drone strike on the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland — a story covered in the morning digest — showing Kyiv is now openly claiming a maritime campaign that stretches from the Baltic to the Mediterranean. For Ukraine, the argument is that Russian military assets are legitimate targets wherever they operate; for its partners, the question is whether such strikes risk drawing third countries into the conflict.

articles.title: UK bought fake C4 explosives for Ukraine, FT investigation finds
articles.description: Britain's Ministry of Defence spent tens of millions of pounds buying explosives marketed as an enhanced version of military C4 for Ukrainian attack drones — but the product contained no RDX, the key ingredient of conventional C4, a Financial Times investigation found. The supplier, Pennsylvania-based Tripwire South LLC, bought a cheaper commercial explosive and resold it at up to 100% markup. The MoD's own tests found no RDX, but it deemed the material fit for use and never told the supplier.
articles.body: Britain bought tonnes of explosives for Ukraine that were marketed as an enhanced version of military-grade C4 but contained no detectable trace of its principal ingredient, a Financial Times investigation published on November 24 found. For almost three years, Britain's Ministry of Defence signed contracts worth tens of millions of pounds with Tripwire South LLC, a Pennsylvania company run by former part-time police officer Ryan Morris, for a product called "Enhanced Demolition Compound-4," which Tripwire claimed was a more powerful version of C4 made by mixing chemicals into RDX, the key ingredient of conventional military C4. The explosives were shipped from Kentucky to be packed into Ukrainian attack drones. But the FT's supply-chain analysis and chemical testing found the product contained cheaper PETN, a commercial explosive, instead of RDX — and the MoD's own independent tests also found no RDX. Tripwire appears to have bought an existing white-label explosive and resold it to Britain at up to 100% markup; one contract covered an initial 36 tonnes with an option to rise to 204 tonnes, worth about £26.3 million. The MoD defended the purchases, saying the explosives performed as expected and the contract did not require RDX, but it could not explain why it paid such premiums to a middleman, or why supplier safety documents appear to be contradicted by its own testing. The safety paperwork also omitted warnings present in the original manufacturer's documents, raising risks for the Ukrainian troops handling the material. MP Mike Martin, a member of the Commons Defence Committee, said the purchase could have jeopardised the safety of Ukrainian troops and demanded an explanation, while the MoD's national armaments director told lawmakers the circumstances sounded like fraud. Tripwire and Morris deny wrongdoing, say every batch contained RDX, and have threatened the FT with legal action. The purchases were made through Task Force Kindred, a fast-track procurement programme once praised as a model for defence supply reform.

articles.title: Putin removes film director Alexander Sokurov from Russia's Human Rights Council
articles.description: President Vladimir Putin has removed film director Alexander Sokurov from Russia's Human Rights Council, according to a decree updating the council's membership. Sokurov, one of Russia's most acclaimed filmmakers, had been one of the council's few independent voices. The decree also removed lawyer Vladimir Ryakhovsky and added television presenter Tutta Larsen.
articles.body: President Vladimir Putin has removed film director Alexander Sokurov from Russia's Human Rights Council, according to a decree updating the council's membership, Meduza reported on November 24. Sokurov, 75, is one of Russia's most internationally acclaimed filmmakers — director of "Russian Ark" and "Faust" — and had been one of the few independent voices on the council, a body that advises the president on human rights but has been steadily stripped of dissenting members since the full-scale invasion. The same decree removed lawyer Vladimir Ryakhovsky and added television presenter Tutta Larsen to the council. Sokurov has been a rare public critic within the system: in 2021 he used a meeting of the council to tell Putin directly that Russia should let republics that do not want to live in a single state go, a remark that drew a sharp rebuke from the president. His removal is the latest step in the hollowing-out of the council, which once included prominent human rights defenders and now functions largely as a loyalist body. It also fits the broader pattern of the Kremlin removing cultural figures who show even limited independence — Sokurov joins a long list of artists, writers and academics pushed out of state institutions since 2022. No reason was given for the change, and Sokurov has not publicly commented.

articles.title: Russian lawmakers approve tighter monitoring of bank transfers to uncover untaxed income
articles.description: Russia's State Duma has passed a law tightening oversight of bank transfers between individuals, aimed at uncovering untaxed income. The move gives the tax authorities a wider window into everyday peer-to-peer payments. It comes as the Kremlin looks for new revenue while war spending strains the budget, and as the Duma also approved the 2027–2029 federal budget on November 24.
articles.body: Russia's State Duma has passed a law tightening oversight of bank transfers between individuals, Meduza reported on November 24. The legislation is aimed at uncovering untaxed income by giving the authorities a wider view of peer-to-peer payments — the everyday transfers Russians use to pay for services, split bills and move money informally. The measure lands as the Kremlin searches for new revenue while war spending strains the federal budget: the Duma also approved the 2027–2029 federal budget on November 24, and the government has been raising taxes and tightening collection to fund the war. For ordinary Russians, the law means transfers that once flew under the radar may now draw questions from the tax authorities, and it extends the state's surveillance of financial life beyond businesses and into personal transactions. Critics note the irony: while the authorities move to track small informal payments by citizens, the same week saw the detention of a regional governor accused of embezzling over a billion rubles of public money. The law is part of a broader package of fiscal tightening that also includes directing tobacco licensing fees toward regional healthcare funding, passed in the same session. It remains to be seen how aggressively the tax service will use its new powers, but the direction is clear — the informal economy that millions of Russians rely on is coming under closer state scrutiny.

articles.title: UPDATE: Zelenskyy and Magyar agree energy, trade, transport and demining cooperation after Zakarpattia talks
articles.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar concluded their talks in Zakarpattia on November 24 with agreements on cooperation in energy, bilateral trade, transport infrastructure and humanitarian demining. It was the first visit to Ukraine by a Hungarian prime minister since 2015, and it follows Budapest's decision to allow two more EU accession negotiation clusters for Ukraine. Magyar also met representatives of the ethnic Hungarian community in the region.
articles.body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar concluded their talks in Ukraine's Zakarpattia region on November 24 with agreements on cooperation in energy, bilateral trade, transport infrastructure and humanitarian demining, Zelenskyy said after the meeting. The visit — the first to Ukraine by a Hungarian prime minister since 2015 — marks a notable thaw in a relationship strained for years, when Hungary under its previous leadership repeatedly blocked or slowed EU aid and sanctions against Russia and obstructed Ukraine's EU accession talks, citing the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in Zakarpattia. Magyar also met representatives of that Hungarian community during the visit, a constituency at the centre of the bilateral dispute. The trip follows Budapest's decision to allow the opening of two additional EU accession negotiation clusters for Ukraine, unblocking a key step on Kyiv's path toward membership. For Zelenskyy, the meeting was an opportunity to lock in the improved tone and press for continued Hungarian support, particularly on energy and EU funding; for Magyar, who took office promising a more constructive European policy, it was a visible signal that Hungary's approach to its neighbour has changed. The two leaders discussed minority rights, cross-border cooperation and Ukraine's EU accession, and the agreements announced — practical, working-level cooperation rather than grand declarations — suggest both sides wanted the visit to produce concrete results. The test will be whether the new tone survives the next EU vote on Ukraine funding, where Hungary has in the past been the holdout.

articles.title: Ukraine needs €115 billion in 2027, with €25 billion still to find, Zelenskyy says
articles.description: Ukraine will need at least €115 billion ($125 billion) in external financial support in 2027, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told a congress of local and regional authorities on November 24. About €90 billion is already secured from the EU — €45 billion from a 2025 decision plus a further €45 billion loan proposed by the European Commission last week — leaving €25 billion still to find. Zelenskyy said he was confident the gap would be closed.
articles.body: Ukraine will need at least €115 billion ($125 billion) in external financial support in 2027, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday, November 24, addressing a congress of local and regional authorities. The government has already secured about €90 billion in commitments from the European Union for next year: €45 billion from an EU decision last year to provide two years of support at €45 billion a year, plus a further €45 billion loan the European Commission proposed last week. "We need to find another €25 billion. I am confident that we will accomplish this task," Zelenskyy said, adding that the European Commission has already presented a way to secure the funding and Kyiv is now working to ensure the EU supports it. The €115 billion figure is far larger than Kyiv estimated until recently: the draft 2027 budget approved by the government in September put the need for external support at $52.6 billion. Zelenskyy explained the increase after consultations with the defence minister and military leadership revealed a need for another €70 billion on top of the €45 billion originally expected. The Commission's proposed €45 billion loan would send up to €25 billion to military needs and up to €20 billion to direct budget support, borrowed on external markets under EU budget guarantees. The EU is now Ukraine's main financial supporter, and EU leaders meet in Brussels on November 26–27 to discuss the bloc's budget and Ukraine support. The IMF has put Ukraine's additional external financing needs for 2027–2028 at $49–51 billion. Zelenskyy also said Ukraine may need a similar sum again in 2028, underlining that the war's financial burden is not a one-year problem.

articles.title: Ukraine protests appointment of sanctioned Russian official as IAEA deputy chief
articles.description: Ukraine has protested the appointment of Russian official Oleksiy Ferapontov as deputy director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, in charge of nuclear energy. Kyiv's foreign and energy ministries are demanding the appointment be revoked, calling it a threat to nuclear safety and an attempt to legitimise Russian control over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant. Ferapontov is under sanctions.
articles.body: Ukraine has protested the appointment of Russian official Oleksiy Ferapontov as deputy director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency for nuclear energy, demanding the decision be revoked. Kyiv's Foreign Ministry and Energy Ministry issued a demarche and a formal note of protest to the IAEA, calling the appointment a threat to nuclear safety and an attempt to legitimise Russian control over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, Europe's largest, which Russian forces have occupied since 2022. Ferapontov is under sanctions, and Ukraine argues that putting a sanctioned Russian official in charge of the IAEA's nuclear energy department undermines the agency's credibility at a moment when it is supposed to be monitoring the safety of the very plant Russia seized. The protest highlights a long-running tension: the IAEA, led by Rafael Grossi, has maintained working contacts with Moscow and has inspectors at Zaporizhzhia, while Kyiv has repeatedly accused the agency of being too accommodating to Russia. For Ukraine, the Ferapontov appointment is not a personnel matter but a political one — it signals, in Kyiv's view, that the international nuclear watchdog is willing to normalise Russia's presence in the sector even as Moscow's forces hold a Ukrainian nuclear plant hostage. The IAEA has not publicly responded to the Ukrainian protest. The dispute comes as the Zaporizhzhia plant remains in cold shutdown, dependent on external power, and a focus of international concern over nuclear safety in wartime.

articles.title: Russia has lost over 432,000 soldiers in 2026 — a record year, General Staff says
articles.description: Russia has lost more than 432,000 soldiers since the beginning of 2026, the Ukrainian General Staff said — an absolute record for a single year of the war. The figure covers killed and wounded and reflects the grinding offensives around Pokrovsk and other frontline sectors. It comes a day after Meduza and Mediazona estimated at least 720,000 Russian troops had died by autumn 2026.
articles.body: Russia has lost more than 432,000 soldiers since the beginning of 2026, the Ukrainian General Staff said on November 24 — an absolute record for a single year of the war. The figure, which covers both killed and wounded, reflects the scale of Russia's grinding offensives this year, above all around Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka, where Moscow has been pushing for months at enormous cost. The General Staff also reported total Russian personnel losses of about 1.64 million since the full-scale invasion began, with 2,471 lost in a single day earlier this week. The record-year figure lands a day after Meduza and Mediazona published their estimate, covered in the morning digest, that at least 720,000 Russian troops had died by autumn 2026, based on leaked Rosstat mortality data — a toll that includes the missing. The two numbers measure different things: the General Staff counts killed and wounded, while the journalists' estimate counts only deaths. Together they describe a war of attrition in which Russia continues to advance slowly while paying a staggering human price — at least 40,000 dead and injured a month, by some estimates. For Kyiv, the figures are both a measure of the cost Russia is bearing and a warning: Moscow has so far been willing to absorb losses on this scale and keep attacking. For Ukraine's partners, they frame the question of how long Russia can sustain offensives of this intensity before its manpower pool is exhausted.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: US wants a peace deal by December–January, but Ukraine won't trade independence or territory
articles.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the United States wants to wrap up a peace deal on Ukraine by December or January, but that Ukraine will not accept an agreement at the cost of its independence or territory. He added that Putin expects to break Ukraine over the winter, and urged partners to speed up deliveries of Patriot missiles. The remarks came in the same Bloomberg interview in which he threatened to take his case to the new US Congress.
articles.body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the United States wants to conclude a peace agreement on Ukraine by December or January, but that Kyiv will not accept a deal at the cost of its independence or territory. The remarks, from a Bloomberg interview reported on November 24, set out Kyiv's red lines as the diplomacy enters its decisive phase: Washington is pushing for a settlement within weeks, while Putin has said Russia has no interest in a ceasefire and expects to break Ukraine over the winter. Zelenskyy also urged partners to accelerate deliveries of Patriot air-defence missiles, a plea sharpened by the report, covered in the morning digest, that the Pentagon has not approved the transfer of about 60 interceptors already allocated to Kyiv. The president's message is twofold: he is willing to negotiate, but not on terms that sacrifice sovereignty, and he is preparing a fallback — asking the new US Congress to tighten sanctions on Russia — if Trump cannot deliver a deal by year's end. The timing matters because the current negotiating window is narrow: partners are pushing for four-party talks before Christmas, Europeans are insisting on a four-party format in Abu Dhabi, and the Kremlin has a small window before a pro-Ukrainian Democratic Congress takes power and Trump's room for manoeuvre narrows. For Ukraine, the coming weeks will test whether diplomacy can produce a settlement that preserves its independence, or whether the war grinds on into another winter of energy attacks and frontline attrition.

articles.title: EU leaders to meet in Brussels on November 26–27 to decide on Ukraine funding and the bloc's budget
articles.description: EU leaders will hold an extraordinary European Council meeting in Brussels on November 26–27 to discuss the bloc's budget and support for Ukraine. The meeting comes as the European Commission's plan for a €45 billion loan for Kyiv — part of the €115 billion Ukraine says it needs in 2027 — faces resistance from Slovakia and debate over whether it should sit inside the EU budget. The outcome will shape how much of the €25 billion funding gap Zelenskyy flagged on November 24 can be closed.
articles.body: EU leaders will hold an extraordinary meeting of the European Council in Brussels on November 26–27 to discuss the European Union's budget and support for Ukraine, Ukraїnska Pravda reported on November 24. The summit lands at a critical moment for Kyiv's finances: President Zelenskyy said the same day that Ukraine needs at least €115 billion in external support in 2027, with about €90 billion already secured and €25 billion still to find. The European Commission last week presented a plan to borrow a further €45 billion for Ukraine — up to €25 billion for military needs and up to €20 billion for direct budget support — but the proposal faces resistance inside the bloc. Slovakia has refused to support the loan, and the Czech prime minister wants Ukraine aid kept outside the EU budget, leaving Kyiv's supporters increasingly isolated in the debate. The Brussels meeting will test whether the bloc can agree a mechanism to deliver the money, and whether the €45 billion loan can be approved in time to cover next year's needs. The stakes are high: the EU is now Ukraine's main financial supporter, and the €90 billion already agreed covers only part of the 2027 requirement. For Zelenskyy, who told regional officials he was confident the remaining €25 billion would be found, the summit is the first real test of that confidence. The leaders are also expected to discuss the wider EU budget, in which Ukraine funding has become one of the most divisive questions.

articles.title: Steam Awards 2026 nominations open, with a Hall of Fame vote for the best game of the decade
articles.description: Valve opened nominations for the 2026 Steam Awards on Monday, November 23, and this tenth-anniversary edition adds a Hall of Fame category pitting the last ten Steam Game of the Year winners against each other for the title of best game of the decade. Nominations close November 30, finalists are revealed December 17 with the Winter Sale, and winners are announced January 2. Grand Theft Auto VI is not eligible — Rockstar has still not announced a PC version.
articles.body: Valve has opened nominations for the 2026 Steam Awards, the tenth edition of its annual player-voted awards, and this year the event adds a Hall of Fame category that will crown the best game of the past decade. Nominations are open now and close on Monday, November 30, at 10 a.m. Pacific, with the finalists revealed and voting beginning on December 17, when the Steam Winter Sale starts; voting closes on January 2, 2027, and winners are announced immediately. The Hall of Fame ballot pits the ten previous Steam Game of the Year winners against each other: Grand Theft Auto V, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, PUBG, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Red Dead Redemption 2, Resident Evil Village, Elden Ring, Baldur's Gate 3, Black Myth: Wukong and Hollow Knight: Silksong, with GTA V and The Witcher 3 standing in for 2016 and 2017, years when the awards had no Game of the Year category. There are 14 categories in total, including the return of two old favourites — Just 5 More Minutes and Defies Description — and a new one, This Is My Job Now, for games that swallow all your free time. Any Steam account that is not limited can nominate, and taking part earns badges, including a Selection Committee badge for nominating and playing a nominated game. One quirk of this year's ballot: the year's biggest game, Grand Theft Auto VI, cannot be nominated at all, because Rockstar has not announced a PC version. The Hall of Fame vote is the one to watch — Steam's user base does not always vote the way critics do, so a surprise winner among the ten past champions is entirely possible.

articles.title: Resident Evil 10 reportedly in early pre-production for PS6 and Xbox Helix — a soft reboot with a new cast
articles.description: Capcom has reportedly begun early pre-production on Resident Evil 10, according to Rely on Horror, with the game aimed at next-generation consoles — PlayStation 6 and the next Xbox, codenamed Helix — and planned as a soft reboot with an entirely new cast in an isolated European setting, with no ties to Umbrella. Nothing is confirmed by Capcom, and the game is said to be years away, targeting release before the end of the decade.
articles.body: Capcom has reportedly started early pre-production on a new mainline Resident Evil entry, provisionally called Resident Evil 10, according to a report by Rely on Horror based on unnamed insider sources. The project is said to be targeting next-generation hardware — PlayStation 6 and the next Xbox, known by the codename Helix — and is planned as a soft reboot: an entirely new cast of characters, an isolated European setting, and a story with no connection to the Umbrella Corporation or previous games. The working title may change before any announcement, and the game is still in the earliest stage of production, with a release reportedly aimed at before the end of this decade. The report lands on the back of Resident Evil Requiem's huge launch — the game has reportedly sold more than seven million copies in less than two months — while Capcom has already confirmed a Resident Evil Code: Veronica remake targeting a launch next year. Capcom has not commented on any of the Resident Evil 10 claims, so the platforms, setting and timing should all be treated as unconfirmed for now. If the report is accurate, it would mean Capcom is already planning two generations ahead, betting that the next Resident Evil can reinvent itself for hardware that does not exist yet.

articles.title: Gothic 3 Classic reaches PS5 and Xbox today with the community patch built in
articles.description: THQ Nordic is releasing Gothic 3 Classic today, November 24, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, priced at €29.99. The console version of the 2006 cult RPG integrates the fan-made community patch 1.75, adds gameplay improvements and a tailor-made gamepad interface, and is optimised for current hardware. It gives a new generation its first proper console version of Piranha Bytes' sprawling fantasy epic.
articles.body: THQ Nordic is bringing Gothic 3 Classic to current-generation consoles today, November 24, with the cult 2006 role-playing game launching on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S at €29.99. The console version integrates community patch 1.75 — the fan-made fix package that has kept the PC original playable for years — along with further gameplay improvements, a tailor-made gamepad user interface and controls, and advanced optimisation for the smoothest Gothic 3 experience yet. The original, developed by Germany's Piranha Bytes, was famously ambitious and famously buggy at launch, but its open world of Myrtana, its faction politics and its freedom to side with orcs, rebels or Hashishin earned it a devoted following that has kept it alive for two decades. THQ Nordic's Classic edition is the first time the game has been properly rebuilt for consoles rather than simply emulated, and it arrives in a quiet release week — one of the few notable launches between the GTA VI storm and the December rush. For players who never touched the PC original, it is a chance to play one of the most influential European RPGs in a form that finally works as intended; for veterans, the community patch integration is the detail that matters most, since it preserves two decades of fan fixes inside an official release.

articles.title: Stellaris: Willpower expansion launches, turning ethics into galaxy-shaping ideologies
articles.description: Paradox released the Willpower expansion for its sci-fi strategy game Stellaris on PC on November 23, priced at $24.99 or included in the Season 10 Expansion Pass. The expansion, developed with Abrakam, adds an Ideology system that lets a fanatical ethic grow into a galaxy-spanning ideology, a movable Galactic Hall, a new Ambition and three Origins. A free 4.6 Corona Borealis update arrived alongside it.
articles.body: Paradox Interactive has released Willpower, the latest major expansion for its science-fiction grand strategy game Stellaris, on PC on November 23, priced at $24.99 separately or included in the Season 10 Expansion Pass. Developed with Abrakam, the expansion is built around Ideologies: an ethic held with fanatical conviction can now grow into a boundless ideology that shapes diplomacy, warfare and the identity of an entire empire. A Galactic Hall can be moved around the map as the visible embodiment of that ideology, and the expansion adds a new Ambition — a peaceful victory path based on willpower rather than conquest — plus three new Origins: Golden Generation, which trains promising students at a Golden Academy to become future leaders; Lost Makers, in which a machine intelligence searches the stars for its creators; and Great Khan. The free 4.6 Corona Borealis update arrived at the same time with balance and systems changes for all players. Willpower is the first Stellaris expansion since the game passed its tenth anniversary, and it lands as Paradox continues to support one of the longest-lived strategy games on PC — a title that has grown through dozens of expansions and updates into something far larger than the game that launched in 2016.

articles.title: Counter-Strike 2 becomes the first game ever to pass 10 million Steam reviews
articles.description: Counter-Strike 2 has passed 10 million user reviews on Steam — the first game on the platform ever to do so. As of November 23 the shooter had 10,002,894 reviews, 85 percent of them positive, putting it far ahead of second-placed Dota 2 on around 2.82 million. The milestone underlines how the 2023 successor to CS:GO still dominates PC gaming three years on.
articles.body: Counter-Strike 2 has become the first game in Steam's history to pass 10 million user reviews, according to 3DM, which reported the milestone on November 23. As of that afternoon the shooter had 10,002,894 user reviews, 85 percent of them positive, keeping its overall rating at "Very Positive". The gap to the rest of the platform is enormous: the second-most-reviewed game, Dota 2, sits at around 2.82 million reviews, meaning Counter-Strike 2 has more than three times as many. The game launched in 2023 as a free update replacing Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, which had run since 2012, and it inherited one of the largest player bases in gaming along with the esports scene that surrounds it. Ten million reviews is a measure of sheer scale rather than quality — review counts track how many people felt moved to write something, and Counter-Strike's huge, vocal community has always been prolific — but the number still captures something real: no other game on Steam has ever been played, argued about and reviewed by so many people. For Valve, the milestone is also a reminder of the platform's own history, since Counter-Strike began life as a Half-Life mod before becoming the backbone of Steam itself.

articles.title: Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii sails into PS Plus Extra and Premium
articles.description: Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii joins the PlayStation Plus Extra and Premium catalogues today in the US, UK and Japan, as part of the month's new additions. The spin-off stars Goro Majima as a shipwrecked pirate captain, mixing ship battles, island exploration and the series' trademark brawling. It is one of the bigger day-one catalogue additions of the year for subscribers.
articles.body: Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii is joining the PlayStation Plus Extra and Premium catalogues, available to subscribers in the US, UK and Japan from today. The spin-off, released earlier this year, stars series favourite Goro Majima as a shipwrecked pirate captain building a crew, fighting naval battles and brawling across the beaches of Hawaii — a deliberately absurd premise even by this series' standards, and one that reviewers enjoyed. Its arrival in the Extra catalogue is one of the bigger subscription additions of the month, giving PS Plus members a full, recent Yakuza adventure without buying it outright. The timing also fits Sony's monthly rhythm: new catalogue titles land as older ones leave, with at least six games — including Granblue Fantasy: Relink — scheduled to depart the Extra tier on December 15, a story already covered in the morning digest. For subscribers weighing whether to keep the Extra tier through the holidays, a fresh Yakuza game is a strong argument, and for Sega it puts Majima's pirate adventure in front of the millions of players who never picked it up at launch.

articles.title: PS5 exclusive Destruction AllStars shuts down tomorrow after a quiet four years
articles.description: Destruction AllStars, the PlayStation 5 exclusive vehicle-combat game from Lucid Games, will shut down on November 25 and has already been delisted from the PlayStation Store. Launched in February 2021 as a PlayStation Plus title, it never found a lasting audience despite its car-combat arena concept. The shutdown is a quiet end for one of the PS5's earliest exclusives.
articles.body: Destruction AllStars, the PlayStation 5 exclusive from Lucid Games, will shut down on November 25, and the game has already been removed from the PlayStation Store. The vehicle-combat arena game launched in February 2021 as a PlayStation Plus title — one of the earliest exclusives of the PS5 generation — built around drivers who fight on foot as well as in armed cars, with a cast of colourful characters and a games-as-a-service structure. It never found a lasting audience: player numbers faded quickly after launch, updates slowed, and the game drifted into obscurity while Sony's other live-service bets grabbed the attention. The shutdown closes the book on a game that was meant to show off the PS5's early promise but instead became a cautionary tale about launching a multiplayer-only title without a strong hook. For the few players still active, the end comes with little ceremony — no farewell event, just a delisting and a server switch-off. It is also a reminder of how quickly the live-service landscape moves: a game that was a headline PS Plus offering in 2021 is gone before the generation is halfway through.

articles.title: UPDATE: Army details lead-dust containment plan as FEMA alerts residents ahead of Wednesday's Iowa detonation
articles.description: The US Army on Tuesday detailed its plan to contain lead dust ahead of Wednesday morning's controlled detonation of more than 60 barrels of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, and FEMA sent an Imminent Threat Alert to phones near Middletown warning the blast will take place at 9 a.m. Central. The detonation was cleared by a federal appeals court on Monday after days of legal and political wrangling, including President Trump's temporary halt.
articles.body: The US Army on Tuesday laid out its plan to contain lead dust ahead of the controlled detonation of explosive material at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, now scheduled for Wednesday morning at 9 a.m. Central Time. Residents of and people near Middletown, a community in the rural south-eastern corner of Iowa, received an Imminent Threat Alert on their cellphones on Tuesday from the Federal Emergency Management Agency warning of the planned blast. The detonation is meant to deal with more than 60 barrels of lead azide, a material used to detonate munitions that has become particularly unstable after long-term storage at the World War II-era plant. "We have continuously added to the mitigation measures throughout the entire time we've been working on this, and we're going to continue to add today," an Army official told CNN's Julia Vargas Jones on Tuesday. The operation was cleared to proceed after a federal appeals court on Monday rejected environmental groups' bid to stop it over fears of lead contamination. It had become a political flashpoint: President Trump temporarily halted the plan, then said it should not proceed until the Eighth Circuit agreed and incoming Democratic Governor-elect Rob Sand agreed — while warning he would hold Sand responsible if the material exploded spontaneously. The Army had postponed the detonation from November 20 to November 23, then to November 24, before settling on Wednesday morning. The government argues the choice is between a planned detonation and an unplanned explosion at any moment; environmental groups counter that no evidence of an emergency has been published.

articles.title: Republicans break from Trump over Jensen Huang's Nvidia reinstatement
articles.description: Republican pushback against Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO is growing, despite President Trump downplaying any blowback from his own party. Several Republicans, including Senators John Cornyn and Pete Ricketts and Representative Don Bacon, have criticised or questioned the move. The split shows the limits of Trump's sway even inside his own party when a president intervenes directly in a corporate boardroom.
articles.body: Republican pushback to Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive is growing, despite President Donald Trump earlier downplaying any blowback from his party. CNN reported that several other Republicans have criticised or questioned the move, including Senators John Cornyn and Pete Ricketts and Representative Don Bacon. The criticism is striking because it comes from Trump's own side: the president spent days stewing over the stock market sell-off, then orchestrated an unprecedented West Wing pressure campaign to convince Nvidia's board to bring Huang back just 11 days after he resigned under pressure. Trump said on CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to the board "directly and indirectly", and Nvidia said the reinstatement was based on "input from senior levels" of the government. For Republican critics, the problem is twofold: the governance scandal itself — Huang resigned amid allegations of an affair with a major customer executive and a reported relationship with an employee, with a board investigation still open — and the precedent of a sitting president leaning on the board of the world's most valuable company to reverse a corporate decision. The episode also sits awkwardly alongside the administration's own national-security concerns: the Director of National Intelligence said on Sunday that China had illicitly obtained advanced Nvidia chips despite US export controls. The growing Republican dissent suggests that even a market rally — the Nasdaq surged 6.5 percent on Monday — may not be enough to make the intervention cost-free for the president inside his own party.

articles.title: UPDATE: Trump awards Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom in a private Oval Office ceremony
articles.description: President Donald Trump awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honour, to Rudy Giuliani on Tuesday in a private Oval Office ceremony closed to reporters. Giuliani, 82, said he was "honoured and humbled" to receive it from the president. The award, first announced in September 2025, honours the former New York mayor's "lifetime of service" — and comes despite Giuliani's leading role in the effort to overturn the 2020 election.
articles.body: President Donald Trump awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Rudy Giuliani on Tuesday, in a private Oval Office ceremony closed to reporters, completing an honour he first announced in September 2025. Giuliani, 82, received the nation's highest civilian award in recognition of his "lifetime of service to the American people", according to the White House, and said in a statement: "I am honoured and humbled to receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom from my nation and from our Commander-in-Chief, President Donald J. Trump." His son Andrew Giuliani, who served as executive director of the president's 2026 FIFA World Cup task force, told reporters afterwards that Trump and Giuliani each spoke at the small gathering for relatives, friends and supporters, reminiscing about their long friendship. The White House did not explain why the ceremony was closed to the press. Giuliani announced the award himself on Steve Bannon's podcast on Monday, saying the ceremony would take place at 11 a.m. on Tuesday. The honour is deeply divisive: Giuliani became a national figure as New York's mayor during the September 11 attacks, but later served as Trump's personal lawyer and led the legal effort to overturn the 2020 election, was disbarred, and was pardoned by Trump after returning to office in 2025. Trump announced his intention to honour Giuliani in September 2025, shortly after Giuliani was seriously injured in a car crash in New Hampshire. After the ceremony, the president and first lady Melania Trump were due to fly to Florida on Tuesday evening to spend Thanksgiving at Mar-a-Lago.

articles.title: Michigan reverses course on hiring Trev Alberts as athletic director a week after he signed on
articles.description: The University of Michigan has told Trev Alberts he will not be its next athletic director, just one week after he signed a memorandum of understanding to take the job and leave Texas A&M, a person familiar with the situation told the Associated Press on Tuesday. The last-minute reversal throws Michigan's athletic department into fresh turmoil, with no explanation yet given for the change of heart.
articles.body: The University of Michigan's athletic department is in fresh turmoil after a last-minute reversal on hiring its new athletic director. Michigan has informed Trev Alberts that he will not be its next athletic director, one week after he signed a memorandum of understanding to take the job and leave Texas A&M, a person familiar with the situation told the Associated Press on Tuesday. The reversal is unusual in college sports hiring, where a signed memorandum of understanding is normally the final step before a formal announcement — and it leaves both schools in an awkward position. Alberts, who had been Texas A&M's athletic director, had evidently agreed to move, and Michigan had evidently agreed to hire him; a week later, the deal is off, with neither side yet explaining publicly what changed. Michigan is one of the biggest and richest athletic departments in American college sports, and the search for its next leader now starts over at a moment when the department faces pressure on multiple fronts, from the changing economics of college athletics to the performance of its football programme. For Alberts, the episode leaves his future uncertain: he had signed on to leave Texas A&M, and it is not clear whether he will now stay in College Station or look elsewhere. The story broke on Tuesday afternoon, and more details — including any official statements from either university — were still to come.

articles.title: Senators mull deal to fund the military but block money for offensive operations in Iran
articles.description: Top Senate Democrats and Republicans are in high-stakes talks about cutting off funding for future offensive operations in the Iran war in exchange for replenishing the tens of billions of dollars the Defence Department says it urgently needs. Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker said there may be a way for Democrats to make their point "without tying the hands of the commander in chief" — but any deal would be a major constraint on the president's war powers.
articles.body: Top Senate Democrats and Republicans are engaged in high-stakes talks about cutting off funding for future offensive operations in the Iran war in exchange for replenishing the tens of billions of dollars that the Department of Defense has said it urgently needs, according to multiple lawmakers and aides in both parties. The emerging proposal would pair a funding replenishment — money the Pentagon says is urgently needed after months of operations — with a restriction barring the use of those funds for offensive action against Iran. "I think there's a way for Democrats to make their point without tying the hands of the commander in chief and the defense of our country," Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker told CNN when asked about the proposal. The talks reflect the political bind around the Iran war: Democrats want a check on further escalation, while Republicans want to keep the military funded and are wary of constraining the president. A deal of this kind would be a significant assertion of Congress's power of the purse over war-making — the kind of constraint that presidents of both parties have historically resisted. The negotiations are still at an early stage, and it is not clear whether the restriction would cover only future offensive operations or also ongoing ones, nor whether the White House would accept any version of it. But the fact that senior Republicans are even discussing the trade suggests the cost of the Iran operations — in money as well as politics — is now weighing on both parties.

articles.title: Judge denies Designer Shoe Warehouse bid to dismiss Warner Music's social media copyright lawsuit
articles.description: A federal judge has denied Designer Shoe Warehouse's bid to dismiss Warner Music's social media copyright lawsuit, ruling on Monday (November 23) that the Canadian company behind The Shoe Company brand is not an indispensable party to the case. DSW and parent Designer Brands had argued the suit could not proceed without Designer Brands Canada, which is behind 75 of the roughly 200 alleged infringements. The ruling keeps those 75 instances in the case.
articles.body: A federal judge has denied a motion to dismiss filed by shoe retailer DSW and its parent company Designer Brands in a copyright infringement lawsuit brought by Warner Music Group's labels and publishers. Judge Michael H. Watson of the US District Court for the Southern District of Ohio issued the ruling in an order filed on Monday, November 23. The defendants had argued that Designer Brands Canada Inc., a Canadian company not named in the suit, is an indispensable party because it does business as The Shoe Company, one of the brands whose social media posts are cited in the case — Warner attributes 75 instances of alleged infringement to The Shoe Company out of approximately 200 in an exhibit to the amended complaint — and because the court lacks personal jurisdiction over the Canadian company. Judge Watson rejected the argument, finding the Canadian company is not indispensable under Rule 19 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure: "Indeed, in a copyright infringement suit, all infringers are jointly and severally liable, and a copyright plaintiff may choose whom to sue and is not required to join all infringers in a single action." He also rejected claims that Canadian law should apply and that judging the posts without the Canadian company present violates due process, noting the court holds persons liable for their conduct, not posts, and cannot impose liability on a company that is not a defendant. The 16 plaintiffs, including Atlantic, Elektra, Warner Records and Warner Chappell, allege the defendants and their influencer partners used Warner-controlled music without permission in marketing videos on Instagram and TikTok, "misappropriat[ing] over two hundred" works while "failing to pay Plaintiffs a dime"; the complaint also cites videos on channels tied to Topo Athletic (at least 22) and Keds (at least 15). Warner sued on May 1, 2025, seeking statutory damages of up to $150,000 per work, citing tracks including Cardi B's "Up" and Fleetwood Mac's "Dreams." The order does not address a separate September motion for judgment on the contributory and vicarious infringement claims, nor Warner's October 13 request to file a second amended complaint adding more than 270 alleged infringements uncovered in discovery. The DSW case is one of several Warner has brought against brands over music in social media marketing, including an October suit against Luxottica, owner of Ray-Ban and Oakley, over at least 427 works.

articles.title: Eminem co-publisher Eight Mile Style adds 108 allegedly infringing AI tracks to $47.7m Suno lawsuit, calling Suno's denials 'false'
articles.description: Eminem co-publisher Eight Mile Style has amended its $47.7 million copyright lawsuit against AI music generator Suno, adding 108 more AI-generated tracks it says infringe its songs. The amended complaint, filed November 19 in California federal court, covers 26 of the 269 compositions in the case, including "Lose Yourself," "Stan," "Mockingbird" and "Without Me." It calls Suno's public denials that its service trades on artists' names and likenesses "false."
articles.body: Eminem co-publisher Eight Mile Style has amended its copyright lawsuit against AI music generator Suno, adding 108 more AI-generated tracks it says infringe its songs. The amended complaint was filed on Thursday, November 19, in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, 13 days after the original suit, and the new examples cover 26 of the 269 compositions in the case, including "Lose Yourself," "Stan," "Mockingbird" and "Without Me." The damages sought are unchanged at just over $47.7 million: the bulk, $40.35 million, is for copyright infringement at the legal maximum of $150,000 per song where infringement is found to be willful, across all 269 compositions — falling to $8.07 million without a willfulness finding — plus $672,500 over alleged bypassing of access controls and $6.725 million over alleged stripping of songwriter and publisher credits. The filing answers what Suno told reporters after the original November 6 suit, when a spokesperson said Suno exists "to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone's name or likeness," and that it does not allow prompts for specific artists' names and songs. Eight Mile Style calls those statements false, noting that in its October 20 answer to the second lawsuit by Universal Music Group and Sony Music, Suno admitted that "as of January 2026, users may include artist names in their prompts." The complaint says a brief investigation uncovered Suno outputs using the copyrighted lyrics — often verbatim — and protected musical elements of 26 of the works, "many in the voice of Eminem," and calls the examples "just the tip of the iceberg." Despite accusing Suno of stealing Eminem's voice and likeness, the amended complaint adds no claim over them, and Eminem himself is not a party. The publisher wants all unauthorized copies impounded or destroyed, "including copies retained in training datasets, internal repositories, model weights, and server infrastructure," plus a court order barring further infringement. The same lawyer, Richard S. Busch, filed a near-identical amended complaint for Elvis Presley Enterprises on November 13 under Tennessee's ELVIS Act. Suno raised more than $400 million at a $5.4 billion valuation in June; Warner Music Group settled with Suno in November 2025, while Universal and Sony are still suing.

articles.title: TikTok rolls out Likeness Detection deepfake tool globally, launches public AI-content checker
articles.description: TikTok has rolled out its Likeness Detection deepfake tool globally and launched a public AI-content checker, the company announced. The tool is designed to spot videos that use a person's likeness without permission, as deepfake and AI-generated content spreads across the platform. TikTok says its AI labelling tools have now helped label more than 5 billion AI-generated videos, up from 3 billion in July.
articles.body: TikTok has rolled out its Likeness Detection deepfake tool globally and launched a public AI-content checker, the company announced. The likeness tool is designed to detect videos that use a person's face or voice without permission, one of the most sensitive problems created by generative AI, where a convincing fake can be used to impersonate a celebrity, a creator or an ordinary person for scams, misinformation or harassment. The public checker lets anyone verify whether a piece of content was AI-generated, extending transparency beyond TikTok's own app. TikTok says its AI labelling tools have now helped label more than 5 billion AI-generated videos, up from 3 billion in July — a jump that shows how fast synthetic content is multiplying on the platform. The rollout comes as platforms across the industry tighten their AI rules: Tidal announced the same day that it will ban fully AI-generated music outright, Deezer has been labelling and restricting AI tracks, and collecting societies are suing AI companies over training data. For creators, likeness detection matters because unauthorised deepfakes can divert attention and income, and can damage a reputation in ways that are hard to undo once a clip goes viral. For TikTok, which faces constant scrutiny from regulators over content moderation, a global detection tool and a public checker are also a way of showing it can police synthetic media at scale. Whether the tools catch the most sophisticated fakes, and how quickly takedowns follow a detection, will be the real test.

articles.title: $1B from YouTube, record revenues, reduced headcount, and WMG selling assets to its Bain JV: What I learned from Warner Music Group's annual report
articles.description: Warner Music Group's annual report shows it took in $1 billion from YouTube, cut headcount and sold assets to its Bain Capital joint venture, Music Business Worldwide founder Tim Ingham writes in a new analysis of the company's fiscal-year filings. The findings add detail to a record year in which WMG's revenues topped $2 billion in a quarter for the first time. The analysis comes days after WMG reported full fiscal-year revenues of $7.437 billion.
articles.body: Warner Music Group's annual report shows the company took in $1 billion from YouTube, reduced its headcount and sold assets to its Bain Capital joint venture, Music Business Worldwide founder Tim Ingham writes in his latest "Tim's Take" analysis of the company's fiscal-year filings. The findings add texture to a record year: WMG generated $2.001 billion in revenue in the quarter ended September 30, 2026 — the first time its quarterly revenues crossed $2 billion — with subscription streaming up 14.7% year-on-year, and full fiscal-year revenues reached a record $7.437 billion, with net income of $735 million versus $370 million a year earlier. YouTube's $1 billion contribution underlines how important the video platform has become as a revenue source for a major label, spanning official music videos, user-generated content and the licensing arrangements that govern them. The reduced headcount reflects the multi-year transformation strategy CEO Robert Kyncl has pursued to make the company leaner, while the asset sales to the Bain joint venture show WMG reshaping its portfolio and raising cash from parts of the business it no longer wants to hold directly. Looking ahead, WMG has pointed to healthy industry trends, improved streaming terms and new growth vectors including AI licensing as support for its fiscal 2027 outlook. For the wider industry, the filings are a reminder that even in a record year, the majors are cutting costs and selling assets — growth and discipline are happening at the same time.

articles.title: Never mind the PR stunts, here's the Sex Pistols claiming to part ways with Frank Carter
articles.description: The Sex Pistols and Frank Carter are parting ways after their December UK and Ireland tour, the band and singer have announced. Carter has fronted the band since 2024, when three shows to save London's Bush Hall turned into a two-year run. The final show is December 20 at London's Eventim Apollo, closing a tour marking 50 years of punk.
articles.body: The Sex Pistols and Frank Carter are parting ways after their December UK and Ireland tour, the band and singer have announced. Carter, the former Gallows and Frank Carter & the Rattlesnakes frontman, joined Steve Jones, Glen Matlock and Paul Cook in summer 2024 for three intimate charity shows to raise money for London's Bush Hall — and the collaboration turned into more than two years of UK and international tours and festival appearances around the world. The farewell run, the 11-date "Anarchy In The UK" tour, begins December 4 in Leeds and runs through Dublin, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Liverpool, Birmingham, Portsmouth and Bristol, ending December 20 at London's Eventim Apollo. Guitarist Steve Jones said: "It's been a glorious ride with Frankie baby, we've loved every minute. The shows were spectacular and of course, a big shout out to all the fans. Without you lot, it's nothing. This is not the end of the Pistols... but let's see what happens." Carter said he never thought for a second that three shows to save Bush Hall would turn into all this, and looked forward to celebrating the run "one last time around our Bloody Kingdom," adding: "As always, I'll see you in the pit." The December dates mark 50 years of punk and of "Anarchy in the U.K.," released on November 26, 1976. Original frontman John Lydon has dismissed the Carter run as "karaoke," and it remains to be seen whether the three classic members continue with another singer. Carter, meanwhile, could return to Frank Carter & the Rattlesnakes, who last performed in November 2024 behind their most recent album, "Dark Rainbow."

articles.title: Rolling Stone crowns Missy Elliott's 'The Rain' the best female song of the '90s
articles.description: Rolling Stone has published its ranking of the 200 best songs of the 1990s, crowning Missy Elliott's 1997 debut single "The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)" the best song of the decade by a female artist. Aaliyah's "Are You That Somebody" was named the decade's best R&B song. The list, published Monday, allows only one song per artist and mixes hits with deep cuts and flops.
articles.body: Rolling Stone has published its ranking of the 200 best songs of the 1990s, crowning Missy Elliott's 1997 debut single "The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)" the best song of the decade by a female artist. The list, published on Monday, November 23, puts Elliott's debut at No. 1 among female acts, with Aaliyah's "Are You That Somebody" named the decade's best R&B song. The full top 10 of the female ranking runs: Missy Elliott's "The Rain" at No. 1, Liz Phair's "F— & Run" at No. 2, Aaliyah's "Are You That Somebody" at No. 3, Natalie Imbruglia's "Torn" at No. 4, Lauryn Hill's "Lost Ones" at No. 5, Fiona Apple's "Paper Bag" at No. 6, Alanis Morissette's "You Oughta Know" at No. 7, Whitney Houston's "Heartbreak Hotel" at No. 8, Britney Spears' "...Baby One More Time" at No. 9 and Lil Kim's "Crush On You" at No. 10. Further down the 200, TLC's "No Scrubs" sits at No. 17, Destiny's Child's "Say My Name" at No. 21, Madonna's "Ray of Light" at No. 71, Foxy Brown's "I'll Be" at No. 84, Erykah Badu's "Tyrone" at No. 89 and Mary J. Blige's "My Life" at No. 156. The rankings were not confined to hits and included deep cuts, flops and fan favourites, with only one song per artist allowed — a rule that kept megahits from Mariah Carey and Celine Dion off the list entirely, which has drawn the usual debate. The honour adds to Elliott's run of Rolling Stone superlatives: the magazine previously crowned her 2001 smash "Get Ur Freak On" the greatest song of the 21st century and her 2002 album "Under Construction" the greatest female rap album of the century, and her "The Rain" video topped its 150 Best Rap Music Videos of All Time tally. As ever with a Rolling Stone list, the conversation is proving as lively as the ranking itself.

articles.title: Ariana Grande tour doc to show the process behind 'Eternal Sunshine' and 'Petal'
articles.description: Ariana Grande is getting a tour documentary that will show the process behind her "Eternal Sunshine" tour and her "Petal" project, Rolling Stone reports. The film follows the singer's return to the stage behind her 2024 album "Eternal Sunshine." It is the latest in a run of concert films tracing how major pop tours are built.
articles.body: Ariana Grande is getting a tour documentary that will show the process behind her "Eternal Sunshine" tour and her "Petal" project, Rolling Stone reports. The film promises a behind-the-scenes look at how the tour came together, from rehearsals and staging to the performances themselves, alongside the creative process behind "Petal," her next musical chapter. "Eternal Sunshine," released in 2024, marked Grande's return to music after a period focused on acting, including her role in the "Wicked" films, and the tour brought the album's songs to the stage with the elaborate, theatrical production her shows are known for. Tour documentaries have become a staple of the streaming era, with artists from Beyonce to Taylor Swift using them to extend a tour's life and give fans access to the work that goes into a stadium show. For Grande, whose fans follow every step of her creative process, a film that covers both the tour and the making of "Petal" bridges two eras at once: the closing of the "Eternal Sunshine" chapter and the opening of whatever comes next. No release date or platform details were given in the initial report, but the announcement alone is enough to set the fanbase speculating about what the "Petal" footage will reveal.

articles.title: Metallica wraps 2026 touring year at Mohegan Sun, returns to the Sphere in January
articles.description: Metallica wrapped up their 2026 touring year on Saturday at Mohegan Sun Arena in Connecticut — their first show in the state in 28 years. The band returns to the Sphere in Las Vegas in January before a final North American tour leg in May. The Mohegan Sun date closed a year of touring behind their long-running M72 world tour.
articles.body: Metallica wrapped up their 2026 touring year on Saturday at Mohegan Sun Arena in Connecticut, their first show in the state in 28 years. The date closed out a year of touring behind the band's long-running M72 world tour, which has carried them around the world since 2023 with its two-night, no-repeat setlist format. Playing Connecticut for the first time in nearly three decades was a notable footnote for a band that has toured relentlessly for more than 40 years — even Metallica still has markets it rarely visits. The band is not slowing down: they return to the Sphere in Las Vegas in January, bringing their stadium-sized show into the venue's immersive format, before a final North American tour leg in May. The Sphere run follows a wave of major acts treating the Las Vegas venue as a destination in itself, with residencies becoming a major revenue stream for legacy rock and pop headliners. For Metallica, the January dates and the May leg frame the closing chapter of the M72 cycle, which has been one of the most successful tours of the band's career. The Mohegan Sun show was a fitting way to end the year: a rare market, a full arena, and a band still playing at the top of its game more than four decades after forming.

articles.title: Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds release previously unseen footage of 1986 Manchester performance
articles.description: Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds have released previously unseen footage of their 1986 performance at Manchester's International II, celebrating the 40th anniversary of the album "Your Funeral... My Trial." The footage captures the band in their mid-1980s incarnation, at the height of their post-punk intensity. It is a gift to fans as the band's early catalogue continues to be reassessed.
articles.body: Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds have released previously unseen footage of their 1986 performance at Manchester's International II, celebrating the 40th anniversary of "Your Funeral... My Trial." The album, the band's fourth, was released in 1986 and remains one of the defining records of their early period — dark, literate and intense, recorded as the band was finding its voice after Cave's departure from The Birthday Party. The newly released footage captures the band in that mid-1980s incarnation, playing the material live in a Manchester venue at a moment when their reputation was built almost entirely on the ferocity of their shows. For fans, unseen footage from this era is rare: the band's early years were documented far less thoroughly than their later, arena-sized period, so every recovered tape adds to the record. The release also fits a wider pattern of anniversary activity around classic albums, with labels and artists mining archives for footage, demos and live recordings that give longtime listeners something new. Cave remains one of rock's most prolific and revered figures, still touring and recording with the Bad Seeds four decades on, and the 1986 footage is a reminder of how long and how strange that journey has been — from Manchester's International II to the biggest stages in the world.

articles.title: Zwan, the Billy Corgan and Jimmy Chamberlin-led supergroup, to reissue 'Mary Star of the Sea' in deluxe form
articles.description: Zwan, the supergroup led by Billy Corgan and Jimmy Chamberlin, will reissue their debut album "Mary Star of the Sea" in deluxe form. The reissue features a full remix of the album plus "Rooms Full of Salt," a two-LP collection of 19 unreleased demos and outtakes. The original album came out in 2003.
articles.body: Zwan, the Billy Corgan and Jimmy Chamberlin-led supergroup, will reissue their debut album "Mary Star of the Sea" in deluxe form, featuring a full remix of the record and "Rooms Full of Salt," a two-LP collection of 19 unreleased demos and outtakes. Zwan formed after the first split of the Smashing Pumpkins, bringing together Corgan and Chamberlin with David Pajo, Paz Lenchantin and Matt Sweeney for a brighter, more melodic sound than the Pumpkins' heavy grandeur. "Mary Star of the Sea," released in 2003, was the band's only studio album — Zwan broke up the same year, making the record a one-off snapshot of a short-lived supergroup. The deluxe reissue gives fans a fuller picture of that brief existence: a full remix of the album plus 19 unreleased demos and outtakes across two LPs, offering a look at how the songs developed. For Pumpkins fans, the reissue is also a piece of the band's wider history, since Corgan and Chamberlin went on to reunite the Smashing Pumpkins, while Pajo, Lenchantin and Sweeney each built substantial careers of their own. Archive reissues of short-lived side projects have become a steady part of the catalog business, and Zwan's lone album — beloved by a devoted cult following — is a natural candidate. The announcement was reported alongside the week's other music news, with the reissue landing as the band's legacy gets a fresh look more than two decades on.

articles.title: El Michels Affair and Clairo team up for a cover of MF DOOM
articles.description: El Michels Affair and Clairo have teamed up for a cover of an MF DOOM song, Billboard reports. The collaboration pairs the retro-soul band's cinematic sound with one of indie pop's most distinctive voices, reworking the late rapper's material. It is the latest in a steady stream of tributes keeping DOOM's catalogue alive.
articles.body: El Michels Affair and Clairo have teamed up for a cover of an MF DOOM song, Billboard reports. The collaboration pairs two very different musical worlds: El Michels Affair, the retro-soul outfit known for cinematic, instrumental reinterpretations, and Clairo, one of indie pop's most distinctive voices, whose soft, intimate delivery is a long way from DOOM's dense, masked flow. That contrast is the point — a good cover finds something new in a song, and putting DOOM's writing through El Michels Affair's warm, analogue soul sound with Clairo singing is a genuine reimagining rather than a straight tribute. MF DOOM, who died in 2020, remains one of hip-hop's most influential and mythologised figures, and his catalogue has been kept alive by a steady stream of covers, samples and tributes from artists across genres. For El Michels Affair, the collaboration continues a run of high-profile reinterpretations that have made the band a go-to for artists wanting their songs rebuilt in soul form. For Clairo, it is another step in a career that has moved steadily from bedroom pop to more ambitious collaborations. The track arrives as DOOM's music continues to find new audiences, more than two decades after his most celebrated records.

articles.title: 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' soundtrack debuts at No. 1 on Billboard's Soundtracks chart
articles.description: The soundtrack to "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" has debuted at No. 1 on Billboard's Soundtracks chart. It is the franchise's third chart-topping soundtrack album. The film is the latest instalment in the Hunger Games series, which has long paired its releases with high-profile music.
articles.body: The soundtrack to "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" has debuted at No. 1 on Billboard's Soundtracks chart, marking the franchise's third chart-topping album. "Sunrise on the Reaping" is the latest film in the Hunger Games series, a prequel that returns to Panem and has drawn audiences back to the franchise's world of tributes and rebellion. Music has been a core part of the franchise's identity since the first film, whose soundtrack featured Taylor Swift's "Safe & Sound" and became a major commercial success in its own right, and later instalments continued the pattern of pairing the films with high-profile artists. A No. 1 debut on the Soundtracks chart shows that the music is still a significant draw, not just an afterthought to the film's release. For the artists involved, a Hunger Games placement remains a valuable showcase, reaching the franchise's large and loyal audience. The chart-topper also underlines how soundtrack albums continue to perform as a category, even as streaming has changed how people listen to film music — a strong opening week can still put a soundtrack at the top of its chart. The debut lands on the charts dated November 28, a week in which holiday music and the GTA VI album are also dominating the rankings.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo scores fourth Pop Airplay No. 1 with 'Stupid Song' as Bruno Mars, Latto and Doja Cat top airplay charts
articles.description: Olivia Rodrigo has captured her fourth Pop Airplay No. 1 with "Stupid Song," while Bruno Mars has landed his third Adult Contemporary chart-topper, Billboard reports. Latto and Doja Cat claim a Rhythmic Airplay No. 1 together, and Remi Wolf has achieved her very first Billboard chart-topper. The moves come on the charts dated November 28.
articles.body: Olivia Rodrigo has captured her fourth Pop Airplay No. 1 with "Stupid Song," Billboard reports, while Bruno Mars has landed his third Adult Contemporary chart-topper. Latto and Doja Cat claim a Rhythmic Airplay No. 1 together, and Remi Wolf has achieved her very first Billboard chart-topper. The moves come on the charts dated November 28, reflecting tracking data for the week ending November 19. Rodrigo's Pop Airplay crown adds to a strong run for "Stupid Song," the single from her third album "you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love," which also holds a top-10 place on the Hot 100 — though the Hot 100 story itself was already covered in the last digest. For Mars, the Adult Contemporary No. 1 is another reminder of his staying power across formats, years after his imperial phase. The Latto and Doja Cat pairing at Rhythmic Airplay shows the format's appetite for big-name collaborations, while Remi Wolf's first-ever Billboard No. 1 is a breakthrough moment for an artist who has built her following steadily rather than arriving overnight. Taken together, the airplay charts show a healthy mix: established superstars holding their ground, collaborations dominating rhythmic radio, and a newer name breaking through for the first time. The chart week also saw holiday songs surging on the Hot 100, with Mariah Carey and Wham! climbing back into the top five as the Christmas season begins.

articles.title: 355 Ukrainian drones flew toward Moscow overnight, prompting flight restrictions at two airports
articles.description: Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 355 Ukrainian drones flew toward the Russian capital overnight on November 24, in one of the largest drone waves aimed at Moscow of the war. Flight restrictions were imposed at two Moscow airports as air defences engaged the incoming drones. The attack came the same night Russia launched 96 drones of its own at Ukraine.
articles.body: Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 355 Ukrainian drones flew toward the Russian capital overnight on November 24, in one of the largest drone waves directed at Moscow since the full-scale invasion began. Flight restrictions were introduced at two of the city's airports while air defences worked to intercept the drones, disrupting early-morning air traffic. The scale of the raid underlines how Ukraine's long-range drone campaign has grown: Kyiv now regularly sends large swarms deep into Russian territory, targeting the capital as well as refineries, airfields and logistics hubs. The overnight exchange was two-sided — in the same hours, Russia launched 96 strike drones at Ukraine, 64 of them jet-powered, killing two people in Zaporizhzhia. Ukrainian strikes on Russian soil have increasingly focused on energy and military infrastructure, and Moscow has become a recurring target as Kyiv seeks to impose costs on Russia far from the front line. Russian officials routinely report shooting down most incoming drones, though independent verification of interception rates is rarely possible. The raid also shows the war's reach into everyday life in the Russian capital, where airport closures and air-raid alerts have become a regular feature of the conflict.

articles.title: Russian strikes kill two in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia, injure dozens
