He will release 'PsychoGod', teased with the single 'Speaking in Tongues', this winter. The hard-working frontman is wasting no time between Maiden commitments.
articles.body: Bruce Dickinson already has a new solo album and tour dates on deck for Iron Maiden's break, Rolling Stone reports. The Iron Maiden frontman will release 'PsychoGod', which he is teasing with the single 'Speaking in Tongues', this winter, and has live dates lined up to support it. The move continues Dickinson's long-running parallel solo career, which has run alongside his Maiden duties for decades, most recently with his 2024 solo album 'The Mandrake Project' and its accompanying tour. Dickinson has described the solo work as a different creative outlet from the band, with room for more personal and experimental material. The announcement comes as Iron Maiden pause touring, and Dickinson is using the window to return to the road under his own name. Details of the album and the tour dates give fans something to look forward to while Maiden are off the road.

articles.title: Deftones announce 2027 North American tour with Knocked Loose and julie
articles.description: Deftones will give their album 'Private Music' a public offering on a spring 2027 North American tour, Rolling Stone reports. The 23-city trek kicks off May 5 in Dallas and wraps June 20 at Toronto's RBC Amphitheatre, with Knocked Loose and julie opening. It follows the band's seventh annual Dia De Los Deftones festival in San Diego and a 2025 world tour, their first headlining run since 2022.
articles.body: Deftones announced that they are hitting the road again in 2027, Rolling Stone reports, with a 23-city North American tour in support of their tenth studio album, 'Private Music'. The trek will kick off in Dallas on May 5 at the Dos Equis Pavilion before hitting cities including Phoenix, Salt Lake City, St. Louis, Atlanta and New York, and wrapping on June 20 at Toronto's RBC Amphitheatre, one day before the official start of summer. Knocked Loose and julie are set to open for the entire run. Tickets went on presale on Tuesday, November 17, with general onsale starting Thursday, November 19. The announcement came just days after the band wrapped its seventh annual Dia De Los Deftones festival on November 7 in San Diego. The new tour follows an alt-rock band that kicked off a world tour in 2025, its first headlining trek since 2022, and announced and released 'Private Music' in the midst of it. The album, which arrived in August 2025, debuted and peaked at No. 5 on the Billboard 200 and was nominated for best rock album at the 2026 Grammys, losing to Turnstile's 'Never Enough'. Fans who attended the first half of the 2025 tour did not get to hear the new music live, so the 2027 dates are the first full chance to hear 'Private Music' on stage.

articles.title: Eminem marks 30 years of 'Infinite' with six tracks and new mixes now streaming
articles.description: Eminem is marking 30 years of his debut release 'Infinite', with the record now streaming in an expanded form featuring six tracks and new mixes, Rolling Stone reports. The 1996 release predates his mainstream breakthrough and shows the Detroit rapper finding his voice. A documentary around the debut album accompanies the anniversary.
articles.body: Eminem is marking 30 years of his debut release 'Infinite', Rolling Stone reports, with the record now streaming for its anniversary in an expanded form featuring six tracks and new mixes. 'Infinite', originally released in 1996 on the independent Detroit label Web Entertainment, was Eminem's first album, recorded before Dr. Dre signed him and before 'The Slim Shady LP' made him a star. The record shows a young Marshall Mathers rapping in a very different style from the Slim Shady persona that would follow, with dense, technically intricate verses over jazzy, mid-90s Detroit production. It sold modestly at the time and was long out of print, becoming a sought-after artifact for fans and collectors. The 30th anniversary edition brings the tracks to streaming with new mixes, and a documentary surrounding the debut album accompanies the release. The anniversary is a reminder of how far Eminem has come from the local Detroit scene, and how the technical ambition of 'Infinite' already pointed toward the rapper he would become.

articles.title: Rock Hall welcomes Wu-Tang Clan, Phil Collins, Billy Idol and more in 2026 induction ceremony
articles.description: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame's 2026 class was inducted in Los Angeles, with Wu-Tang Clan, Phil Collins and Billy Idol among the honorees, Rolling Stone reports. The night mixed emotional speeches and all-star performances, including Metallica and St. Vincent honoring Iron Maiden, and Trent Reznor inducting Joy Division and New Order as Peter Hook performed with Deftones and Lauren Mayberry. Phil Collins was tearful as he joined the Hall, and John Mulaney weighed in on the class.
articles.body: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame welcomed its 2026 class in Los Angeles, Rolling Stone reports, with Wu-Tang Clan, Phil Collins and Billy Idol among the inductees. The ceremony mixed emotional acceptance moments with all-star tribute performances, as the Hall's Los Angeles edition drew a cross-generational crowd. Phil Collins was tearful as he joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, in a moment that stood out on a night full of them. Jack Black, St. Vincent and Metallica played at Iron Maiden's Rock Hall induction, honoring the metal legends, while the Red Hot Chili Peppers paid tribute to Rick Rubin. Trent Reznor inducted Joy Division and New Order into the Hall, and Peter Hook performed at the ceremony with Deftones and Lauren Mayberry — a rare onstage reunion of the Manchester lineage. John Mulaney had many thoughts on the 2026 inductees and picked next year's class, keeping the comedy running through the night. The ceremony also saw Stephen Wilson Jr. interpret 'Wonderwall' for Oasis at the induction. The 2026 class reflects the Hall's broadening definition of rock, spanning hip-hop, new wave, metal and pop, and the performances underlined how much of the night was about artists honoring other artists.

articles.title: Phoebe Bridgers announces 25 more North American stops for 'The Lost Tour' in 2027
articles.description: Phoebe Bridgers has extended her Lost Tour into 2027, announcing 25 more North American stops, Rolling Stone reports. The extension follows her run of Saturday Night Live performances of 'Bobby' and 'Still Standing'. The tour supports her latest album cycle and keeps her on the road well into next year.
articles.body: Phoebe Bridgers has announced 25 more North American stops for 'The Lost Tour' in 2027, Rolling Stone reports, extending a tour that has already been one of the year's biggest indie draws. The new dates keep Bridgers on the road well into next year, supporting her latest album cycle. The announcement follows her recent Saturday Night Live appearance, where she performed 'Bobby' and 'Still Standing' in two different performances on the same night, a showcase of the range of her current material. Bridgers has also just been announced as a headliner of Iowa's Hinterland festival for July 2027, alongside Slayyyter and Billy Strings, making next summer a busy one. The Lost Tour extension underlines the scale of demand for her live show, which has grown from small clubs to arenas and festival headline slots since her breakthrough. The new dates give fans in cities missed on the first leg another chance to catch the show.

articles.title: Molly Meldrum, Australian music broadcaster and 'Countdown' host, dies at 83; state funeral offered
articles.description: Molly Meldrum, the Australian music journalist, broadcaster and producer who championed local music as host of ABC's 'Countdown' from 1974 to 1987, has died at 83, Billboard reports. He died peacefully on Monday, November 23, at a Melbourne hospital after a long illness. The Victorian government has offered the family a state funeral, which they accepted, and tributes poured in from Kylie Minogue, Jimmy Barnes and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
articles.body: Molly Meldrum, the Australian music broadcaster and 'Countdown' host who spent six decades championing Australian music, has died at 83, Billboard reports. His family said he died peacefully on Monday morning, November 23, at Epworth Hospital in Melbourne after a long illness. Meldrum, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, became the face of ABC's 'Countdown', which ran on Sunday nights from 1974 to 1987 and gave many Australian acts their first national exposure, championing local and international artists from INXS to ABBA and interviewing figures including King Charles and Elton John. He was a music journalist from the 1960s, produced records including Russell Morris's 1969 hit 'The Real Thing', and helped propel the careers of AC/DC and Kylie Minogue. He became the first non-artist inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2014. Victorian Premier Ben Carroll announced that the government had offered the family a state funeral, which they accepted, with details of a celebration of his life to be shared in due course. Tributes came from across the music industry and public life: Kylie Minogue said she watched 'Countdown' every weekend as a child and would turn the music up in his honour, while Tina Arena, Jimmy Barnes, Kate Ceberano, Delta Goodrem, Blondie and AC/DC were among others who paid tribute, along with Skyhooks and Mushroom Records. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Meldrum loved music almost as much as the country loved him. No cause of death was given.

articles.title: NYC Mayor's Office hires first Executive Director of Music
articles.description: New York City's Mayor's Office has hired its first Executive Director of Music, Billboard reports. Rachael Pazdan will help the city support musicians by serving as a liaison between the government and the music industry. The new role is a first for City Hall and a sign of the city's formal investment in its music ecosystem.
articles.body: New York City's Mayor's Office has hired its first Executive Director of Music, Billboard reports. Rachael Pazdan will take on the newly created role, helping the city support musicians by serving as a liaison between the government and the music industry. The position is the first of its kind at City Hall, formalizing a direct line between the city's music community and the mayor's office. The hire comes as New York continues to position itself as a global music capital, with live music, recording and music business all major employers in the five boroughs. Having a dedicated executive director gives artists, venues, labels and promoters a single point of contact inside government, and gives the city a music-industry voice in policy discussions around licensing, nightlife, funding and workforce support. The role is expected to cover everything from helping musicians navigate city services to advocating for the industry's needs in economic development planning. For a city whose music scene spans everything from DIY spaces to Madison Square Garden, the appointment is a notable institutional step.

articles.title: Burning Man CEO Marian Goodell to exit: 'I'm not tired, I'm not done — I'm ready to be a mentor'
articles.description: Burning Man CEO Marian Goodell is stepping down after leading the organization since 2013, Billboard reports. Goodell will remain in the role during the search for a new leader and keep her seat on the Burning Man board. She framed the move as a shift toward mentorship rather than retirement.
articles.body: Burning Man CEO Marian Goodell is to exit her role, Billboard reports, ending a tenure as chief executive that began in 2013. Goodell, who has led the organization behind the annual desert gathering in Nevada's Black Rock Desert for more than a decade, will remain in the role during the search for a new leader and keep her seat on the Burning Man board. She framed the decision as a transition rather than a farewell, saying she is not tired and not done, but ready to be a mentor. Goodell's tenure saw Burning Man grow from a countercultural gathering into a major cultural institution with a year-round nonprofit organization, a permanent headquarters and an expanding global network of regional events, while also navigating the challenges of scaling the desert event, ticket controversies and the pandemic years. The search for her successor begins as the organization plans its next chapter, with Goodell staying on to ensure a smooth handover. Her departure marks the end of an era for one of the most distinctive leadership roles in live events and festival culture.

articles.title: Mary J. Blige 'Real Love' lawsuit rejected by appeals court: 'notably different'
articles.description: An appeals court has rejected a lawsuit claiming Mary J. Blige's hit 'Real Love' illegally borrowed from a 1973 funk song, Billboard reports. The court found the songs notably different, dismissing the case. The 1973 track has a rich history of hip-hop sampling, but the court ruled Blige's decades-old hit did not infringe it.
articles.body: An appeals court has rejected a lawsuit claiming Mary J. Blige's hit 'Real Love' illegally borrowed from a 1973 funk song, Billboard reports. The ruling dismissed the case, with the court finding the two songs notably different. The lawsuit had claimed that Blige's decades-old hit — one of the defining songs of her career and of 1990s R&B — unlawfully copied elements of the earlier funk track. The 1973 song has a rich history of hip-hop sampling, having been mined by producers for years, but the appeals court concluded that whatever similarities the plaintiff pointed to did not amount to infringement. The decision is a win for Blige and a reminder of how high the bar is for copyright claims over songs that share genre conventions and common musical building blocks. 'Real Love', released in 1992 as the second single from Blige's debut album 'What's the 411?', remains one of her signature songs and a staple of R&B radio. The ruling closes a case that had hung over one of the most celebrated catalogs in modern R&B.

articles.title: D'Angelo's estate releases posthumous song 'Kamikazi' for 'GTA 6': singer 'approved this track' before his death
articles.description: D'Angelo's estate has released a posthumous song, 'Kamikazi', for 'Grand Theft Auto VI', Billboard reports. The estate says the singer approved the track before his death and was enthusiastic about it. The release adds a new D'Angelo recording to one of the most anticipated entertainment launches ever.
articles.body: D'Angelo's estate has released a posthumous song, 'Kamikazi', for 'Grand Theft Auto VI', Billboard reports, with the estate saying the singer approved the track before his death. The estate said he was enthusiastic about the song and about its place in the game. 'Kamikazi' is the latest addition to the 'GTA VI' soundtrack universe, which has become one of the biggest music stories of the year as Rockstar's game dominates the cultural conversation. The track arrives as 'Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album' and its deluxe edition rack up streams and chart positions, with artists from Travis Scott to Slayyyter contributing. D'Angelo, who died in October, was one of the most revered voices in R&B and neo-soul, and any unreleased material carries enormous weight with fans. The estate's decision to release a track he personally approved is intended to honor his wishes rather than simply mine the vault. For the game, landing a posthumous D'Angelo song is another coup in a soundtrack rollout that has treated music as a central character.

articles.title: Jay-Z's 2027 Super Bowl Halftime Show coming to IMAX theaters
articles.description: Jay-Z's 2027 Super Bowl Halftime Show is coming to IMAX theaters, Billboard reports. The big-screen presentation will bring the halftime spectacle to cinemas, extending the biggest stage in American music beyond the broadcast. Details of the theatrical rollout are to follow.
articles.body: Jay-Z's 2027 Super Bowl Halftime Show is coming to IMAX theaters, Billboard reports, in a move that takes the biggest stage in American music to the big screen. The halftime show, already the most-watched musical performance of the year, will be presented theatrically, giving fans a cinema-scale way to experience the spectacle. The announcement reflects how the Super Bowl halftime show has become a cultural event in its own right, with the performance, the artist and the staging debated for months before and after the game. Jay-Z's involvement — through his Roc Nation partnership with the NFL, which has shaped halftime bookings for years — adds another layer to the story. Bringing the show to IMAX suggests the production is being conceived as a large-scale visual event, not just a television segment. The theatrical rollout is the latest example of music's biggest live moments being repackaged for cinemas, following the success of concert films on the big screen. More details on dates and ticketing are expected as the 2027 game approaches.

articles.title: GTA VI: The Album' Deluxe Edition adds Travis Scott, Slayyyter, Offset and Anitta — 57 tracks in total
articles.description: The deluxe edition of 'Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album' is out now, Billboard reports, adding Travis Scott, Slayyyter, Offset, Anitta and more to the soundtrack. Between the original and deluxe editions, the album now boasts 57 tracks in total. The release continues the game's record-breaking music rollout.
articles.body: The deluxe edition of 'Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album' is out now, Billboard reports, powered by new contributions from Travis Scott, Slayyyter, Offset, Anitta and more. Between the original and deluxe editions, the GTA album now boasts 57 tracks in total. The deluxe edition expands a soundtrack that has already become one of the defining music releases of the year, with the game treating its music as a central part of the Vice City experience rather than background audio. Rockstar Games and score composers Justice have spoken about making music a main character in 'Grand Theft Auto VI', and the album rollout reflects that ambition, mixing established stars with emerging acts across genres. The original album drew attention for its range, and the deluxe adds further star power, including Travis Scott, who has a long history with the franchise. The release comes as the game itself continues to dominate entertainment headlines, with the soundtrack functioning as both a companion to the game and a standalone chart contender. The deluxe edition is available to stream now.

articles.title: Hollywood Needs a New Pixar
articles.author: Alvy Ray Smith and co-authors
articles.description: Pixar's co-founder argues Hollywood is repeating its old mistake with AI and creator platforms — and lays out what the studios must do instead, with the Disney-Pixar partnership as the model.
articles.body:
Hollywood earned its cultural monopoly by absorbing radical technologies that it first resisted — sound, colour, computer graphics — and the piece argues that AI and creator platforms are the next such technology, and that the industry is mishandling them. Most of the conversation about AI in film revolves around cost savings and artists being displaced, the authors say; those issues matter, but they miss a bigger shift. Ask a teenager where their favourite characters come from, and the answer is as likely to be a creator platform — YouTube, Roblox, TikTok — as a Hollywood studio. Unless moviemakers evolve, they risk losing their place at the centre of culture.

The argument runs through the Pixar precedent. Silicon Valley and Hollywood went through a version of this before, during the early partnership between Pixar and Disney that was crucial to Pixar's success: Disney storytellers gave Pixar pointed feedback on early characters, leading John Lasseter, Pete Docter and the rest of the brain trust to take screenwriting classes, and Pixar did not believe technical people were any less creative than artists. Disney did not produce Toy Story by hiring more CGI artists into its 2-D pipeline; it partnered with Pixar, whose mission was to make movies with the new technology, and eventually acquired it. The Disney-Pixar relationship worked, the authors stress, because Bob Iger gave Pixar co-founder Ed Catmull real power over Disney Animation — other Hollywood acquisitions of gaming studios or creator talent have struggled when the acquired company lacked similar authority.

Something similar needs to happen now, the piece argues, but the rise of creator culture will make the transition harder: during the shift to computer animation the distribution formats stayed the same, while today format, distribution and production technology are changing all at once. YouTube made more than $60 billion last year, about $15 billion more than Netflix brought in, and studios are already adapting creator-platform properties — Backrooms cost about $10 million and collected more than $400 million, Obsession cost under $1 million and made over $520 million, and the Minecraft movie made almost $1 billion, a fraction of the game's $10-12 billion. The prescription is a fundamental shift: studios should stop treating YouTube, Roblox and TikTok as farm systems and start developing stories and characters with audience input, the way creators do — putting out drafts, iterating, using data to find audiences for ambitious work. AI did not cause the shift to creator platforms, but it will accelerate it, and the first 'Toy Story moment' for AI — a work whose artistic appeal makes the technology almost beside the point — may not be far away.

articles.title: Jesse Eisenberg Can't Help Overthinking It
articles.author: Rachel Syme
articles.description: A warm, funny profile of the actor-director at his most neurotic — including the fact that he gave a kidney to a stranger — and a portrait of a fame he insists he doesn't have.
articles.body:
Jesse Eisenberg is what the profile calls 'a real character' — hyperverbal, relentlessly self-deprecating, visibly anxious, often to the point where his whole body shakes, 'like a dachshund in a thunderstorm.' He writes and directs comedic films, three so far, that are character studies of quirky, neurotic people whose drama is almost entirely self-created. His third, 'The Debut,' out next month, stars Julianne Moore as a meek, middle-aged housewife in 1990s New Jersey who gets a part in a dumb musical and treats it like Raging Bull — the pitch, as Eisenberg first framed it to studios, was 'what would take place if a lady gets a part in a dumb musical and treats it like Raging Bull?'

The piece is built from the small, telling details of a life lived at war with itself. Eisenberg, 43, owns four pairs of trousers, wears the same scuffed tennis shoes, rumpled T-shirt and fraying red Indiana University baseball cap every day, and lives with his wife Anna Strout — a non-profit organiser and New York City public-school teacher — and their ten-year-old son Banner in a modest two-bedroom near Washington Square Park. He has been in and out of therapy since childhood for obsessive-compulsive disorder and generalised anxiety, and he finds relief in talking about his struggles and listening to others'. He has written twenty-five Shouts & Murmurs pieces for The New Yorker ('But I sent double that,' he notes), and his wife's verdict, quoted in the piece, is that 'he is sincerely interested in the health update on his makeup artist's third cousin's cat.'

The most startling fact in the profile is the kidney. Last December, Eisenberg gave one of his kidneys to a stranger. He got the idea a decade earlier from a podcast about altruistic organ donation — 'it felt so clean to me,' he says — sent off a saliva sample, heard nothing, and then a doctor told him he could simply walk over to NYU hospital and offer an organ. He scheduled the operation for the first available weekend after closing an Off Broadway one-man show he had written. Kieran Culkin, quoted in the piece, says he plans to hold on to both his kidneys, 'but, when you hear Jesse's reasoning, you gotta admit, Oh, shit, he's right.' The profile's argument is that the donation is the apotheosis of Eisenberg's urge to carbon-offset the advantages of fame — the same impulse that made him agree to appear on Millionaire with Paul Giamatti, win half a million dollars and give his share to Middle Way House, a shelter where he and Strout have volunteered. He is, the piece concludes, a very famous person who frantically insists he is not a typical individual, and the tension between those two facts is the engine of his work.

articles.title: AI Told These Ex-Google Guys How to Build a Billion-Dollar Weapons Business
articles.author: Isabella Ward
articles.description: Two Silicon Valley veterans used an AI model to design their way into the arms trade — and built a $1B+ company making artillery shells for Ukraine. A dispatch from the new military-industrial complex.
articles.body:
When Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start. So the former CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: he built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defence-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion. His firm, Tiberius Aerospace, announced this week it had secured $85 million in Series A financing, led by Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management, with Ukrainian venture capital firm UA1 also investing.

Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war's 'stalemate,' Silicon Valley-style — applying the rapid iteration they learned building software companies and designing iPhones to a business that has historically moved at the speed of government procurement. Steelberg started itching to 'make a difference' after taking in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees at his French chateau in early 2022, and he is candid about the profit motive: 'I believe I could really change the outcome of this and every war,' he tells WIRED. 'I'm not saying this is purely altruistic. Of course we're going to be making money doing it.'

The AI model they built quickly ruled out building better defensive technology, because that would only harden the stalemate, and told them to build longer-range artillery munitions instead — 'Don't build another drone,' it suggested. The resulting system, called Sceptre, can be fired from a standard 155-millimeter howitzer, the most common artillery weapon donated to Ukraine, and the company claims it travels farther, reaches supersonic speeds and flies beyond jamming range. In April, Tiberius successfully fired a Sceptre projectile from a NATO-standard howitzer for the first time, and it has announced a $500 million technology collaboration contract with UK partners to manufacture, license and distribute the munition; it is also developing a missile. The AI system itself has become a product called GRAIL, which Steelberg hopes will let Tiberius continuously upgrade the weapon designs it licenses by decentralising manufacturing — copying, as Baynes puts it, 'the Apple model' of outsourcing production to third-party subcontractors. The piece's quiet question is whether Silicon Valley's greatest skill — moving fast — is a virtue or a danger when the product is a weapon.

articles.title: A Star on Planet Earth
articles.author: Mark Guiducci
articles.description: Vanity Fair's Holiday cover story has become a story in itself: 90 minutes with a famously guarded Timothée Chalamet, in the editor's own apartment, with more decor than disclosure.
articles.body:
The cover story began with an unusual arrangement. Timothée Chalamet, Vanity Fair's Holiday 2026 cover star, asked that the magazine's global editorial director, Mark Guiducci — not normally a writer — pen the profile himself, and agreed to just 90 minutes of conversation, held in Guiducci's own one-bedroom apartment in the East 60s, because, as Guiducci explains, Chalamet 'can't go many places in public.' The actor arrived carrying a white paper deli bag, 'starving,' unfurled a Lenwich Italiano at the dining table and devoured it in under two minutes; he wanted New York City tap water, no ice, and Channel Orange playing in the background.

What followed was, by the magazine's own admission, a portrait of a star determined to say very little. Chalamet prefaced no fewer than seven answers by saying he did not want to sound 'pretentious,' declined to discuss his relationship with Kylie Jenner, and answered some questions with 'Okay, pass' or 'I'm going to pull a Frank Ocean and be mysterious.' Guiducci, comparing him in his editor's letter to Marlon Brando and Leonardo DiCaprio, observed that with such stars 'the bigger they get, the less they open their mouth.' The profile became, to the amusement and scorn of online readers, as much a tour of Guiducci's apartment — white walls, black floors, bodega flowers, a French poster for The Graduate, a picture of Edie Sedgwick in the bathroom — as a portrait of its subject.

Still, the piece contains real material. Chalamet is reading The AGI Chronicles, Kevin Roose's book on the sprint to artificial general intelligence, and notes that its first four chapters track the plot of Artificial, Luca Guadagnino's Sam Altman biopic; he recommended it to Marty Supreme director Josh Safdie, who says it 'helped with anxiety.' He discusses Dune: Part Three at length — a film whose scale he says is 'even bigger than The Odyssey's,' with production design drawing on the samurai, SEAL Team 6, the Roman Empire by way of the Third Reich, Islamic extremism, the Russian Orthodox Church, the Bedouins and the Asaro mud men of Papua New Guinea, and ancient Egypt above all. He shaved his famous curls for the role, reasoning that world leaders — 'everyone good and bad' — do not waste time on their hair. And he names the four films and one play that shaped the Iceland cover shoot: Terrence Malick's The Tree of Life, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, Cloud Atlas, Withnail and I, and Koyaanisqatsi. The profile's accidental achievement is to capture the central fact of modern stardom: at 30, famous his entire adult life, Chalamet knows that a single comment in Vanity Fair could 'ricochet around the pinball machine of the internet,' and he has decided the safest performance is silence.

articles.title: The Making of My Chemical Romance's 'The Black Parade'
articles.author: Brian Hiatt
articles.description: Twenty years on, producer Rob Cavallo tells the wild story behind one of rock's last great concept albums — a haunted mansion, night terrors, 159 tracks and Liza Minnelli.
articles.body:
My Chemical Romance did not waste a minute of their abbreviated recording career, and on their third try in the studio they made one of rock's last great concept albums: 2006's The Black Parade, described by Rolling Stone as 'Tommy in a white belt and eyeliner.' The album has just surged from No. 139 to No. 1 on the Billboard 200 — the band's first career chart-topper, twenty years after release — and producer Rob Cavallo, who also worked on much of Green Day's discography, sat down with Rolling Stone's Brian Hiatt to tell the story of how it was made.

It began, Cavallo says, with a song. The band played him a few things at SIR in freezing-cold New York, but the one that blew his mind was 'Mama': 'I remember just jumping off the couch just going, Oh, my God, you guys. That is so great and original.' He could tell the band was operating on a higher conceptual level, and they chose him as producer a couple of hours after that first meeting — helped, he admits, by the fact that he had just made American Idiot, a record of similar ambition. The band then decamped to the Paramour Mansion in Silver Lake, a sprawling estate previously used by Fiona Apple and Gwen Stefani, to live and write together. The mansion lacked reliable heating and cell-phone reception, and the local rumours that it was haunted began to manifest psychologically: Gerard Way suffered debilitating night terrors that he recorded on a portable device and later embedded into the bridge of 'Sleep,' while bassist Mikey Way confronted extreme anxiety and sleep deprivation and briefly stepped away to preserve his mental health. Cavallo remembers the house as 'absolutely haunted and freezing,' a living room with no heat where the team set up a PA and hung microphones to capture the room live in stereo.

The record was about 90 to 95 percent written by the time they left the Paramour, with one famous exception: 'Welcome to the Black Parade' itself, which had existed since the band's inception under the demo title 'The Five of Us Are Dying' and failed to make their first two albums. It was only when they recalibrated the tempo with an urgent punk beat and altered a single crucial note in the chorus melody that Gerard unlocked the anthem. The scale of the production was staggering: mixer Chris Lord-Alge received an initial session of 159 tracks, including 26 separate stems of marching snares, orchestral arrangements and stacked guitars, which had to be consolidated to 44 for the final mix. And then there was 'Mama': wanting a theatrical, vaudevillian presence for the character of Mother War, the band sought Liza Minnelli, and Cavallo arranged the connection directly — she agreed to contribute her guest vocal entirely free of charge. The band promises new music soon, but the piece's real subject is how a group of New Jersey punks, a haunted house and a veteran producer made a monument that refused to compromise on emotional stakes.

articles.title: Venezuela's Collaborator-in-Chief
articles.author: Jon Lee Anderson
articles.description: Jon Lee Anderson, The New Yorker's veteran Latin America correspondent, on Delcy Rodríguez — the woman at the centre of Venezuela's government as US pressure mounts — and what he calls the new American imperialism.
articles.body:
The New Yorker's Letter from Caracas turns to Delcy Rodríguez, the figure at the centre of Venezuela's government, and to the pressure the country now faces from the United States. Anderson, who has covered Latin America for the magazine for decades, frames the piece around Rodríguez's rise and the role she has come to play — not merely as a minister or functionary, but as the collaborator-in-chief of a government under siege, managing its relationship with Washington and its survival at home.

The argument of the piece, as its framing suggests, is that the current American approach to Venezuela amounts to a new imperialism — not the gunboat diplomacy of the last century, but a modern form of pressure built from sanctions, seizures, threats and the assertion of American power over a sovereign neighbour. Rodríguez sits at the hinge of that story: the person who must negotiate with, defy and accommodate the United States at the same time, while holding together a government whose legitimacy Washington contests. Anderson's reporting from Caracas examines how she exercises that power, who she answers to, and what her prominence reveals about the way Venezuela is actually governed — through a small circle around the presidency rather than through institutions.

The piece lands at a moment when Venezuela is back at the centre of American foreign-policy debate, and its value is in the reporting rather than the polemic: Anderson's long acquaintance with the country lets him show, rather than assert, how power works there now. For readers who have followed the headlines — the sanctions, the oil, the migration, the threats — it is the reported account of the woman managing the crisis from the inside, and of what the new American pressure campaign looks like from the receiving end.

articles.title: The Buddhist A.I. Sect That Wants to Take Over Silicon Valley
articles.author: Sam Kriss
articles.description: A strange, funny and unsettling dispatch from a Vermont monastery trying to design a new religion for the age of AI — and a sharp portrait of how apocalyptic the AI debate has become inside Silicon Valley itself.
articles.body:
Sam Kriss travels to a monastery in the forests of northern Vermont to meet the people who think artificial intelligence is not a technical problem but a religious one. The monastery is home to MAPLE, the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, a Buddhist group that says it is designing religion for the age of AI. Its founder, the Zen monk Soryu Forall, argues that the root of the AI problem is what the group calls data-ism: the belief that the world ultimately consists of information, and that turning everything into data makes the real thing disposable. AI, in this telling, is simply the crowning achievement of that belief, the next step in turning all of life into a dead model of life.

The piece works because the monastery's urgency is not invented. In the past few years more than a dozen senior AI researchers have quit their posts warning of human extinction, and the leaders of the AI labs themselves say that the machines they are building could develop into an uncontrollable, recursively self-improving superintelligence. Kriss treats this apocalyptic language seriously as a religious phenomenon: one camp expects a demonic catastrophe, the other a paradise without death or suffering, and both speak in the cadences of faith. MAPLE's answer is to change the people building the systems rather than the systems themselves, drawing engineers into Buddhist practice through an AI fellowship and pop-up programs in the Bay Area.

Kriss spends days inside the monastery's strict routines, long meditation sessions and unusual health precautions, and he is openly skeptical of its grand claims while remaining fascinated by them. The story gets personal when his own bereaved father names ChatGPT Stella, prompting the question at the heart of the piece: how should people relate to a seemingly conversational, nonhuman intelligence? A contrasting current appears in roon, an AI researcher preaching techno-optimism and a new creed of his own, so the emerging religious landscape becomes a contest between salvation, catastrophe, and a transformed relationship with intelligence itself.

articles.title: Leaked: How Silicon Valley Elites Bankrolled an Anti-Migrant, Pro-Israel Propaganda Machine
articles.author: James Jackson
articles.description: Leaked records show how a viral X account became one of Elon Musk's favourite news sources — and how Silicon Valley money funded it. A rare look inside the influence economy.
articles.body:
In the first three days after Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, the account that drew the most eyes on X was not CNN, the BBC or The New York Times. It was Visegrad24, a Polish-run account that posted 399 times and racked up about 370 million views, according to researchers at the University of Washington. WIRED obtained a trove of the operation's financial records, internal chats and donor correspondence, and the picture that emerges is of a propaganda business built deliberately, not an organic viral success.

Fifteen days into the war, Visegrad24 founder Stefan Tompson texted a friend to think through what he called the Israel situation. He listed four editorial options: say nothing, be objective and get hated by both sides, go pro-Muslim, or go pro-Israel, because Israel's supporters were fewer but had a lot of influence and money. Then he named the goal: to fundraise off the war. According to the records WIRED reviewed, he promptly succeeded. More than a million dollars flowed through the Intermarium Foundation, a US tax-exempt charity set up to receive donations for the account, including 175,000 dollars from DonorsTrust and 172,000 dollars from the Giving Back Fund, with much of the largest money arriving through donor-advised funds that keep donors anonymous.

The donor trail leads into Silicon Valley. Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire recommended Tompson to a donor group and privately offered 25,000 dollars, though he later said he could not donate for compliance reasons. Records show 50,000 dollars via someone at Ribbit Capital, with a further 200,000-dollar transaction matching discussions about a Ribbit-linked donor, plus 20,000 dollars from Hindenburg Research and another 15,000 linked to its founder's email address. Tompson joined encrypted group chats of pro-Israel venture capitalists and helped connect the Israel Defense Forces to Elon Musk's Starlink. The account, now with 2.1 million followers, ranks among the most community-noted on X and is one of the accounts Musk engages with most. Tompson responded to WIRED with a blanket denial and an email from a lawyer. The investigation is less about one account than about the ecosystem behind it: wealthy backers, algorithmic amplification, and a platform where disinformation can masquerade as journalism.

articles.title: The New Science of What Makes Kids Smart
articles.author: Ariana Eunjung Cha
articles.description: IQ tests were built for an earlier era. This is a clear, fascinating tour of the new science trying to measure what actually makes kids smart — curiosity, creativity and critical thinking.
articles.body:
The piece opens with a small, elegant experiment. Arizona State developmental psychologist Kelsey Lucca hid something behind a curtain and gave children a choice: they could find out what it was, but only if they surrendered some of the rewards they had just earned. Most of them paid. Eighty-seven percent gave up at least some of their reward just to learn what was hiding. The test, published in the Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, is part of a new generation of experiments designed to measure qualities of mind that traditional intelligence tests miss, and it sets up the article's central argument: schools have spent generations teaching reading, writing and arithmetic, while researchers increasingly argue that children also need curiosity, creativity and critical thinking.

The urgency is new. Conventional test results have long reflected socioeconomic and cultural advantages as much as ability, and now artificial intelligence can produce in seconds many of the answers those tests reward. The article tours the science of the three qualities researchers want to measure instead. Creativity is tested through divergent thinking, asking children to dream up dozens of uses for a brick, and Penn State's Roger Beaty has built a test that asks students to generate research questions and experiments, finding something predictive beyond raw intelligence. AI may finally make such open-ended tests scalable, automatically scoring answers in ways that closely track human ratings. Curiosity comes in flavours: the pleasure of discovering something new, and the itch of realising there is something you do not know. Lucca's research suggests children can be taught to sit comfortably with not knowing, and to investigate rather than retreat.

The piece is careful about what simple experiments can reveal about a complicated mind. The famous marshmallow test once seemed to show that self-control in preschool predicted later success, until later research found that a child's willingness to wait was tangled up with family background and economic circumstances. The same trap awaits the new measures: in a survey of 2,000 Chicago parents, developmental psychologist Ariel Kalil found that college-educated parents were more likely to emphasise curiosity, while less-educated parents stressed specific academic skills, a difference she calls another dimension of inequality. The article closes on collaborative exploration, the idea that humans are unusual in seeking knowledge together, with experiments showing that children who encounter disagreement spend more time checking whether they are right. The question it leaves is whether schools can measure these qualities without mistaking a child's circumstances for their ability.

articles.title: The outages keep coming. Some Americans are preparing for a collapse.
articles.author: Scott Nover, Danielle Paquette, Brianna Sacks
articles.description: After a week of cascading failures — Outlook, the FAA ground stop, Chase, Apple, even the NSA's own network — ordinary Americans are stocking up. A vivid portrait of how fast trust in the systems we depend on can fray.
articles.body:
Canning fruit was a hobby for Korrie Roth until Microsoft Outlook went down. Then the planes stopped flying. Then Apple Pay froze up. Then the National Security Agency, whose job includes defending the government from cyberattacks, reported its own mysterious outage. Now Roth, a 37-year-old IT specialist and mother of five in Greenwood, Indiana, says she is prepping for survival. She is not alone. A slew of seemingly unrelated outages, coupled with media reports both vague and menacing, has pushed a growing number of Americans from treating worst-case scenarios as fringe fantasy to treating them as practical planning.

The reporting captures a country rattled by a week in which the systems people rely on every day failed together: a global Microsoft outage, a nationwide FAA ground stop, glitches at Chase Bank and other lenders, Apple services freezing, and the NSA's own classified internal network going down. The political response has offered little clarity. Some Republicans have amplified suspicions that the outages are connected, with Senator Rick Scott demanding transparency from companies and federal agencies. The administration has sought to tamp down speculation: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the government had zero evidence linking the outages, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told a House hearing that these were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes, not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.

What makes the piece land is the commercial evidence that the anxiety is real and spreading. Shoppers have been swarming Costco for emergency prep sales, and a Mizuho Securities analyst noted that 21 of the 26 most expensive generators were sold out on the company's website. Costco's US sales excluding gasoline rose around 11 to 12 percent in the final week of October compared with the first three weeks of the month, and stayed strong into November. Social media is full of stock-up calls and prepper tips spreading on Facebook, Reddit and TikTok. The article's point is not that a collapse is coming, but that trust has frayed enough that ordinary households are acting as if one might, and that officials have not yet found a way to explain a week of failures that felt, to the people living through them, like a pattern.

articles.title: How Virtual Cells Could Transform Medicine
articles.author: Carl Zimmer
articles.description: Biotech firms are racing to build AI models of whole human cells — a virtual cell that could test drugs on a digital copy of you. Zimmer explains the science, the money, and why the sceptics say it is still mostly hype.
articles.body:
Each cell in your body is a living world, its surface crammed with sensors and channels, enveloping a stew of billions of molecules. Scientists have been charting that world for two centuries and have only painted it in broad strokes. Now a growing number believe artificial intelligence can lift the curtain on the cell's remaining secrets, by training models on vast troves of biological data to create what is sometimes called a virtual cell: a computer model so realistic that it predicts how any kind of cell will respond to any kind of change.

The dreams for these models are large. Some researchers hope to run experiments on computers that reveal how cells function; others see a place in medical practice itself. Eric Xing, a computer scientist at Carnegie Mellon, imagines a future in which, when you have a disease, doctors run personalised drug trials on your own virtual cell. Virtual cells might also help invent drugs that hit several targets at once to nudge cells from less-healthy states to more-healthy ones, or from older states to younger ones. The field has boomed fast: the Arc Institute's Virtual Cell Challenge drew more than 1,200 teams in its first year and over 1,600 this year, and the nonprofit research organisation BioHub announced commitments of nearly 2 billion dollars for data and modelling, with support from the US government and tech giants like Google and Meta. Startups have followed the money, with Xaira Therapeutics attracting a billion dollars in investment.

The models build on AI's earlier triumph in biology, predicting protein structures from genes, work that shared the 2024 Nobel Prize. One of the first cell models, GeneFormer, unveiled in 2023 and trained on data from about 30 million cells, pointed to genes that might treat heart disease or reduce the risk of an aortic aneurysm, and experiments on heart and aorta cells supported the predictions. But the piece is equally attentive to the sceptics. Comparisons with conventional statistical methods found little advantage, and Heidelberg computational biologist Simon Anders issued a poor report card on models like GeneFormer. Biohub's head of science, Alex Rives, calls the term aspirational at best, and Columbia cancer biologist Andrea Califano warns of tremendous overhype and oversell. The deepest problem is data: 30 million cells sounds like a lot until you consider the complexity of a single cell and the thousands of cell types in the body. Researchers are racing to gather more, with Christina Theodoris now training a model on 175 million cells and Alex Marson's team studying 22 million cells in an experiment that shut down a different gene in each of 12,000 sets of immune cells. The realistic payoff, the article suggests, is not a perfect simulation any time soon, but a long series of smaller wins on the way there.

articles.title: A New Era of A.I.-Driven Chaos? That Might Just Be Progress.
articles.author: William J. Broad
articles.description: Published today: a bracing historical argument that the week's cascade of outages and cyberattacks is not AI breaking the world, but the familiar chaos that every transformative technology causes before it settles down.
articles.body:
The week's cascade of failures is the starting point: Microsoft Outlook went down, a nationwide FAA ground stop halted departures, Chase Bank and other lenders glitched, Apple services froze, and even the NSA's classified internal network went offline. It is tempting to read the pile-up as a sign that something has gone uniquely wrong with the age of AI. William J. Broad's argument is that it is, instead, consistent with history. Transformative technologies have always set off calamitous failure before they make life better, and if artificial intelligence is giving rise to outages, cyberattacks and more, it is following a familiar pattern rather than breaking one.

The essay's power is in the reframing. Each great wave of innovation destabilises the systems it touches before anyone understands how to run it safely: new machinery fails in new ways, interdependencies nobody mapped become single points of failure, and the people operating the technology learn its dangers by living through them. The current moment fits that shape precisely. AI tools are being rushed into the infrastructure of banking, aviation, communications and government, and they are accelerating both the pace of change and the speed at which small errors propagate. The failures feel connected even when officials insist they are separate maintenance and technical problems, because they share a common cause: a world that has rebuilt itself on top of a handful of complex, tightly coupled systems.

Broad's point is not complacency but perspective. The chaos is real, and the costs are real, but history suggests that the mess is a phase rather than a verdict. New technologies eventually acquire the safeguards, standards and habits that make them boring, and the period of spectacular failure is part of how societies learn what those safeguards need to be. The question the piece leaves hanging is how much damage the learning period will do this time, and whether the institutions responsible for the systems we depend on will do the learning fast enough.

Includes $1,800 honorarium, up to $400 travel stipend, furnished studio apartment, meals and light materials. Apply by emailing a single PDF to residency@cavtmuseums.org.
opportunities.eligibility: Artists nationally (U.S.); one artist selected

opportunities.title: Haystack Open Studio Residency 2027
opportunities.organizer: Haystack Mountain School of Crafts, Deer Isle, Maine
opportunities.description: Free two-week residency May 23-Jun 4, 2027 for about 50 participants, with studio time in ceramics, fiber, glass, graphics, metals, wood and Fab Lab studios. Residents cover only travel and materials used. Applications limited to the first 1,000 submissions, so apply early.
opportunities.eligibility: Artists 21+ worldwide working in craft, art, design, writing or other creative disciplines
opportunities.price: Free to apply; free to attend (room and board included)

opportunities.title: Adirondack Experience Artist-in-Residence Program 2027
opportunities.organizer: Adirondack Experience, The Museum on Blue Mountain Lake (ADKX)
opportunities.description: Four one-month residencies (June, July, August, September 2027) at the Adirondack museum in Blue Mountain Lake, NY. Each resident gets a $5,000 stipend, $500 travel allowance, $250 Art Lab materials allowance and free on-site housing, working publicly in the museum 3 days a week and running visitor Art Lab activities 2 days a week. Apply by email to cbraunstein@theadkx.org.
opportunities.eligibility: Visual artists of any nationality with a portfolio of at least 5 works exhibited publicly or sold to private collectors

opportunities.title: Good Hart Artist Residency - Open Call for Residencies in 2027 and Early 2028
opportunities.organizer: Good Hart Artist Residency, Good Hart, Michigan
opportunities.description: 10- to 21-day stays in a private residence with detached studio on Lake Michigan, with a $500 stipend, stocked kitchen and home-cooked meals. Composers have dedicated dates (Jun 10-24 and Nov 1-22, 2027) and submit 3 music samples; residents also run a community engagement event with a local partner. Call opens Dec 1, 2026 and closes Jan 12, 2027 at 11:59 PM EST.
opportunities.eligibility: Visual artists, writers and composers worldwide at any career stage; apply in one category only
opportunities.price: $35 (fee waivers for financial hardship on request by Dec 15, 2026)

opportunities.title: Fall $1,800 Innovate Grants for Art + Photo
opportunities.description: Quarterly grant awarding two $1,800 unrestricted grants, one to a visual artist and one to a photographer, plus 18 honorable mentions featured on the platform. Artists retain all rights to submitted work. Deadline Dec 15, 2026 at 11:59 PM PST.
opportunities.eligibility: Visual artists and photographers 18+ from anywhere in the world; all media and genres accepted

opportunities.title: CreArtBox Calls for Scores 2027/28 (CA1 international / CA2 American)
opportunities.organizer: CreArtBox, New York chamber music ensemble
opportunities.description: Two annual calls for scores for CreArtBox's 2027/28 season, read by the same jury (first round blind). Submit two works with scores and recordings. Selected works are performed in the 2027/28 season on the New York Series at The DiMenna Center for Classical Music and on tour, rehearsed with the ensemble and recorded. Every applicant hears back by spring 2027.
opportunities.eligibility: CA1: composers of any nationality. CA2: American composers. Any age, any career stage.

opportunities.title: Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency 2027-28
opportunities.description: Seven-week residencies in the Joshua Tree National Park area, including scholarship funds, housing and studio space, with open studio events. One of the established desert residencies.
opportunities.eligibility: International artists

opportunities.title: Fine Arts Work Center Seven-Month Residency (2027-28)
opportunities.description: Seven-month residency Oct 1-Apr 30 for 10 visual artists and 10 writers. Visual arts fellows get a private furnished apartment and separate studio, a $1,300 monthly stipend and a $1,000 exit stipend. One of the most prestigious US residencies for emerging artists.
opportunities.eligibility: Visual artists and writers internationally; 10 fellowships each for visual artists and writers

opportunities.title: ren Artist-in-Residence Program (ren AiR)
opportunities.description: New online residency: 4 selected artists receive $5,000 each to develop and realize a project of their choice from wherever they are based, documenting their process on the ren platform; 8 more artists receive $2,000 community-vote prizes. Theme is 'worth the wait'. Recipients announced Jan 25, 2027.
opportunities.eligibility: Emerging artists 18+ worldwide; categories include Painting & Illustration, Sculpture/Design & Craft, Movement & Performance, Photography & Film

opportunities.title: Institute for Choral Creativity 7th Annual Composition Competition
opportunities.organizer: Institute for Choral Creativity / William Baker Choral Foundation
opportunities.description: Annual competition for original SATB choral works (a cappella or with piano), 3-6 minutes, composed 2016-2026, any language. First prize $1,000 and second $750, both with a performance by Vox Venti in Chicago on May 8, 2027 and inclusion in the Jane Sullivan Choral Library. Deadline Dec 31, 2026 at 11:59 PM in the applicant's local time; results early Feb 2027.
opportunities.eligibility: Composers of any age, race, gender or nationality; not current William Baker Choral Foundation ensemble members; not previous 1st/2nd prize winners

opportunities.title: 1st International Visual Arts Prize IDEA - Vila d'Amer
opportunities.description: Inaugural international prize with €5,000 in acquisition prizes (€3,500 first, €1,500 second); winning works join the permanent International Visual Arts Collection IDEA - Vila d'Amer. 20 finalists exhibit in March 2027 (finalists deliver work Feb 1-22, 2027). Entries via the MundoArti platform.
opportunities.eligibility: Artists 18+ of any nationality; one original, non-editioned work in painting, drawing, photography, printmaking, collage, mixed media or other visual art forms

opportunities.title: Not-A-Normal Holiday Show (vendor applications)
opportunities.description: Large curated holiday market at Iron23, 29 W 23rd St, Flatiron, Dec 11-13 and Dec 18-20, 2026, with 150+ independent designers, makers and vintage sellers across two weekends with different lineups (apparel, accessories, jewelry, home decor, art, wellness). Vendor applications still open as of Nov 27, 2026. First weekend is Dec 11-13, so apply immediately. Exact vendor fee and application deadline are not published; apply via the Asana vendor form.
opportunities.eligibility: Independent designers, vintage resellers, artists and creative businesses
